Chapter  XXV
BACK  RIVER  AND  THE  PONDS
How can we make a  survey of  Wessagusset in  1622 or 1623?    We
can only do it in imagination,    but as Morton made journeys through
that  town,      we can  best  do  it  by going  with  him,    and  seeing  in
fancy what he saw.            The course of procedure may be imaginative,
but the descriptions  are real,   and taking the journeys with  Morton
gives  them life.
On the trip  up Back River,    with  the help of the young Indian,
we were provided  with  a  canoe,     that  being the easiest  way to  go
up  the  river  and  through  the  streams.           Starting  in  the  morning
near the mouth of Back River,  just around the point where Bradley's
plant now stands,    we set out on our expedition.        With the Indian's
skill  in the use of the paddle we moved easily along on the surface
of the river,     with the densely wooded banks on each side.
It was a bright,   clear day and the water was smooth,   and skimming
along  all   nature was  beautiful,    and we seemed to  be gliding  on a
river  of  Paradise.               Sea  birds  were flying  around us,    the fish  in  the
water beneath were swimming about,    occasionally jumping out of
the  water  for  flies .           We passed  what is  now Stoddard's  Neck on
the left,       which was then well wooded,  and the trees  were reflected
in  the  water,     making  what  seemed  like  a beautiful  underground
island,       and  all  around  us  there  was the  sweet stillness  of  nature,
with a little  harmonious  sound that  might be called  the  music of
the air.              The river had become so wide that it  was like a bay,    and
in  after  years ships  came up there.
Onward  still  we glide  in  quiet  and  rhythmic motion,    the  river
rounding  around a little ,    and the canoe traveling in a sort of circle
as  we  followed  the  river.            We passed  what  is   now Gillam  Hill,
and bearing  a little  to  the left  we came to  a place where an Indian
trail  led  down to  the  river,     and  the  Indians  were  accustomed  to
cross  the  river  here in  canoes.         At this  place in later years a bridge
was built  which was called  London bridge  by the  earlier  settlers ,
and in  still  later years  the  Hingham bridge,    the Back River being
one of the boundaries between Weymouth and Hingham.
Back River in  1922 is  still  very beautiful,   but in  1622 its  beauty
was  far  greater.                 It  was  a wild  beauty,    it  is  true,    but it  was the
beauty of  Nature,     and nothing can surpass  nature in loveliness.
Having passed  the  place  where  the  bridge  was  built,      we for  a
long  time have on  our left  a  region  which is  now occupied by the
government  naval  station,       but  in  the  old  days  the  public  had
access  to  this  region,    and it  was full  of Nature's  attractions .           On
both sides of the river there were wonderful places for camping and
fishing.             One  of  these  was  called  Aunt Nabby's  Grove.              To  this
 - 133 - 
BACK  RIVER  AND  THE  PONDS                   125
grove many of Weymouth's citizens  came from time  to  time,    as  it
was a most lovely place to  spend the day in the shade of  the  trees
on the river bank,    and a most excellent  spot for  fishing.
But Aunt Nabby's Grove is cut off from the public,   and the naval
men have it all  to  themselves.             We pass Beal's Cove on the left and
Whale Island on the right,   to which for many years the Whale Island
Club came for pleasure and rest,    but as  the government took pos-
session of the island the club had to seek a new home,    and they took
possession of Burying Island  in the  Fore River,   giving it  the addi-
tional name of Whale Island.           We pass by what was later the French
estate  where Mrs.  Frederick T.  Hunt now resides,     but in  spite  of
all the beauty of the river in these spots we must skim along,    pass-
ing where in later years Leonard had his wool scouring mill,    and in
time come to the falls .
The river  was  navigable  as far  as the falls,    a distance  of  three
miles  from its  mouth,   and a smaller  river  or  stream connects Back
River  with  Whitman's  Pond,   called  by the  early  settlers   Fresh
Pond.          At the falls we had to carry the canoe around,    but this  was
easy,   as  canoes  are  very  light.        After  this  the  river  was  only  a
stream,     but it  led us into  Whitman's  Pond.         Near here later  was
the  Fulling  Mill  and the  Weymouth Iron  Works.
For a mile  we paddled  through  this  pond  which  is  half  a mile
wide,      then,      through  a continuation  of  the pond,   till  we ran  into
what was afterwards  called  Mill  River.        The journey through  this
pond was a very pleasing one,    as the water was clear and pure,    and
it  seemed to  be embowered in woods,   and made one think of the
beautiful descriptions  of lakes by some of our famous poets.             Mill
River winds around the fields  and through marshes,    and sometimes
the banks were so  near that we could  almost reach  out and touch
them as we passed.          There is  another river which empties into Whit-
man's  Pond;      this  was called  Old Swamp River,     and is  about three
miles long and takes its  rise in Hingham,    but  through this  river we
cannot go,    as our journey is  through Mill  River to the Great Pond.
This  river  is  seven miles  long  and formerly  a quarter of a mile
wide  and  makes  a  beautiful  and  romantic  trip  in  a  canoe.            It
winds  around  in  curves  at  many places,      and  the  meadows  and
marshes  are  cut in  spots by little  streams  or  creeks.        If one has
ever  journeyed  through  some of  the  salt  water  creeks  along  our
coast he can form some idea  of what it  was.
Agood time to follow the course of  Mill River in our day would
be to  take  it  in  the winter  time,   when the  ponds  and  river  are
frozen.             With a pair  of  skates  on,    one  could  skate  from  the  end
of  Whitman's  Pond  at  East  Weymouth,     over  the  pond  and  all
through  Mill  River,     and over  Great  Pond.         This  could  have been
easily  done last  winter,    and  the writer  has taken part  of  the  trip
to  refresh  his  memory.
The  river  is  called  Mill  River  because  at  several  places  mills
were  built  during  the  history  of  Weymouth.        The  trip  on  the
surface  of the river was a most interesting  one to  Morton and his
 - 134 - 
126                    THE  EARLY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
two companions,   and Morton was so  pleased  that  he  always  had
something  good  to say about Weymouth.
The citizens  of Weymouth to-day do not realize the many beau-
tiful  and interesting  places  to  be seen,    and in these days of  auto-
mobiles  it   would  be  easy  to  journey  over the  town and get  out
where  many  of  these  wonderful  things  can be  seen  by walking.
How many,     for instance,   have seen Fresh River,    Marsh River,     Old
Swamp  River,      Soap  House  Swamp,    Wigwam Hill,    Ragged  Plain,
Huckleberry  Pond,     Judgment  Valley,      Puddle  Meadow,     Haunted
Rock,         Honey  Hill,       Lovers'       Lane,     and other  places  too  many to
mention here?
The  canoe  bearing  Morton,       Peddock  and  the  Indian   glided
noiselessly  along the river  and passed  into Great Pond.          This lake
is   a mile  and a half  long,    and about  a  mile  wide.      Around  the
pond they journeyed,   circling  the shore and enjoying the wonderful
scenes  of  the wooded banks with the varied colors of the  trees  and
beautiful  stretch  of water.
In  the journey  around the pond they  passed  three  islands,     one
of which was called  Hawk Island because it was a great gathering
place  for  hawks.            On this  island  lived  the  last  Indian  in  Wey-
mouth,      Aaron by name.
They saw  several  little  streams  that  ran out of the lake  which
served  as  an  outlet  for  the  water,     and later  were  utilized  by the
settlers   for  mill  purposes.        Fish  were  also  plentiful  in  the  pond,
and iron ore was obtained from the bottom,   and became an article
of  commerce.           Having fully  explored  the  pond they  came to  the
entrance into  Mill River,   and started on the return journey,    gliding
along  with  pleasure  through  the  fields  and  marshes,      and  looking
off  into  the distance they  saw a great deal  of what is  now South
Weymouth,    and at last  coming to the first  part of Whitman's Pond
they  left  the  canoe  and  walked  up the  bank for  some  distance
through the  trees  to see  one of the curious things in  Weymouth.
This  has been  called  Cavern  Rock.          This was a very large  rock
or  cliff ,       almost like  a  house.             It  seems  to have been a great  ledge,
and at  the  time of the upheaval  in  the  early  days  which  caused
an explosion,     this  rock was split  or rent in two,   and a large boulder
that had been thrown up had fallen  into the wide crevice or crack
made by the explosion,  holding the two parts of the ledge apart,    thus
forming a sort  of  chamber,     or  cave.            On the  outside  the  crack  or
crevice was narrower than the inside,  and a man passing through this
crack as though it were a door found himself in a rocky chamber with
the sky and the boulder for a roof,     and all around him a rocky wall.
In our day people go  to  see  this  curiosity,   and some call  it  the
house in  the  rock,    but  the  more common name is  Cavern  Rock.
When a party  goes  to  see  it  there  is  sometimes  much merriment
if  there  should  be  a  very  large,    fat  man in the company,     for  the
entrance is  so  narrow that some fat  men cannot get  through,     and
it  is  amusing to  see  them  try,     without  success .            Morton  and his
companions having seen this  wonderful cave returned to  the canoe
 - 135 - 
BACK  RIVER  AND  THE  PONDS                   127
and took their journey back to the place where they started from,
and they felt  when they had reached the Weston settlement  that
they had become familiar  with Wessagusset,      and  would not  need
to take any more journeys.        It would be well if all  the citizens  of
Weymouth should visit these places,    as it would give them a greater
love for  their  town.
TREES,       ANIMALS  AND  FISH.
We learn much about the region in which Weymouth is  situated
from  Morton's book " The New Canaan, "  as  he tells  us about the
trees,      shrubs,      animals  and fish.        People sometimes  ask,     what were
the  things  in  Weymouth in early days?    From Morton we learn
that of trees  there  was  an  abundance of  red  and white oak,       also
elm,       beech,       walnut,     chestnut,      pine,     cedar,      cyprus,     spruce,      alder,
birch,     maple,    elder,    hawthorne.         Of vines  there  were white,    black
and red plum trees,    cherry trees,   musk roses,    sassafras,     sarsaparilla,
gooseberries,            raspberries   and  other   berries.           Then  there   were
potherbs,   potima goram,    thyme,   Angelica,   purslane,   violets,    aniseed,
honeysuckle and balm.
The fish  in the river and bay in those days were cod,   bass,    mack-
erel,     sturgeon,     salmon,   herring,   eels,    smelts,     halibut,     place  hake,
pickerel,     lobster,    oyster,    mussels,    clams,   mussel cockles and scallops .
Bradford,       in  his  history  of  Plymouth,     mentions  a river  in  Wey-
mouth  which  he  calls   an  alewife  river.             These  are  the  herring
Morton writes of,    and the river was Back River and its  tributaries,
In the early days the herring ran up the river and got up over  the
falls  into  Whitman's  Pond,   but mills  were built  on the river  and
a great  one was called  the Fulling  Mill,    which afterwards  became
the plant of the Weymouth Iron  Works .
In some way,      because  of  these  mills,      the herring  got  stamped
out,    as they could not get up to the pond to spawn.          But about the
year  1700  the  pond was  restocked  with  herring,   and by order  of
the  town  the  mill  owner had to  make  a  passage  so  that  the  fish
could get up to Whitman's Pond to spawn.        Since then the herring
have been plentiful.
Morton also  tells  of the birds in Weymouth.          There were swans,
geese,       white  and  gray  ducks,      gray  and  black  pied  teals,       both
green-winged  and  blue-winged,    widgeons,     snipe,      cranes,       turkeys,
pheasants,   partridge,    quail,    owls,    crows,    hawks,    goshawks,     martins,
sparhawks and sea gulls .
Then,      of  animals,  there  were three  kinds of deer,    as elks ,     moose
and common deer.        The Indians were in the habit of catching deer
in  traps,      and  on  one  occasion  Governor  Bradford  got  caught  in
one of these  traps.             This  was when he went on an expedition  in
1621.    There were wolves,     beaver,   otter,    wild cat,    martin,   raccoon,
fox,    bear,   porcupine,   hedgehog,   conyer,   squirrels and flying squirrels,
snakes and rattlesnakes.
Of stones  there were chalk,    slate,   iron-stone granite and lead ore,
black and red in color.
 - 136 - 
128                   THE  EARLY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
Thomas  Morton  must  have  made  a  very  complete  survey  of
Wessagusset to learn  all  these things  about it,    and there are many
people living  in Weymouth to-day who could not tell  half so much
about the town.
Weymouth as a town is  about nine miles long,   from the Abington
line  to  the sea,      and on an average about three miles  wide,     and has
a water front of nine miles.       On the north are the waters of Boston
Harbor;    on  the east it  is  bounded by Hingham;     on the west by
Holbrook and Abington;    and Rockland on the south.
It is  the oldest town in the  Massachusetts  Bay Colony,     and its
boundaries  have  not  been  changed  since  the  first.        It  contains
upwards  of  sixteen  square miles,    and its  surface  is gently  rolling;
that is,     it  consists of many hills  and valleys,   and in some places  the
soil  is   very  fertile,    and in  early  years  it  was a good farming  and
dairy town.
There  are  many hills  in  Weymouth,     but the  largest  are  Great
Hill and King Oak Hill.          These hills  are the result of glacial action.
They are  lenticular  in  shape,    and some are kames,   both of which
belong to the ice  age,     and are formed by the melting of glacial  ice.
Much could be said about the geological features of Weymouth,
the solid  rocks  underneath,    which are pierced  by amygdaloid  trap,
and  the  glacial  scratches  on the  uncovered  ledges,     but that does
not belong  to  my subject,    but  to  the  person  who  writes  on  the
geology of Weymouth.
The early  settlers  in  Weymouth devoted themselves to  farming,
and the  part  of the town in which they  located  was  called  " Old
Spain .    "     Why it  was so  called  is  not known,    but there  have been
various  speculations  or  theories,    and there may be some truth  in
them.
Fishermen and traders visited the New England coast before 1620
to  carry on  their  trade with  the  Indians,   and to  engage in fishing.
Camps were made by them on the territory that is now Weymouth.
The old  Indian  trails  from  the regions  in  the south,    which  are
now  Bristol,         Plymouth  and  Norfolk counties,     had their  center  in
what is  now Weymouth.          It was a point easily reached by sea and
land,    and as  the  Indians  made it  a place  for gathering  it  was of
great  value  for  trading  with  them.         We know that  among these
fishermen  who visited  the  place  there  were different  nationalities ,
and  there  is   a  tradition  that  a  party  of  Spaniards  had  a camp
there,      and hence it was called " Old Spain.  "    Then Sir  Ferdinando
Gorges  was  supposed  to  be  a  Spaniard  by some because  of  his
name,      and  for  that  reason  his  settlement  was  spoken  of  as  the
settlement  of  that  old  Spaniard,     Gorges;        hence  came  the  term
" Old Spain .   "
Then it  has been common on the New England coast for  people
to  say :          " There is  nothing between us and Spain."    So some would
say as they went down to the seashore, " Let us go down and look
at  Spain .     "      The region  in  North  Weymouth may have  received
its name in that way.
 - 137 - 
BACK  RIVER  AND  THE  PONDS                   129
The theory of a camp of Spanish fishermen seems to  be the most
plausible,       however,       and  it   is   supported  by  the  incident  of  the
French  vessel  anchored  off   Peddock's  Island.          In  this  region  of
" Old Spain "   we find in the early days the names of many settlers ;
thus  there  was  John  King,         Nicholas   Phillips,     John  Whitman,
Richard Sylvester,      Leonard Peddock,     Benjamin Owen,  John Pedro,
William  Bibble,     Thomas  Morton,     John  Upham,      John  Richards,
Edward  Bates,        Thomas  Alger,        Bennet   Wills,         Edward  Baker,
Nicholas  Rouse,    Joseph  Shaw,        Thomas Applegate,       John  Hollis ,
Nicholas  Byram,     Matthew Pratt  and others .
These  early  settlers  in  Weymouth  we find  by grants  of  land
spreading out beyond " Old Spain "  into other parts  of  Weymouth,
and we find  in  later years  the following  names of settlers  having
land  in  " Old Spain: "   John Green,     Nicholas  Ford,     John  Torrey ,
William Pitty,   John Bicknell,    Benjamin Richards,   Jonas Humphrey,
Ebenezer  Pratt,      Henry Waltham,    James  Smith,    Maurice Trufant,
John  Whitman,       Nicholas  Phillips,      John  King  and  Samuel  King.
Then in  the  region  now called  Weymouth  Heights  we have  the
names  of Thomas  White,      Richard  Webb,   James Nash,       Nathaniel
Humphrey and Robert Lovell.
The writer  hoped  to  discover  where  the land of all  these  early
settlers  was located,   but he has found it  a long  and difficult  task,
the  records  are so  meager.       Members of the Weymouth Historical
Society have tried  to do so,    but they seem to  have met with little
or no success.         One way to learn something of this matter would be
to trace the title of these lands back as far as one can go,    but that
would be an endless  task.
Any one who has had experience  in  these  matters  knows what
a long  job  it  would be,   and when we think  of the cost  to  pay a
lawyer to look up the title of one piece of property even for twenty-
five  years back,   we can realize the time and expense for looking up
all  the  real  estate  in  " Old Spain,"  or  the  " Lower  Plantation"  of
Weymouth,       as  it  is  sometimes  called.          This  is  a work that  ought
to be accomplished by some one before it  is  too late.
The work  of  Gilbert  Nash  in  reference  to  the  early  property
owners  in  Weymouth  will  help  in this  matter.          Then  there  are
such  terms  as  the  " Ferry  Field,"   the  " Mill  Field, "   and  other
terms  in  old  wills,     which  would  be  of  great  value  in  the  search.
The " Ferry  Field"  was on the way to  the  ferry;    that  is,     it  was
near  the  ferry,      and  there  was  a  road  that led  to  the  ferry  which
ran through the Ferry  Field,    and was called the way to the ferry.
The ferry we know was at King's Cove,    and as John King owned
ten acres  of  land,    which  included  King's  Cove,     some of  his  land
must have been on the  Ferry  Field,      and we find  by old  wills,     such
as that of John Whitman,     for  instance,    the date of which is  1685,
something  about  the  " Ferry  Field.   "     We learn  from  these  wills
that  John  King,      Samuel  King  and  John  Whitman  had  land  in
the  Ferry  Field.      An examination  of  all  the old wills  would  give
much information on these points.

THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
By T.  H.  CLARK
INTRODUCTION
The geology  of Weymouth offers  nothing  spectacular;          no  cliffs
or  chasms,       no  mines  or  mountains  diversify  its  simple  contours.
Acouple of pretty lakes,   two small rivers,   widening at their mouths
into  salt  water harbors,      a ledge  or  two of ancient  granite,     and a
few of the rounded hills  called drumlins make up its salient features.
And yet  if  we take the trouble  to  study a little  deeper,      we shall
find  many things  of geological  interest.
TOPOGRAPHY
The shape of the  town of  Weymouth is  that of a long parallelo-
gram,      extending  practically  north  and  south,  and the  boundaries
are  artificial  except  in the northern  third,    where the  two  streams,
the   Fore   River  and  the  Back  River,    define  the  lines   between
Hingham  and  Weymouth  on  the  east,      and  between  Quincy  and
Braintree  and  Weymouth on  the  west.               Both  of  these  rivers,      as
far  as  they  are  town  boundaries,      are  salt  estuaries,    and  the fresh
streams which run into them are small and are not navigable above
tidewater.
The  surface  of  Weymouth is  a fairly  level  plain,    relieved  here
and there by glacial hills  or by ledges of rock;      and there is  a general
slope  to  the  north  of  about  one hundred  and ninety feet  from  the
Abington-Rockland  line  to  tidewater.          The drumlins,     or  glacial
hills,       of which King Oak Hill  and Great Hill are the best  examples
(respectively ,       about  one  hundred  and  one hundred and fifty  feet
in  height) ,      are confined to the northern part  of the town,    and from
the tops of  these hills  a good view of  the level skyline  is  obtained,
which  proves  the  general  flatness  of  the country.          The southern
half of the town is a flat plain,  one hundred feet or more above the
sea  level .              A good growth of white pine,    which favors  sand plains
for  its  locations,      has always been a feature of the southern part  of
the  town.           There is  no  elevation  in the  town  over  two  hundred
feet.
Our two small rivers,    the  Mill  River and the Old Swamp River,
both  running  into  and  through  Whitman's  Pond  into  the  Back
River,         are  all  that is  left  of the  great glacial  streams  which once
filled  their  valleys.            The Back  River,    where it  runs  through East
Weymouth,       is  famous for  its  herring  fisheries.        From  the  earliest
dates  these  rivers  have furnished  power for  all  kinds  of mills.
 - 139 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 131
Weymouth has two beautiful ponds within its  borders,    -Great
Pond,      at  the  extreme  southern  end,      and  Whitman's  Pond,       near
the  center.             Great  Pond  is  the  largest,      and  is  of  greater  extent
than most of the ponds in the surrounding  towns.          The shores  are
wooded and picturesque,    and there is  a pretty island  in the middle.
If  the contemplated driveway around the  shore is  achieved  it  will
be an added attraction to the town,    even though boating and fishing
are prohibited.       The pond is  the source of the town's water supply,
and because of the dam at its  northern  end  is  of  larger  area  than
formerly.         It is  related  that the late  Mr.  Quincy L.  Reed tried  for
a number of years to find  an old  road,    of which there was a  record,
on the western side of the pond,   and finally  found  traces  of  it  six
feet under water,   owing to the enlargement of the pond.         Whitman's
Pond  is   even  more  picturesque  and  pleasing  than  Great  Pond,
owing to the hills  and bold rocky ledges  on its  shores.            Camp and
bungalow  sites  have been  developed  here  which  are  enjoyed  by
many summer visitors.           This  pond has  furnished  excellent  water
power to  the  various  East  Weymouth industries  for  many years,
and,     with Great  Pond,    an ample supply of ice for the town.
GEOLOGY
The geology of Weymouth is  mainly concerned with two aspects,
the underlying bedrock,   and the surface covering of loose  material,
mostly glacial deposits.
The bedrock underlying the  surface is  of two kinds,    slate in  the
northern  part,     and  granite  and  similar  rocks  in  the  south.             The
boundary between these two areas  is  roughly  along  the line of the
New  Haven  Railroad   from  the   Weymouth  station   eastward.
Inasmuch as  the  slates  are  known to  be much older,     geologically
speaking,     than the granites,   it  is  logical to study them first.           There
are three kinds  of slates  represented in Weymouth.         Of these,    one,
in  North Weymouth at  Mill  Cove and Pearl  Street,    and another,
in  the railroad  cuts  near  Weymouth Landing,  belong  to  the  Cam-
brian  Period,   but are quite distinct  in  character,    while the  third  at
Slate Island belongs to the much more recent  Carboniferous Period .
Mill Cove Slates
The most northerly  outcrop  of  rock  on the mainland is  at  Mill
Cove  and along  Pearl  Street,      North  Weymouth.            The  rock  here
exposed is  a purple slate  very well shown  around the  shores  of  the
cove,       and  extends  eastward  along  Pearl  Street  to  a  point  a  few
hundred feet beyond North Street.             It  consists  for  the  most part
of a reddish or purplish calcareous  slate,    with one or two thin beds
of white limestone up to  two feet  in  thickness,     and an occasional
bed of gray sandstone.          The locality  in which this  slate  is  found is
already well mantled with glacial drift,   but Nature has conveniently
neglected  to  cover  these  few  outcrops,    though  it  is   becoming  so

thickly  settled  that even now many of the  outcrops  are  being  ob-
scured,     and in a few years  more most of them will be covered with
buildings.
The slates  are  relatively  soft  and non-resistant  to  the  weather,
a condition  which  probably  explains  why they  are  not  seen  at
more places where they are  supposed  to  exist by logical  inference.
Along Pearl Street  they are protected,  " sheltered "  so  to speak,    by
the  hard  resistant  " everlasting"  granite,      which  outcrops  only  a
few score of feet  south of Pearl Street as high ledges.     It  has been
estimated  that  there  are  about  seven  hundred  feet  of  strata  ex-
posed  in  this  vicinity.        Professor  Crosby  measured  the  dip  and
strike  of  these  rocks  and records  them as follows :        dip,     70°  to  80°
to  the south;     strike,     N.  75°  to  80°   W.   It  is  apparent,     then,     that
these  rocks,     which,    like  all  other  sedimentary  rocks,     originated  in
a nearly  horizontal  position,   have been tilted  or folded  until  they
are  now practically vertical.
Many layers  of the  slate  contain holes from half an inch  to  an
inch  across,     occasionally  larger,    resembling  eye sockets,    formed by
the  weathering  out  of  calcareous  concretions.          These  are  usually
flattened so that when they are broken across  they have the shape
of  an eye.             Hence the  name " eyed stones "  for  fragments  of  this
kind of rock so frequently found in the gravel pits  of the southern
part  of  the town.          These concretions  are  of  similar  formation  to
the clay dogs or clay stones of the beds of many of our larger rivers ,
the  Connecticut,    for  instance.             They  occur  so  thickly  in  some
places as  to form a continuous band in the slate.       The slate  itself
represents  the  fine  limy  mud which  once  formed  the  sea  bottom
of  the ocean  which  covered  this  region  in  the  early  part  of  the
Cambrian Period.
The only  mineral which  is   conspicuous  among  the  Mill  Cove
slates   is   epidote.         It  occurs  in  two  principal  modes:      first,      as  a
hard,    green,    outer  shell  about the fossil clay stones,    and secondly,
as  a  secondary mineral developed on slickensides,                  surfaces  along
which the rocks have slipped and slid,  the heat and pressure gener-
ated  by this  movement being  sufficient  to  form  new minerals,      in
this   case  epidote.         Here  the  epidote  occurs  as   a  striated  green
facing  on the  plane  along  which  the  rocks  must  have  slipped.
Frequently  this  movement is  so intense  that  the  rocks  receive  a
mirror  polish,    well  deserving  the  common name miner's  mirrors.
Examples of this  last  type of epidote can be seen best at the out-
crops  along the north side of  Pearl  Street.
There  is   a low  inconspicuous  outcrop  on  Pearl  Street  scarcely
rising  above the  ground,    opposite  the  home of the  late  Richard
Ash.             This ledge  is  especially  interesting  from the  fact  that  about
1900,            fossils  of the  Lower  Cambrian  Period,    the  most ancient  of
the fossil  bearing  periods,    were  here discovered.             Mr.  H.  T.  Burr,
who found them,    being  then  a  student  at  Harvard,     published  an
account of his discovery  the  same year  (see  Bibliography) .          Since
then no further  investigations  have been made until  1913,     when  a

Harvard  party,   while exploring  the  same ledge,    discovered  a  very

but it  places  the  name of  our town in  the scientific  literature  for
alltime.
A list  of the fossils  that have been found at this  locality  follows .
Of these  the  only  ones  that  are  by  any  means  common  are  the
Obolella,    Holmia and Strenuella.
Brachiopods:
Obolella  atlantica.

Urotheca pervetus.
Orthotheca  cylindrica.
Trilobites:
Callavia bröggeri.
Callavia hurri.
Callavia  crosbyi.
Strenuella  strenua.
Weymouthia nobilis .
These trilobites  were a  race of small crab-like  crawling creatures
which lived in  the mud along  the shores,    and  were the  scavengers
of the Cambrian seas .           Their shells  were like those of the horseshoe
crab in texture,    and the  impressions  of  them were well preserved
in the fine mud.        They ranged in size from a foot or more in length,
such  as  the  Paradoxides found over in  Hayward's quarry in  Brain-
tree,     down to  the minute specimen above described,    and form the
subject of many erudite volumes in scientific  libraries.              Their heads
were curved,     or semi-circular  in  shape,    and  adapted  to  burrowing
in the mud,    and are  the signs  by which they are most easily  recog-
nized  in  the  fossil  state.           The little  specimen  recently  found  and
named of this  large family of fossils  is  about  the  shape of a dumb-
bell,    and less  than a  quarter of an inch long.       They all  have their
crab-like  legs  curled  under  them,     so  they  rarely  show in  the  im-
pressions  in  slate,    which are  usually  of  their  backs .
Weymouth Landing  Slates
A second  area  of  slate  occurs  in  a  well -defined  but  narrow belt
stretching  from  the  Monatiquot  River  in  Braintree  eastward  to
the vicinity of  King  Oak Hill.         This belt  of slate  is  exposed  only
in  a few localities,    such  as  both  banks  of  the  Monatiquot  River,
the railroad cuts at Weymouth station and White's Neck ( Idlewell) ,
and one or  two small cuts  around the  base  of  King Oak Hill.          In
all  these places the slate is  essentially the same.            In  contrast  to the
more massive purple slate  of the Mill Cove area,    this  belt  is  com-
posed of black fissile  slates,   which may readily be cleaved into very
thin  laminae.            Most of  the  natural  surfaces  are  stained  with  the
mineral  limonite,     but  this  is   a  natural  consequence  in  any  rock
which contains even a fraction of  1  per cent of iron,    when exposed
to  the weather.        In addition to the eminent slaty cleavage,     several
subordinate directions  of splitting  are  always  present,    so  that it  is
 - 144 - 
136                        THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
impossible  to obtain large slabs of thin  slate such as might be useful
for  roofing  purposes.        The innumerable  cracks  and crevices  in  it
provide  ample  space  for  water,     so  that  wells  sunk  into  the  slate
are  seldom  dry;     this  is  in  contrast  to  the  granite  which  occurs
closely  associated with the slate .
The most extensive  exposure is in the cut at Weymouth station.
This  cut,       about  1,050 feet  long,    is  almost entirely  in  slate,    but at
the station end of the south side there is  a minor amount of granite.
The relation  between the slate and the granite is what is  called  a
fault;       that  is,   the two kinds  of rocks  have been forced  past  each
other,     the granite moving upward and the slate slipping downward.
An even more interesting  cut has been bared where the  railroad
crosses  White's  Neck,     under  the  bridge  now leading  to  Idlewell.
Here  the  slate   occurs  in  another  long  cut,    associated  with  the
granite  under  similar  conditions.        The  granite  here,       though,        is
found at the eastern end of the cut,    and the slate immediately ad-
joining  the  granite  shows  the  effects  of  the  contact  with this  in-
tensely hot igneous rock,   for it  is bleached almost white and trans-
formed into  a crumbly,    incoherent mass.           Further from the granite
the slate  has  been  fractured,     and great gaping  fissures  have  been
formed in  it  which must have been originally filled  with intensely
hot  vapors  from  the  contiguous  molten  granite.        These  vapors
brought with  them an abundance of silica  in solution,    which,   when
the granite and its  vapors cooled,   deposited the silica as the mineral
quartz in the fissures.           In  almost every case  the  fissures,     or  veins,
were completely filled by the quartz.           The veins are very numerous,
and of all  sizes,    from a fraction of an inch up to several feet  wide.
These  veins  are  noticeable  from  the  train  windows  as  prominent
white bands running down the sides of the cut.
From  a  mineralogical  point  of  view  the  veins   are  extremely
interesting,       for  they  have  yielded  some  very  fine  crystals.            Ap-
parently  the veins  were filled  by the growth of quartz  crystals  on
their walls,     and as  long as the vein remained not entirely filled,    the
free  and  perfect  crystals  stood  out  into  the cavity.          Most of the
veins   are  filled   entirely,      and  give  up  nothing  but  structureless
masses of white quartz.          Here and there a place can be found where
the  process  of  deposition  was  halted  before  the  veins  were  quite
filled,    for we find cavities up to  a foot  or so in diameter containing
beautiful perfect crystals  of quartz.          Most of the available cavities
have been  explored,     and  their  contents  adorn  collectors'     cabinets
all  over the country.        The largest  collection of specimens from this
locality  is  that  of  Mr.  Clarence  W. Fearing  of South Weymouth,
who was fortunate enough to have been on the ground when blasting
was done in  order  to  put a second track through the cut.          During
this  operation Mr. Fearing gathered some fine  crystals  and crystal
groups.             None of  these  are  of  exceptional  size,   the  largest  I have
seen  being  five  inches  long  and  three  inches  thick.        Some of the
specimens  are  of remarkable clearness,     while  others are clouded by
the green mineral  chlorite.      All the crystals  are of simple form,
 - 145 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 137
hexagonal prisms  capped by hexagonal  pyramids,     with  only  here
and there exceptional faces.           It should be said,  however,     that  the
collector  must not expect  to  find  the  crystals  in  perfect  condition
when they come from the rock.           They are almost invariably coated
with  limonite,     a  mineral  which  is  identical  in  composition  with
iron rust.             This  can  be  scraped  off   with  a knife  without  much
danger of damaging the crystals,    for  they are harder than the best
steel,      but a better  method of cleaning  them is  to soak them for  a
day or  two  in  either  weak hydrochloric  acid  or  in  concentrated
oxalic  acid,      preferably the latter.           The acid  dissolves  the  limonite
but does not attack the quartz,    so that the crystals become perfectly
clean and free from stain.         Large masses of the soft green granular
mineral chlorite help  to  fill  the veins,   and Mr.  Fearing has  in  his
possession a single crystal of the rather rare mineral monazite from
this cut.           Monazite is used in the manufacture of Welsbach mantles
for  gas  lighting.
North and east of King Oak Hill  are a few small outcrops of  this
same slate,    but its  appearance and relations  are  substantially  the
same as  in  the other cuts.
The cuts  on both sides  of  the  road  above  and  north  of Wash-
ington  Square  are  actually  across  the town line  in  Braintree,      but
they  are  so  well  known  and  often  seen  by Weymouth  residents
that  they  deserve  mention  here.         The  higher  of  these  two  cuts
consists of three kinds of rocks,    but they are all so deeply weathered
and iron- stained that the difference can be made out only by careful
study.         Slate makes up the  northern  part of the cliff,     granite  the
southern part,    and in between is  a dike of diabase,    described below.
These slates  belong to the  Middle Cambrian  Period,     and thus  are
slightly younger than the  Mill  Cove slates.           No fossils  have as  yet
been found in them.
Slate  Island  Slates
The  two  islands  in  Boston  Harbor  belonging  to  the  town  of
Weymouth are both  characterized  by slate.          In  each  case  it  is  a
fine,       soft,     dark gray rock,    extremely  broken up by slaty  cleavage
and joint  planes.          Slate  Island  is  almost wholly composed of  slate
ledges,     while  Grape Island,    the  remnant of  a wave- torn  drumlin,
has  small  outcrops  of  slate  on its  northern  and southern  borders.
The  slate  has  no  counterpart  on  the mainland of this  town,     but
Professor   Crosby  concluded  that  it   belonged  to  the  same  slate
series  as  outcropped at Huit's  Cove and Beal's  Cove in Hingham.
If this is  so,    then the Slate Island slate belongs to the Carboniferous
Period,    and is therefore millions of years younger than the Cambrian
slates  of the mainland.          No fossils  have been found in it yet.
This  slate  is   extremely  fissile,     and  besides  is  much  contorted.
The layers of slate  are so closely  bent that pieces  broken at  a right
angle are occasionally met with,   and these can be still  further split .
It  is  broken in so many directions  that  it  is  unsuited  for  roofing
slates.
 - 146 - 
138                          THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH
Granite
If  we draw a line  from Weymouth station  along  the railroad  to
East  Weymouth  station  we have  divided  the  town  geologically
into  two  parts,   -  a  northern  part  of  slate,     and  a  southern  and
much larger  part  of  granite  and allied  rocks.         The difference  be-
tween  the  relative  resistance  to  weathering  in the  two  regions  is
apparent,      since  the  slate  never  stands  up in  bold  ledges,      but  is
always  subdued where it  is  exposed,    while  the granite  frequently
makes high  precipitous  ledges.
To  be  granite,    an  igneous  rock  must contain  the two  minerals
quartz  and  orthoclase  feldspar;         in  addition,     it  may contain  any
one or more of a great variety of minerals,    the commonest of which
are mica and hornblende.         Most of the granite  of Weymouth is  of
the hornblende variety,   but some biotite  (black mica)  granite  and
some muscovite  (white mica)  granite  are  occasionally  found.          All
these varieties of the granite grade into each other almost insensibly.
Technically,       this  granite  is   all  known  as  Dedham  granite,       and
stretches  from beyond Dedham eastward to  Cohasset,     though it  is
far  from homogeneous,     even within the limits of this  town.
In the  main,     the granites  of  Weymouth are quite  uninteresting.
The most abundant kind,   the hornblende granite,    is  a dull gray in
color which even  on a fresh  surface  is  not attractive.          To be used
successfully  as  a building  stone  a rock  must possess,   beside  dura-
bility,     one or  both of  the  following  attributes :       ease of  quarrying,
as  the  Indiana  limestone,     or  attractiveness  of  appearance,     such  as
the  Milford granite.         The Weymouth hornblende granite  possesses
neither of  these  qualities.         Near the Abington line,   however,    there
is   a variety  called  Brockton  granite,    which consists  of about one-
third  red  to  pink  orthoclase  feldspar,     a fact  that  imparts  a very
pleasant soft  tone to  the  rock  on  a  fresh  surface.             If ledges of this
variety of granite could be found in sufficient  quantity,   and I  have
never  seen  such  in  Weymouth,      though  this  granite  is  especially
abundant  in  Abington,    it  could  profitably  be  quarried  as  an  at-
tractive  building  stone.
There is  one other variety  of granite  that  needs  especial  notice.
This  is  the  seam- face  granite,    a mica granite.         It is  now being  ex-
tensively   quarried  along  Washington  Street  in  Weymouth,        and
even  more  so  across  the  town line  on Whiting  Street,      Hingham .
The feature to which this  granite  owes its  chief interest  and value
as a building stone is  the remarkably perfect parallel joint structure.
These joints,    or seams,    vary from half an inch to two feet  or  more
apart,       thus  dividing  the  granite  into  perfectly  plane  sheets  easily
quarried.                The blocks  require but little  trimming before  they  can
be used as building stones.         The grain of the granite is  exceptionally
fine and smooth,   and in color it  is  almost pure white or a light  gray.
This solid  color,     unvaried  by the content of any black minerals,      is
no detriment,     however,    because the fresh  surfaces  are  seldom  used
 - 147 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 139
as  outside  surfaces  in  buildings.          The joint  faces  are  almost  all
colored by stains of iron oxide,   which,   far from rendering the blocks
so  discolored   useless   as   at  the  Quincy quarries,    gives  an  added
attraction  to  the  stone,     since  the  deep  and  rich  yellow,      red  and
brown stains  of iron oxide are used as  exterior surfaces in building.
This  arrangement  gives   a  beautifully   variegated   effect   to   the
granite,      and  as  far  as  I   can  ascertain  the  colors  are  permanent .
The stain  is  due to  the  rusting  of  small  grains  of  iron  pyrites,      a
mineral occurring in the granite.
Professor  Crosby wrote of the seam-face granite as follows :
a
The earliest instance of the use of the seam- face granite was in the construction
some seventy- five  years  ago of the  stone house on the north side  of Washington
Street,      in  Weymouth,    less  than one-fourth  of      mile  from  the  Hingham line ;
and the little  quarry  from which the material  for this  house was obtained  may
be seen on the south side of the street between the house and the town boundary.
This house shows to good advantage the ready adaptation of the granite to archi-
tectural  uses,       the horizontal  surfaces  of  the  blocks  being  in  every  instance  the
natural joint faces.      In the  more modern use  of the  seam-face  granite,    however,
both beauty and economy have been consulted by placing the stones,     as a rule,
onedge.
Diorite
Diorite is  an igneous  rock differing  chiefly  in the lack  of  quartz
and the  substitution  of  plagioclase  feldspar  for  orthoclase.             Horn-
blende  is  invariably  present  too.        It  is  exposed  at  comparatively
few points  in our town.           The largest  outcrop  is  along  the  eastern
shore  of  Whitman's  Pond  for  about  half  a mile,     having  a width
about half as great.          This is  a much darker rock than granite,     and
is unsuited for building stone,     since its  constituent minerals,     chiefly
plagioclase  and hornblende,     decompose  and  become discolored  so
readily   under  the  influence   of  the  atmosphere.              Fragments  of
diorite may be seen in almost every granite ledge as small  rounded
dark  green  or  black  so-called  inclusions.             It  is  supposed  that  the
diorite was once more extensive than it  is  at present;      in  fact,    all
the South Shore towns were once composed of it.            The granite was
thrust up into the diorite  in  a molten condition by a paroxysm of
the  earth's  interior,     absorbing  much of it,     or displacing  it,      so  that
the  granite  now  occupies  the  place  where  the  diorite  once  was.
The  area  near  Whitman's  Pond  represents  some  of  the  diorite
which escaped complete effacement.           In this  process,     which  must
be conceived  of as happening thousands  of  feet  under  the  surface
of the earth (and since exposed by the constant erosion and wearing
away  of  the  rocks  by  the  elements) ,      and  millions,     yes,        perhaps
scores  of  millions  of years  ago,     blocks  of the  diorite  were  broken
off from the parent mass  and dropped into  the  fiery  underground
reservoir  of  molten  granite,    to  be  held  prisoner  there  when  the
granite solidified by cooling.
 - 148 - 
140                         THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
Dikes
Penetrating  both  the  granite  and the  slate,     and in all  parts  of
the  town,     are  a great many black dikes from a few inches wide up
to  two or  three  hundred feet.           This last  figure  is  exceptional,     and
there  are  very few dikes  over ten feet  wide.      Since these dikes  cut
through  both  granite  and  slate,     it  follows  that  they  must  have
been  formed  after  these  two  kinds  of  rocks  were  formed.              With
one or two exceptions,   the dikes of black trap rock belonged to the
Triassic  Period,                     the  time  when the  red  sandstones  of  the  Con-
necticut  Valley  were being  accumulated,    and reptiles  fifty  feet  in
length  roamed over the  land,     and lava  flows  interrupted  the  mo-
notony of  an otherwise quiet  time.
Adike appears on the surface of a ledge as a wide band of another
material.               It  is  formed by molten matter being forced up from the
interior  of  the  earth  into  a  fissure.            A splendid  example of a dike
may still  be seen at  Central Square,    though I hear it  is  shortly  to
be blasted  away.            A very  large dike forty to fifty feet wide can be
seen in The Rocks,    South Weymouth,   crossing the Bay State Street
Railway  Company power line  at its  highest point between Middle
Street  and  Park Avenue.        A somewhat  smaller  dike  crosses  the
power  line  a  few yards  further  south.          This one is  remarkable  for
its   coarse  porphyritic  texture.         The rock  is  quite dark,       and  con-
tains  large,      perfectly  formed  plagioclase  feldspar  crystals,        which
are  sometimes  plainly  twinned.        It  is  difficult,     however,      to  free
them from  the  parent  rock.             The largest  dike  in  Weymouth may
be  inspected  in the  cuts  in  the  street  just  north  of  Washington
Square and across  the town line  in Braintree.       Although this  is  in
Braintree,      it  is  the best place to see this  large dike,    which may be
traced with difficulty  eastward into Weymouth.
In  addition  to  the  black dikes  of  trap  rock,     there  are  a  great
number of dikes of aplite,     the variety of aplite of which the  seam-
face  granite  is  composed.        These  are  white  or  gray,      never  more
than ten feet  wide,    and seem to  radiate out from the  main aplite
body near the Hingham line.          They are made of practically nothing
but  quartz  and feldspar.          A good example of this  type of dike  is
the  one  which  cuts  through  the  ledge  of granite  in  front  of  the
Pratt Schoolhouse.
Glacial Geology
In common with the rest of the New England towns,  Weymouth
shares  the  effects  of  glacial  erosion  and deposit,    and its  hills  and
valleys  may all  be said  to  be due ultimately to  that cause.       Prior
to  the advent of  the  glacial  ice-sheet,     the soil was much like  that
of our southern states,   which were never glaciated.         The great ice-
sheet,       slowly  grinding  its  way southward  from  the  wilderness  of
Canada,    sheared off  and carried away the virgin soil of the previous
geological  periods,    and left  us with deposits  of boulders  and clay,
 - 149 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 141
or  gravel  and  sand,     from  its   rushing  streams.          It  rounded  and
smoothed  off  the  rock  ledges,    and  cracked  off  and carried  away
detached  pieces.        Such  pieces  of  rock,      worn  smooth  somewhat
during  their journey  as  glacial  freight,     are  now strewn  across  our
countryside,      for  the most part covered  by later  outwashings  from
the glacial  streams.         These boulders  as  a rule  occur in connection
with what our farmers call yellow dirt,     or hard pan,   a mixture com-
posed mostly of clay and boulders compacted into a hard substance
by the weight of the ice which rode over it.          This combination has
made farming a difficult  process,     and has been the  origin,     too,     of
most of the mileage of stone walls,    made from these glacial boulders
with which  the  fields  were covered,     in  some cases  so  thickly  that
plowing was impossible  until  they were removed.
Two very interesting  specimens of ledges  worn and polished  by
glacial  action  are  to  be  seen,    one  at  the  junction  of  Main  and
Winter  Streets,     continuing  across   Front  Street  to  a  point  just
north of the  Reed Cemetery,    and another near the East Weymouth
car barn.               We must not forget to mention the fine view of polished
ledges  on  a grand  scale  which  can  be  seen  from  Pleasant  Street
looking eastward,   especially from the rear of the Pratt Schoolhouse.
Boulders.                       When the  ice  melted,    it  was forced  to  drop all  the
boulders  and  finer  material  which  it  carried.         Occasionally,    when
the  ice  was carrying  particularly  large  boulders,    these  have  been
left  stranded,    so  to  speak,     far  from their  parent  ledge.            The best
example of  these  stranded  boulders      erratics,       as  they  are  called
in geology      is  House Rock,    just  east  of  Essex  Street  and south
of   Broad  Street.           Of this  boulder  Professor  Crosby  notes  that  it
rests   upon  a  northward  sloping  and  distinctly  glaciated  ledge  of
granite.           It  is  therefore  a true  erratic,     and not  in  any sense  a re-
siduary  mass.               Viewed  from  the  northeast  the  boulder  presents  a
rather  striking profile,    first  noted by Mr. John J.  Loud,    which has
caused  it   to  be known  locally  as  the  Weymouth  Sphinx  (House
Rock is  the more generally used name) .          The maximum horizontal
dimensions of  the boulder  are :         north  side,    thirty- seven feet ;        east
side,       twenty- five feet;      south side,    forty-two feet ;      west side,     forty-
two feet.               Its  circumference six  feet  above the ground is  one hun-
dred and twenty-six  feet.          In volume House Rock must approxi-
mate a cube  thirty- five  feet  on  an  edge,      or  over  forty  thousand
cubic  feet.             At one  hundred  and  seventy  pounds  per  cubic  foot
the weight  is  about three  thousand  five  hundred tons.             It  is  thus
nearly  half  as  large  as  the great  Madison boulder of  New Hamp-
shire.          This  is  an undoubted glacial  erratic,    and the  probabilities
are very great that it  is  not far  traveled;     in fact,   the parent  ledge
is  quite  certainly  one  of  the  group of  ledges  on  the  west  side  of
Essex Street  on the  north side of the  almshouse,     and the rock  is
now probably between one- half  and three- quarters  of  a mile from
its birthplace.
Another notable  stranded  boulder  is   the  Perched  Rock,       which
stands  on a ledge  of  granite  off  Park  Street,      near  the  Hingham
 - 150 - 
142                         THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH
line.                This  rock  is  thirteen  feet  long,   six  to  eight  feet  wide,     and
seven  to  eight feet  high.     It  cannot  weigh  much less  than  fifty
tons.
Caverns.    -Another  striking  example  of  the  power  of  the   ice-
sheet is  to be seen on the east side of Whitman's Pond in the woods.
The western face of a high bold ledge of granite has been sufficiently disrupted
by the last efforts of the ice to form what is  virtually a roofless  cavern which may
be entered through a narrow crevice about twenty- five feet long and closed above.
In view of these facts  it  is  plain that in the production of its  freight  of boulders
the ice- sheet  must in some instances have quarried away whole hills  of solid rock,
so that it  is  not  surprising  that  in the case  of  such  a giant  as  House Rock,      the
parent  ledge  was  destroyed  in  the  making,     and nothing  remains  to  mark the
site.            (Crosby. )
In this same locality can be seen a perched boulder on the high
cliffs   facing  Whitman's  Pond,    weighing  perhaps  ten  tons.             It  has
been moved by the ice only a short distance,   because it  is  composed
of the same material as  the rock upon which it  rests,    diorite,    which
has an extremely limited distribution.
Mr.  Fearing  has  told  me in  a letter  of another cave,      to  which
I  shall  take  the  liberty  to  refer  by quoting  Mr.  Fearing's  words.
I am told  there  is  a sort  of cave  not very far  south  of the  Hingham bridge,
large enough to hold a number of people,    and that tradition tells  of its  use by the
Indians  as  a shelter  or  meeting place.      There is  also  a story  that  about twenty
years ago or so it  was for a while a rendezvous for hoboes.
This  cave  is  evidently  on the  land  now owned by the  United
States government,    and at the present time,   even if it is not already
destroyed,     it  is  probably inaccessible.        It would be very instructive
to   hear  a  description  of  this  interesting  cave  from  one  who has
actually visited  it.
