Drumlins
The hills  of  Weymouth are  all  glacial.           Even the rock hills  owe
their present configuration  to  the scouring action  of the ice.        King
Oak Hill  and  Great  Hill  are  both  of  the  type known as  drumlins ,
smooth,         beautifully  rounded  hills,     all   deposits  of  the  ice-sheet.
 - 151 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 143
They  are  made  up  of  a  heterogeneous  mass  of   clay,     sand  and
boulders  called till,   which was pushed  and rolled  along  under  the
moving  ice,      and  perhaps  lodged  upon  some  convenient  bedrock,
whereupon the ice  finally overrode it,    smoothing it  into the pleasing
form we see to-day.       Great Hill,    the finest of the Weymouth drum-
lins,     is  about one hundred and fifty- three feet  above sea level,    from
which it  rises  directly.        King Oak Hill,   ten feet  higher  (one hun-
dred and sixty- three feet,    more or less)  commands a view of all  the
rest of them,    and one of the most beautiful views of Boston Harbor,
which is  itself  dotted  with drumlins.           Their  gentle  slopes  make
these  hills  pleasant to look at,     easy to  cultivate,   and give graceful
contours to  the skyline.
Sand  Plains.                     In  contrast  to  the  rounded slopes of  the  drum-
lins  are  the  level  stretches  of  sandy and gravelly  soil,    the  ancient
flood  plains  and  outwash  plains  of the  turbulent  streams  issuing
from the melting ice.      The main roads of this town run for the most
part  over  these  plains,    avoiding  the  rocky  ledges.          Some  of  the
plains  extend over  into  Hingham,   where they are far more evenly
developed  and  more  extensive  than  their  interrupted  nature  in
Weymouth.              Thomas Corner,     Lovell's  Corner,    Pleasant Street  and
Mosquito  Plain  are good examples  of this  type of  glacial  deposit.
Amarked characteristic of sand and gravel deposits  is  the growth
of pines and cedars which prevail on them.        It will be noticed that
all the cemeteries in  the town are  located  on such deposits,     rather
than upon the hard,    bouldery till .
Such deposits as these plains,    as well as eskers and kames,    which
are described below,  are often included under such terms as modified,
stratified  or  assorted drift,    to indicate  that,   while their  material  is
strictly  of  glacial  origin,   it  has  suffered  considerable  modification
or   assorting  at  the  hands  of  the  glacial  streams,      and  is   always
arranged  in  strata.             It  is  almost  always  composed  of  material  of
medium or  fine  grain,   that  is,    of  gravel  or of sand,    and  probably
constitutes  the town's  most valuable  natural  resource.
Eskers.    -Eskers,     or  serpentine ridges of modified drift,     are very
noticeable  in  some parts  of  the town,    particularly  the  region  west
of  the  Back River,    where a complicated system of these ridges can
be seen.      A second  system runs  practically  north  and south,    from
Washington Square  to  Nash's  Corner.             The latter  system  is   seen
to  best  advantage on Winter Street  and the Austin  Tirrell  Farm.
Like  sand plains,    these  eskers  are  composed of layers  of  fine  ma-
terial,    sand and gravel mostly,   with no clay and only a few boulders ;
and some of the most valuable gravel pits  have been developed  in
this   type  of  deposit.          Their  sinuous  course  brings  to  mind  the
winding course of  a river,    and such is  indeed the case,   for it  is  sup-
posed that these eskers  mark the sites  of the greater  streams  either
on or  under  the  glacier,     whose  beds  were  constantly  being  filled
by material slumped into them by the melting  of the  ice  and the
release  of its  encaged load  material.
Infinite  pleasure may be enjoyed by the naturalist  in  examining
 - 152 - 
144                        THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
the varied and often beautiful types of boulders and pebbles in the
gravel  pits.            Porphyry,     greenstone,     quartz,     purple and green  slate,
fine   specimens  of  puddingstone,      and  occasionally  a  beautifully
banded  boulder  of  red  sandstone  or  amygdaloid  may be  the  re-
ward of  a  short  search.          A veritable  collection  in a nutshell of all
the kinds  of  rocks  existing  for,    say,     twenty miles  to  the  north  of
us.          Here,      too ,       are often  found good specimens  of the eyed stones,
whose place of origin is  the ledge of slates  around Mill Cove.
Kames.                   A third   type  of  stratified  drift  is  that  technically
known as kames.          These are hills  of more or less  irregular  shape,
but usually approximating a conical form.          Three beautiful examples
of them may be seen just over the town line south of High Street.
Where several  occur  in close  proximity,    as  east  of  Pleasant  Street
and north of Washington Street,    they give a very pleasant variety
to   the  topography,      which  has  frequently  earned  for  them  the
descriptive  name of dumpling hills .
Economic Geology
The economic aspect  of  a town's  geology  is  to  some of us  the
most  important  aspect.             The  resources  of  Weymouth in  this  line
have  consisted  chiefly  of  building  stone  from  the  granite  ledges,
boulders  from  the  glacial  till  for  its  stone  walls,   gravel  from  the
modified drift deposits,     and,   early in our history,   bog iron ore from
the bottom of  our  ponds.           Of all  these,    granite  of  the  seam-face
type is  the only one which has been sent outside the  town to  any
extent.
Granite.    -The only kind  of  granite  which has become of  com-
mercial  importance is  the seam-face  granite  of Washington Street.
This has been described on page 138 above.        The seam-face stone is
of  more importance  to  Hingham than  to  Weymouth,     because  the
joint  structure which makes for easy quarrying is  better developed
there  than  in  Weymouth.         Only one quarry  is  active  now in this
town.               Since  the  development of  these granite  quarries  a score  or
so  of years  ago  there  has  sprung up a substantial demand for  this
beautiful  stone in many sections  of  the country.
Bog  Iron  Ore.   -In  the  early days New England manufactured
almost all  of  her iron from the deposits  of  bog iron  ore  (limonite)
which were found in the swamps and ponds.         This is  a yellow or
brown mineral  which  usually  forms  an encrusting  mass upon the
twigs,      roots  or stones  on the bottom of streams and ponds,    whence
it  used  to  be pulled  up by means of long  rakes.        It  occasionally
forms  the  bottom  layer  of  swamps.             When the  vegetable  matter
around which the  mineral gathered decays,    the limonite  is  left  as
a spongy looking  mass,   which is  its  usual appearance.        It has its
origin in the iron  contained in  small quantities  in the rocks  of this
region,     and thence dissolved  in  the  stream waters.           In solution  in
streams  the  iron  is  in  the  form of  iron  carbonate  (FeCO3) .            This
mineral  is   unstable  in  waters  which  are  being  evaporated,      and
 - 153 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 145
under  such  conditions  loses  its  carbon  dioxide  (CO₂) ,     leaving  iron
oxide  (FeO) .                   This  compound,    again,     is  not stable  in  the  presence
of water,      but " rusts "  readily  by the addition  of  both  oxygen  (O)
and  water  (H₂O)     to  form  the  mineral  limonite  (2Fe2O3.3H2O) ,      or
bog iron  ore.        This  industry  was  sufficiently  large  to  supply  the
inhabitants   of  New England  with  iron  for  a  considerable  time,
ceasing  only  when it  became  more  profitable  to  import  the  rich
Michigan  ores .             The  record  of  the  existence  of  numerous  forges
and furnaces  all over the  town proves how large a quantity of this
ore  was  extracted  from the ponds by our forefathers .
Mr. Joy has  kindly furnished me with the following memoranda
concerning the early  state  of the iron industry in Weymouth :
In 1771  iron ore  in sufficient  quantity  to  pay well for  gathering  was  found  in
the ponds of the town,    and a contract was made with Thomas Hobart 1   of Abing-
ton,   by a public sale,   for the ore found in Great Pond at 40 shillings per ton,     with
an agreement to defend him against  any claims  for  damages that  might be ad-
vanced by other parties.     Acommittee was also chosen by the town to prosecute
any others who should be found taking ore from this pond.        This contract remained
in force until May,    1773,   when a lease was given to Mr.  Hobart for  thirty years,
at  £60 per year,    for the privilege  of taking ore from all the ponds of Weymouth.
In 1806 the town agreed to let  Thomas Hobart of  Pembrook dig one hundred
and fifty  tons of iron from Weymouth Great  Pond,    for 3 shillings  per ton,      as  it
is inthe pond.
In  1807  there  was  an  account  of iron  ore  dug out  of Great  Pond by Isaiah
Lucas  and Samuel  Reed.
In  1809,      September 2,     Mr.  Stetson  was granted  permission  to dig ten tons of
iron from Great Pond for 60 cents per ton.
Sand and Gravel.   - Probably the one resource which has brought
the  most profit,   with the possible exception of bog iron  ore,    is  the
series  of gravel pits  widely scattered  over the town.          Scarcely  any
deposit of modified drift has escaped being dug into,   either to furnish
road  material,      or grading  for  houses.            To list  the  gravel pits  is  in-
advisable,     for while some of the larger pits will continue to furnish
gravel  for years  to  come,    the  usual procedure is  to  abandon a hill
half dug in favor of a new pit closer to the place where the  gravel
is   needed.              Because  of  their  height,       eskers  are  more  frequently
used  than gravel  plain  deposits,     probably  because  of  the  ease  of
digging and loading.
Attempts have been made recently to  use sand from these  esker
deposits  in  the  making  of  cement,    but  these  have  not  yet  been
highly  successful,      as  the  best  quality  of  cement  requires  a  sand
whose grains  are  angular in  shape,    while  most of  the  sand  grains
of  our  eskers  are  more  or  less  rounded  and  water- worn.
Field  Boulders .                                In  the  early days  the building  of  stone  walls
composed  of  these  boulders  served   two  purposes,                 the  process
cleared  the  land  and made farming  easier,      and  saved  the  tedious
labor of splitting out fence rails.          Some of the lower stones in these
walls were dug out from the fields  where they were buried a foot or
In the  Boston Gazette,    March 12,    1770,    Aaron Hobart of Abington advertises a " Bell Foun-
dry," where bells  of various  sizes  were cast .
 - 154 - 
146                         THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH
more under the surface,   for whose borders they were used in fencing.
The farmers  used to  take special days with oxen and stone boat to
help build each other's walls,   and the boys were employed in picking
up the smaller  stones  to  fill  in at the top.          These picturesque  and
familiar  features of the New England landscape are fast disappear-
ing  from  our  more  thickly  settled  communities.          These  boulders
were also  very useful in the building of cellar walls,   for they saved
the cutting of foundation stones,   or the bringing of cut stone from
a  distance.               These little  rounded  pasture  boulders  have certainly
been of economic value to all  the New England towns in the past.
Clay  and Lime.                 Neither  of  these  two  raw materials,    essential
for   building  with  brick,      occurs   in  appreciable  quantities.             The
chimneys  of  the  earliest  houses  were  built  of  brick  brought  from
near- by towns  (perhaps  Bridgewater,    where there were brickyards
from the earliest  times) ,    and mortar,    whose lime was obtained from
seashells  pounded up on the beach.          The beds  of limestone at  Mill
Cove are  too  thin to  be  of  any use.
Peat.                     A small  amount of peat has in  times past been cut and
burned  here,      but  it   was  never  much  used,      nor  economical  as  a
fuel.             New methods  of  cutting,    drying  and compressing the peat
may ultimately make the peat of value,    though the possibility  is
remote.               It  occurs in the swamps along both Mill and Old Swamp
Rivers.
Infusorial  Earth.  -This  fine  white  powder,    composed  of  the
microscopic skeletons of minute unicellular plants called diatoms,     is
much used as  a polishing  powder on account of its  excessive hard-
ness  and fineness.         Mr.  Fearing  found a thin bed of this  material
in the easement ditch not far from the station at South Weymouth.
It  is  likely  to  occur  in  connection  with  any fresh-water  deposits,
such  as  our sands  and peat.
Geology of the  Highways
It  has  occurred to  me that the  average visitor or citizen in Wey-
mouth sees  the geology of the town only  as  he traverses  the high-
ways.                So  it   seems  a good plan  to  give  a brief  sketch  of what is
to  be  seen  along  some of  the  principal  highways.             We will  select
for  our  first   trip  the  route  from  Washington  Square  by  the  old
turnpike,    now Main Street,    to South Weymouth,    returning by way
of  Pleasant  Street  and East Weymouth.
Main  Street.    -Starting   from  Washington  Square  and  going
south  on  the State  road  up the hill,   we are  leaving  the  slate  area
behind us,      and are  entering into the granite country,    which every-
where is  higher than the much less  resistant  slate  area.          Hence the
rise  of  about one hundred feet to  the top of the hill.         Halfway up,
and back of the Weston property,     one may see  a  very good esker,
with  steep  sides  and  a  serpentine  form.            Numerous  outcrops  of
granite occur on both sides  of  the  road,   especially  on the left  near
the top  of  the  hill.         When the  summit is  reached,     above  Lincoln
 - 155 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 147
Square,      we  are  on  a flat  sand plain,  with  here  and there  a rocky
ledge off  to  the  east.               These ledges  are  much more apparent when
we come to  the fork where Washington Street  branches  off.               Just
beyond the fork we see a ridge,    or  esker,    on the left.          At present  it
has  a  row  of  cedars  on  its   crest,                      a  characteristic  growth  on
eskers.           It is  soon lost to sight in the woods,    reappearing at intervals
in  its  serpentine  course  on  Winter  Street,     and  especially  on  the
Austin Tirrell  Farm,    and finally  ending in the gravel pit  south  of
Nash.                  Continuing  up Main  Street  there  is  nothing  of  interest
until  we arrive  at the junction of  Main and Winter Streets.              In
the  northwest corner  of  these  crossroads,       and  about  two  hundred
feet from the same,   there is  a rather extensive flat outcrop of granite
covered  by a  network of  ridges  an inch  or  two wide and about  as
high.             These are  mostly veins  of quartz  or of aplite  granite,     both
of  which  are  more  resistant  than  the  granite  itself,      so  that  the
granite weathers  away,    leaving  the other material in relief.          In the
southwest  angle  of  the  crossroads   and  westward  along  Winter
Street  the polished ledges  referred to on page 141 are found.           These
are  of  coarse  granite,    but they will be seen  to  include many dikes
of aplite,    which is white in color and of finer grain,    so that it  takes
a better polish than the coarser granite.         If possible,   it would repay
one  to  study  the  ledges  off  Front  Street,    just  north  of  the  Reed
Cemetery,    only a few hundred feet away.        In the opposite direction ,
a short  trip  up Winter Street will bring us to a cut across  an esker,
which if  we could walk along  it  would prove  to  be the  same ridge
which we saw a half- mile back at the fork.
Descending into the valley of the Mill River we must notice how
small  the  river   appears  when  compared  with  the  width  of  the
valley.        We should remember that the valley was once filled  to the
brim with  the  stream  swollen  by waters  from  the  great  rain  and
snowfall of  the  glacial  period.        Just  before  we reach  the river,     we
pass a gravel pit dug into our esker,   which is  here somewhat modified
in form.           The steep  hill we now ascend  up to  Stetson's  factory  is
really an ice contact hill,   where the ice front of the glacier  lay stag-
nant for  a while,    and from which poured out southward the streams
carrying  sand  and pebbles  which  made the  gravelly  plain  beyond
the  top of  the hill.     Ice contacts  are  usually very steep,    and if  we
have time  to  make a  side  trip  along  Middle  Street,      beyond  the
old  Orcutt estate,    we may see as good an ice  contact slope as  there
is  in  the  town along the  path  which runs  to  Whortleberry  Pond.
This  slope  rises  up very  steeply  to  the  right  of  the  path.              The
pond itself  occupies  the  low ground  (fosse)   which  was  left  when
the ice melted,   and is  all  that is  left of a once more extensive glacial
pond;   while above and to the south of the contact is  a good though
small outwash plain on which was deposited the sands  and gravels
carried  out from the glacier when it  lay  up against this  contact.
Going back to the turnpike we travel for about three- quarters of
a mile to  Park Avenue between two very different kinds of scenery.
On the left we get glimpses of the rocky ledge  called  " The Rocks, "
 - 156 - 
148                         THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
while  on  the  right  we see  the  wide  flat  bed  of  the  ancient  Mill
River.                 Mr. Fearing has told me of finding evidences of the original
bed of  the river  on his  land,     showing that the river once filled  the
lowlands  nearly  as  far  eastward as  Main Street.          At Park Avenue
the land begins to rise again,    and if we look off to the left  we can
see   a  very  steep   slope   crossing  both  Torrey  Street  and  Tower
Avenue.                 This  is   another  ice  contact  slope,      and  a  small  stream
runs at  the bottom of  it .               From Columbian Street to the Abington
line  there is  very little  to mention.
Pond Street. -Returning,  let us take  Pond Street and Pleasant
Street   to   East  Weymouth.               Pond  Street  is   situated  upon  Pond
Plain,        a  sand  and gravel  plain bordering Great Pond.            It  is  worth
while,       if   one  has  time  to  walk  down through  the  woods  to  the
pond.              From the point where Oakden Road joins  Pond Street  there
is   plainly  visible  a small  esker  rising  sharply from the  plain,     and,
at present,     it  has a fringe  of  pines  along its  crest.
Pleasant  Street.     - Little  more  of  geological  interest  can be  seen
until  we have  crossed  Columbian  Square.             The  road  soon  begins
to  descend  rapidly  where it  crosses  the  ice  contact up over  which
we  passed   on  Main  Street  below  Columbian  Street.             At  Park
Avenue we come down on  to  a  sand  plain  again.            This  is  well
developed  on  both  sides  of  the  Old  Swamp River,     and doubtless
represents  the old  flood plain of that stream before it  shrunk to its
present  size.                A side  trip  up  Park Street  gives  a  very  instructive
view  of  an  old  glacial  delta,    just  east  of  the  Old  Swamp River,
over which once  ran  torrents  of  icy  water bearing débris  from the
fading  glacier  which must have lain  to  the northeast.            At present
the billowy form of the tongued delta front can be well seen .       Half-
way up  the  hill,      and  on  the  left,      one  of  the  old  water  channels
shows  a  very  remarkable  fresh  gully which was developed  practi-
cally  in  its  present  dimensions  by a single  day's  rainstorm  about
two  years  ago.            The  gully  at  its  largest  part  is  twenty-one  feet
wide  and  seven  feet  deep.            When  we think  of  what  one  single
storm  may  accomplish  it   does  not  require  much  imagination  to
picture  the  removal  of  the  entire  hill  by repetitions  of  such  an
occurrence,       and from  that  it  is  but  a  step  to  understand  how an
entire  region  may be worn down from a mountainous condition  to
a flat  region  like  our own to-day.          We can either  retrace  our steps
or  continue  up the hill  to  the top of the level  delta  plain  at and
beyond Pine  Street.            There  are  a few  sand pits  south of the cross-
roads  which show excellently  well the  steeply inclined  foreset  beds
of the delta.               These beds indicate the  slope over which the waters
ran,    dropping their load as they went.        Going north toward Pleasant
Street we soon come to  the cemetery,    built  on assorted drift,    again,
and then begin to descend the delta front on to the Pleasant Street
sand plain by Oak Street.
Starting  again  on  Pleasant  Street  at   Park  Avenue,       we  catch
glimpses  every  now and  again  of  the  graceful  slopes  of  the  delta
front just described,    off to the right.           Scattering outcrops of granite
 - 157 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 149
occur all  along  Pleasant Street ;       one  of  the largest  of  these  is  the
ledge on the west side  of  the  Fair Grounds.           It  soon becomes  ap-
parent,      though,    that there  is  a continuous  mass of  rocks  off  to  the
west.                This  is   " The  Rocks, "  seen  from  the  east.                 " The  Rocks "
constitute  a  wild  rocky tract  occupying most of the space between
Main  Street,      Park  Avenue  and  Pleasant  Street,      and  are  bounded
on the  north by Middle Street  and  the  Old  Swamp River.              It  is
made up mostly of granite,   and contains many things of interest ,
dikes  of  black  trap  rock  and  of  aplite,     many cliffs   and  perched
boulders,         and  several   high  points   of  rock  from  which  splendid
views  of  the  surrounding  country  may be  obtained.              One  of  the
best  cliffs  in  this  area  may be seen  from  the  vicinity  of  the  Oak
Street turnout on Pleasant Street.           A nearly vertical cliff  of granite
about  thirty  feet  high  stands  out in bold  relief  against  the  low-
lying area to the north.          This cliff  marks the location  of a fault  in
the  rocks,  -   a plane  where  the  rocks  have  actually  moved.            In
this  case  the  north  side  has  slipped  down,     or  the  south  side  has
moved up,    in  response to the ever- varying conditions  of  stress  and
strain existing in  the earth's  crust.           Such an adjustment invariably
makes a considerable jar in the crust,    which we on the surface  feel
as  an earthquake.        The plain,     at this  level,    terminates just  beyond
where the  road  crosses  the  Old Swamp River,     and is  succeeded  by
a similar plain at a higher level.            One or two ledges of granite out-
crop  here,      but the rock is  much weathered,     and its  characteristics
obscured.                  Mr.  Fearing  has  related  to  me  the  finding  of  large
pieces  of slag  built  into  the  stone  walls  near  the  site  of  the  old
tannery on the old  Palmer Loud place.     Whether or  not  there  was
ever a furnace here I  have not been able to find  out,    but the situa-
tion  is  right for the finding  of bog iron  ore.              When we ascend  the
rise  just  beyond the river,    there is  a view well worth looking at off
to  the left.                Below is  a fertile  meadow at  the  level  of the river,      or
slightly  above it;      beyond this  is  the wide  expanse  of  swamp on
both sides of the river;   and still  further  over we can see the  craggy
cliffs  of "The Rocks"  as  they overlook the river.           I  have seen  no
higher  cliffs   than these  in  Weymouth.             They are  of  solid  granite.
At the  Pratt  Schoolhouse  we  see  one  of  the  most  interesting
ledges in the whole town.          The main rock of the ledge is  well shown
in  freshly blasted  portion  abutting on the sidewalk.         It is  a  rather
dark  granite  very  rich  in  hornblende  and  both  pink  and  green
microcline  feldspar.          On  the  top,      especially  where  the  rock  has
been weathered rough,    there are long crystals of hornblende visible,
which in places  are  almost  an  inch  in  length.         Pyrite  is   not  un-
common in  the  granite  as  very  small  cubes,      and  indeed  it   also
occurs  in  the  diorite  inclusions ;         it   is   usually  covered  by  a  dark
brown rust.             Most of the small rusty patches  on the  surface of  the
ledge have a small  crystal  of pyrite  in  their  centers.           The granite
contains  a great many inclusions  of diorite,    for  the  most part  less
than  six  inches  across  and  of a very  fine  grain.         Numerous veins
of epidote  shoot  through  the  rock in  all directions,     and  sometimes
 - 158 - 
150                          THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
the granite breaks along such a vein showing a surface coated with
the pale green epidote.
If  we walk around the  south  side  we shall  find  near  the south-
west  side  a vein  of  almost solid  epidote  about three inches  thick,
and  also  very  many smaller  ones.             Closer  to  the  school  on  the
south side there is  exposed a magnificent dike of aplite six to seven
feet  wide  on  the  surface,     showing  up in  marked  contrast  to  the
darker and coarser granite.        If we look carefully along the southern
contact  about twenty feet  from  where it  disappears  underground
westward,     we may see a small jog in this boundary line,    the western
end of  the dike  having  moved along  a line  northward  about  four
inches.            This  line,    a fault,    can be distinctly  traced across  the dike
to  a  corresponding  jog  in  the north boundary.         On both sides  of
the aplite this fault plane is  marked by the formation of the mineral
epidote,    -an alteration mineral often formed on faults.         Rounding
the ledge  to  the east  side,     we can see  on a vertical  rock face  that
the dike itself  is  very nearly  vertical,     and that therefore  it  would
if  continued  eastward  run  toward the main body of  aplite  on the
Hingham line.           In all  probability  this  was its  place of origin.          On
the  northeast  corner,       near  the  large  cedar  tree,       the  hornblende
granite  again gives  way to  aplite.         This time the aplite  does  not
show very clear- cut boundaries,   but it is a true dike,    just the same.
It  is  an  unusually  wide  one,      however,     for  it  is  at  least  fifty  feet
wide.            On the south side it  is  flanked by a black trap dike,    about
four  feet wide,    and on the north side is  bounded by a body of what
appears to  be diorite.           This may be a part of the ancient diorite,
the  original  rock  of  this  region.           There  are  no  good  striae  visible
on the ledge,     and the only other signs of glaciation  are two or  three
places  on the  south  end where the rocks  have been  smoothed by
the ice without being polished.
Surrounding  this  outcrop is  a wide sand and gravel plain,    called
by geologists  the Whitman Plain,   which extends quite continuously
as  far  as  Lovell's  Corner.             The view  from  the  back  of the  Pratt
Schoolhouse  is   very  instructive.          Across  the  valley  of  the  brook
are  the  bare  glaciated  ledges  of  aplite,     and probably,       too,      of  the
coarse  granite.             On a sunny day these  ledges  are  so  bright  as  to
be almost dazzling.        One or two stranded boulders lie  on the ledges,
but  as  a  rule  they  are  remarkably  bare  and  polished.          In  time,
weather  will  roughen them and frost  will spoil  their  rounded out-
lines  by ripping off blocks.
The steep grassy bank north of the  schoolhouse is  a  kettle-hole,
where  once  there  lay  a huge block of ice,    either  an iceberg  broken
off  from  the  glacier  front  which  floated  away to  ground  at  this
spot,      or  else  a part of the ice- sheet  itself  left  stranded,     as  it  were,
by having the ice  melt away all around it.        It was filled  around by
sands  and  gravel,      and  when it  finally  melted left  a hole  to  mark
its  former site.            There is  nothing  more of interest  except this  level
plain and the polished  ledges  off  to  the right  until we come to  the
granite  ledge  cut  away to  make a  sidewalk where the road  turns
 - 159 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH                 151
to  the left  near  the  Methodist  Church.         This  is  not  such  a dark
granite as usual,     and many of  its  faces  are  stained by a light  film
of iron rust,    giving it a pinkish appearance.            From Lovell's  Corner
the Whitman Plain can be seen  to  splendid  advantage along  each
of the four crossroads .
Beyond Lovell's  Corner the road begins to skirt the rocky ledges
which go down to  Whitman's Pond.           Near the  street  car  turnout,
where some blasting was done a few years  ago,     this  granite  can be
well  seen  and  studied.         It  is  practically  the  same as  the  granite
at  the  Pratt  Schoolhouse,     and  needs  no  further  comment.                It is
dark,      with  plenty of diorite  inclusions  and epidote veins.            All the
way along  this  part of Pleasant Street  one gets  the  impression  of
traveling  between  two  parallel  ledges  of  rock;        in  all probability
the   lowland  in  between  marks  the  bed  of  an  ancient  preglacial
stream  which  flowed  between  granite  banks.          From  the  turnout,
and  for  about  a quarter  of a mile beyond,  we look off  to  the  east
and see that the sand plain has given way to a collection of rounded
" dumpling "   hills,        the  so-called  kames.          These  are  composed  of
sand  and  gravel,      just  as  the  sand  plains  are,     but  they  lack  the
level  surface.
Opposite the  Fairmount Cemetery is  a  small inconspicuous  ledge
which will repay study.       It is  a dike of black trap,   much weathered
so  as  to  appear to  be an outcrop  of  brownish rock.           The trap  was
originally  formed  as  a  dike  about  two feet  wide,    unbroken,     and
with   perfectly   sharp  cut  borders.           It  is  quite  a feat  in  mental
geometry  now  to  reconstruct  this  original  state,     for  it  has  been
cross- fractured  and faulted  to  a great  degree.            The cemetery,      as
usual,     is  built  upon stratified  drift       kame hillocks -for  ease  of
working.             Opposite  the   cemetery   a   new  road   leads   down  to
Whitman's  Pond,     where  great  ledges  of  the  dark,     almost  black
diorite  may be  seen at  and beyond the present  limit  of  the  road
southward.
Continuing,     it is well to notice  the stone wall  on the  left  as  we
descend  from  the  Whitman  Plain  level.           Several  boulders  of  the
near-by granite were evidently split and incorporated into the wall.
Some of them will be seen to  contain an abnormally large number
of  inclusions of diorite.            More plums than pudding !
The road  soon  climbs  up on to  the  Whitman Plain  level  again
just across  the  Back River.        A short trip  up Iron  Hill  Street  will
show  the  few  but finely  polished  ledges  recently  uncovered  from
their  mantle of glacial drift.            The steep descent of the Back River
from  Whitman's  Pond  has  been  explained  by  the  fact  that  the
original  outlet  has  been  dammed by  an  extensive  glacial  gravel
plain developed to  the north of the pond around East Weymouth.
East  Street.     -   When we  reach  Jackson  Square  let  us  go  along
Commercial Street  to  Madison  Square,     and then take  East Street
to Weymouth Heights.          We cross  the railroad near East Weymouth
station,     where there  is  an extensive  cut in granite,   and from  here
can get a good view of the esker,     extensively quarried  for  concrete

152                          THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH
sand  recently.             This  lies  to  the  west  of  the  railroad,      but  is  con-
tinued  eastward  across  the railroad  and may be seen to  very good
advantage  in  a  cut  in  East  Street  less  than  a quarter  of  a mile
from the  crossing.        A deep gravel pit has been dug into  the esker
here,    but  one may still  see  the sharp hog- back crest  rising  steeply
northeastward.             I  know of  no more typical  esker than this  in  the
whole  region.              It  bends  to  the north  in  a few hundred  feet,       and

runs  into  North  Street  at  Weymouth  Heights  we  get  changing

Union Avenue and Weymouth Heights we pass between the drumlin
on the left  and a lobate delta front on the right,  precisely similar  to
the  one  above  the  Old  Swamp River  at  Mosquito  Plain.           There
are  one or  two cuts in the  railroad  along the base of the drumlin,
showing both granite and slate.
Norton  Street.                              When  we  cross   North  Street  on  to   Norton
Street  a good view unfolds itself  on our left.          In the distance is  the
railroad  cut  at  White's  Neck  where  the  quartz  veins  are  to  be
found;      to  the  right  of the cut is  the hill  now known as  Idlewell,
probably  a kame.          North of the cut a few outcrops of granite  can
be seen on the hills  beyond the slate  area.              In the foreground is  the
marshy  lowland  bordering  a cove  of  the  Fore  River.            The road
soon  passes  through  a very deep cut  in  an esker,    upon which Old
North  Cemetery  is   located.           Scattered  outcrops  of  granite  occur
on the east,      but when we descend a slight  grade to  the junction of
Norton  and  Pearl  Streets  we come  to   a  small  outcrop  of  purple
slate,     with a minor amount of gray sandstone.            This is  the area of
the  Lower  Cambrian  slates  of  Mill  Cove,     described  on page 131 .
Pearl  Street.    -   A short  walk along  Pearl  Street  to  the  east  of
Norton  Street  brings  us  to  the  fossiliferous  outcrop.          The main
mass  of  the  slates  may best  be  studied  by taking  the path which
leaves  Pearl  Street  on  the west just after  crossing  Phillips '         Creek.
The remainder of  Pearl Street and all the roads surrounding Thomas
Corner  are  on a sand plain.
Neck Street.   - Crossing this  sand plain and going north on Neck
Street,      it   is   at  once  apparent that the  all- pervading element in the
scenery  along  this  street   is   Weymouth  Great  Hill,      whose  huge
bulk  is  a landmark for  miles  around.             The road passes  along  the
steep  easterly  side of  the drumlin,      too  close  for  us  to  appreciate
fully  the  perfection  of its  form.             Rose Cliff  and the  adjoining hills
are  drumlins,       too,       though  neither  so  large  nor  so  perfect  in form
as  Great  Hill,     and also  somewhat obscured by deposits of modified
drift  on their  flanks.           Upper  Neck is  a  low  drumlin,      and  Lower
Neck a sand and gravel spit,    built out into the harbor by the waves
from débris  worn from the  Upper Neck drumlin.         Bradley's  stands

upon  a  gravel   bar  connecting  the  Rose  Cliff   hills   with  Upper

North  Street. -Returning  we will  follow  Neck Street  to  North
Street.             After  crossing  Bridge  Street  a  wide  diversity  of  scenery
presents  itself.         Immediately  on our  right  is  the  Thomas  Corner
sand plain,     so close that it  can scarcely be appreciated.          Off on the
left  is  the  flat  fertile  meadow which  in  previous  years,       at  least,
yielded  three  crops  of  hay each  year.            Looking eastward  to  Green
Street,    the hill  on the extreme left  is  a drumlin;        south of that  is  a
series  of  kames and  eskers  which  borders  the  Back River.           Off  to

the high  steep slope of an ice contact and the level top of the out-
wash plain  on its  summit.            Beyond  this  level  top  is   the  lobate
delta  front  above  East  Street.          Then  traveling  south  on  North
Street  we pass  through  an  esker  at  the  Old  North  Cemetery,      the
same  one,      of  course,     through  which  Norton  Street  cuts  a  short
distance to the west.          The quickest way back to Weymouth Landing
is   by Commercial Street  direct.            This gives us a chance to inspect
the  cut  at White's  Neck,     and to  study  the  slates  and  the  quartz
veins  there.            An alternative route is  by Commercial (southward) ,
Middle  and  Broad  Streets  to  Lincoln  Square.              By this  route  we
get  a  better view of King Oak Hill,   up whose flank  the  road  takes
us,    and we can also see the  fine  dike at  Central Square.
MINERALOGY
With the exception of the quartz veins in  the White's Neck cut
Weymouth has no mineral deposit in  quantity or in quality sufficient
to   attract  collectors.            Our  minerals  may  be  separated  into   two
groups,                one   containing   minerals   which   are   characteristic   of
veins,     and another minerals which are diffused  through the granite
and other  igneous  rocks generally  as  small grains .
Vein Minerals
Quartz. -Quartz  is  the commonest  of  all  vein  minerals,       if  not
the  commonest mineral of all  types.          It is  white,    hard and  breaks
with a very sharp edge.        When it is transparent it  resembles window
glass  in  many of  its  properties.       Scarcely  any rock  ledge  in  this
town is  free  from  quartz  veins,                    fissures  which  have  been  filled
by  solutions  of  this  mineral  in  times  past.               The  most  notable
examples of  this  formation  is  the  series  of  quartz  veins  in  the  cut
at White's  Neck.
Chlorite.                      A soft   green  mineral,       which  occurs   in   connection
with the quartz in the cut at  White's  Neck.             It  occurs  either  as  a
soft  filling  of  cavities,      or  as  cloudy  inclusions  within  the  quartz
crystals.
Monazite.   -This  mineral  can scarcely be called  a characteristic
 - 162 - 
154                      THE  GEOLOGY  OF   WEYMOUTH
Weymouth  mineral,    since  but  one  small  crystal  of  it  has  been
found here.              This comes from the same cut,    and is in the possession
of Mr.  Fearing .
Pyrite.                 The mineral  pyrite,     or iron  pyrites,    is  the  commonest
metallic mineral,   and being frequently mistaken for gold has earned
the name of Fool's Gold.          It occurs as veins in the aplite  on Wash-
ington  Street,     and small  crystals  have been seen  from  the  quartz
veins  at White's Neck.
Epidote.            Ahard green mineral which is  abundant in the slates
at  Mill  Cove  and  Pearl  Street,     both  as  veins,    and  as  the  filling
of  the  cavities  in the  slates.       It  is  also  common in  veins  in  the
granite.
Calcite.                       Unknown as  crystals  from  Weymouth,    but it  makes
up the beds of limestone at  Mill  Cove,    and also the filling  of some
of  the cavities in the slates  there.
Limonite.                               This is  the mineral which makes the  rusty stain  on
our  rocks.             In fact,    it  is  identical  with  iron  rust.         The beauty of
the  seam-face  granite  depends  directly  upon  this  otherwise  dis-
figuring  mineral.          Most of the  quartz  crystals  from the veins  are
covered by limonite;       in  this  case,     as  in the case of the seam-face
granite,      the limonite is  the result  of the weathering of the mineral
pyrite,     which  is  extremely rich  in  iron.            Limonite  also  makes  up
the beds of bog iron ore (see page 144) .
Disseminated Minerals
Quartz.    -Quartz  is   an  essential   mineral  of  all   granites .                    It
seldom  occurs  in granites  in large grains,     but usually in grains  no
larger  than peas.        It can be identified by its glassy appearance.
Feldspar.              Feldspars of  various  kinds occur in both the granites
and  the  diorites,     and also  in the dikes.      The  common feldspar  in
the  granites  is   orthoclase,     which  is  usually  white,     though  some-
times pink or greenish.            The diorite  contains a plagioclase feldspar,
though in  such small grains that it  is  very hard to  see them.         The
porphyritic dike,     described  on page 140,  contains large crystals  of a
plagioclase  feldspar known as
Hornblende.                    Most  of  the  granites  contain  hornblende;           it   is
the black mineral which is  scattered through the rock.          Care should
be  taken  not  to  confuse  hornblende  with  another  black  mineral,
biotite.             The latter  is   flaky,     and  can  easily  be  scratched  with  a
knife,       or  separated  into  layers,        whereas  hornblende  cannot.             It
occurs  also  as  thin  needles  in the diorite.
Muscovite.                               White mica.                  This is  found only sparingly in Wey-
mouth.               As far  as  I  know,      it   occurs  only  as  small  scales  in  the
aplite.
Biotite .     -   Some of  the granites  are characterized by the presence
of the mineral biotite  instead  of  hornblende.             On West Street  the
granite  contained  biotite   crystals   half  an  inch  or   more  across.
These were  exposed during some blasting  eight years  ago.
 - 163 - 
THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH                 155
Apatite,         Titanite  and  Zircon.  -These  three   minerals   are   all
present  in  granite,    but  in  microscopical  grains.         Zircon  can  oc-
casionally  be  seen  with  the  naked eye,     especially  from  the  dark
granite at the crest of the hill west of Lovell's  Corner on Washington
Street.               It  occurs in small honey-colored  grains.

THE  WEYMOUTH  SPHINX1
The Weymouth Sphinx is  the  name that  has  been  given  to  a
notable facial outline to be seen upon the celebrated glacial  boulder
between  Essex  and  Middle  Streets,      Weymouth,       Mass. ,      known  as
" House  Rock, "  and the following  verses  are  offered  for  publica-
tion at the repeated  request  of  some of  those  who have  heard  or
read them.                JOHN J.   LOUD.
BERLIN,         GERMANY,   Nov. 23,    1893.
MY DEAR MR.      LOUD:   - I  was very much interested  in your letter  that came
yesterday.          It  is  more than an interesting  fact  that  you have discovered -it
is  remarkable.            I  am anxious to  know if  the face can be as distinctly  seen  with
the naked eye,      as  with  the photographic  condensation.           It  must be,    of course,
that the profile would appear to  the greatest  advantage at  certain times of the
daywhen the lights  and shades are right.       Have you ascertained what these times
are?  Does the face look north or east,  or what is  the direction?   Would the photo-
graph suffer  an enlargement without lessening  the  illusion?
I have written some lines upon the subject,   as you requested,    and have dressed
the facts up in an imaginative imagery,   somewhat in the manner of Dr. Holmes'
"Broomstick Train," or his  legend of the Roxbury Pudding Stone.
It  seemed a pleasant thought to associate this " Lady of the  Fields " with the
"Old Man of the  Mountain" and to  describe the contending forces  of heat  and
cold in the prehistoric glacial  and thermal changes,    as a battle in the mountains
and the clouds.        If it pleases you,   and seems worth while,    it  might be of interest
to print it  in the " Gazette, "  with a reproduction of one of the best  photographs.
Do with it  as you judge best.
OLIVER  HUCKEL.
THE HOUSE  ROCK  IS  ANOTHER SPHINX
The president  of  the  Weymouth  Historical  Society,     Mr.  J.   J.
Loud,        in   1893,      made the  interesting  discovery.         He had  asked
one of his  sons  to photograph for him the great  glacial  boulder on
Essex Street,     and one of the photographs  revealed what had prob-
ably  hitherto  been  unnoticed,                 a great  face  in  the  rock.        Later
photographs  taken for  the purpose showed it  with still  greater  dis-
tinctness.          It will be seen from the cut above to be a strong womanly
face,     and some seem  to  see  in  it  a decided  resemblance  to  Queen
Victoria.
It  is  easy  to  imagine the great  bulk behind the face,    as  in  the
Egyptian  sphinx,   to be the visible  portion of  a partly buried  lion .
The sphinx  of  Egypt is  about five  thousand years  old.         It  was
carved in the earliest  dynasty of those kings who are known as  the
pyramid  builders.         It  is  curious  to  meditate  on  what must  be  a
fact,    that this newly discovered sphinx,    a  carving by natural forces ,
is   a  thousand  thousand  years  still  older,     for  it  came here  in  the
glacial  period which scientists  have estimated  was several  millions
of years  ago.             If  such  a fact  seems  incredible,      read  some  of  the
1Reprinted from the Weymouth Gazette,   issues of April 30 and May 21,    1897.
 - 166 - 
158                          THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
late works  on the  glaciers,     such  as  Professor  Wright's,     on  " The
Ice Age of North America. "
This  rock  is  igneous,     or  fire  rock,     like  the  mountains  themselves
which were largely  formed  and  upheaved by volcanic  fires .             This
peculiar  variety  of  rock  has  been  identified  as  belonging  to  some
of  the White Mountain rock of New Hampshire,    so that this  great
stone,     perhaps torn from a mountain cliff by the ice sea,    may have
made  quite  a  long  journey  on  the  back  of  the  glacier  before  it
found its  present resting place.
THE LADY OF  THE  FIELDS.
(A Parable  of  the  Sphinx- like  Glacial  Boulder in the Weymouth Fields .)
Five thousand years ago on Egypt's sands
Amonarch of the earliest dynasty
Gave haughty orders  to his  myriad slaves
To swarm about a massive block of stone
And,   with the clanging might ofarm and iron
Carve out  a royal image in the rock.
The royal word was law.            The slaves obeyed.
Year after year the desert heard the sound,
The dull and ceaseless clinking on the stone.
Slaves died and slaves  were born.          But still  the  sigh
And groan of chisel and the hiss of scourge
Were wrought into the patient mass of stone,
And forth there came a marvel to the world
Aroyal image in the royal stone,
Awoman's face upon a lion's  form,
A suffering patience in surpassing strength,
An image that should breast the shocks of time.
And rest eternal in the whirling sands.
A seer of the mysteries of life,
Aholder of the secrets of the dead,
Aguardian of those royal pyramids,
The tombs of swarthy Cheops and his race.
But what of this,    another rock-wrought Sphinx,
Ruder in  image for  a western world,
This woman's face and lion's  shaggy form
That rests  in massive strength in Weymouth Fields?
Take ladder,    climb the mighty granite breast,
And stand on tiptoe till thou touch the face;
Hold now thy patient ear close to the mouth,
That mouth of stone that  seems to whisper forth
The silent eloquence of all the past
Something of this,   perchance,    may come to thee.
Ahundred thousand centuries  earlier
Than Egypt's sphinx was born,    of myriad slaves,
(What ache of thought is in this stretch of time)
The mystic monsters of the realm of Fire
That swarm within the molten depths of earth
Black,     save the whirl of heavy fiery  glow,
Hadburst their prison with volcanic rage,
Andmade themselves a kingdom in the light,
Had reared with  massive force and master- skill
Alofty castle,    grouped of mountain heights,
Resplendent in the gleam of precious stones.
Fine-wrought within their forges'     shimmering heat.
This massive castle,     towered with many summits,
 - 167 - 
THE  WEYMOUTH  SPHINX                       159
unheard;
Should be the fortress  of the race of Fire
And lord it  over all  the realms of earth.
The race of Fire was jubilant in strength;
Theirmyriadswrought their tasks unseen,
They winged their  flight  in vapors of the air,
Orgrovelled inthe molten depths of earth;
And here within their  stronghold of the mountains,
With eager homage and supreme devotion,
They throned aloft  a noble king and queen,
Born of themselves,    and of the mountain granite
That they had wedded in  a fiery  love.
Splendid and noble were the king and queen
And held high revel in the lofty halls
Whose many turrets pierced the roofing  sky.
They showed their granite birth by massive forms,
Royal in feature and of royal calm,
And yet  from out the eyes there seemed to glow
The glory of their flaming hearts of fire,
And when he looked with kingly grace toward her,
It  seemed as if his eyes were purpling sunrise
That found in hers a sunset,    crimson-gold.
Thus were the sovereigns of the realm of Fire
Who dwelt in glory in the mountain heights.
Cycles of ages passed.        The myrmidons,
Whowrought themagic of the realm of Fire,
Had filled the changeful earth with wondrous deeds.
And still  supreme within their  mountain halls,
High- throned,     reposed the sovereigns of the Fire.
The sweet sun kissed the blushing mountain- mist
And gave them aureole crowns of rainbow light ;
The strong-winged winds took up their mountain- harps
And sang the glories of the realm of Fire,
They lauded high their noble King and Queen,
They shouted of their powers and their might,
With harp and voice they gave a sovereign blast,
And roared defiant challenge to the world.
Sudden outpealed the trumpets of the north,
Distant at  first,   but louder now and fierce.
The challenge had its  answer.       And a host,
That long with envious eyes had seen aloft
The mountain-towers and flaming flags  of light ,
Bore down upon them from the frozen seas.
Onward they came in glittering  array,
The serried armies of the realms of Frost.
Clad in the heaping snows they marched,
With waving banners of the ice-cold  mists,
With spears and axes of great  icicles,
With mighty cannonade of giant hail.
Earth trembled as the countless  host came on,
The mountains shivered as the icy hordes
Clomb its  steep sides  and stormed the castle walls,
Andwhen,   with front unchecked,   they met
The red-hot swarms that from the castle rushed,
Then all  the air grew thick in vaporous cloud
There,    where the fierce primordial  passions  strove
And stormy waged the elemental war.
Sudden from lofty towers of  mountain peaks
Athousand bolts of lightning hurled themselves,
And loud the thunders roared from height to height .
 - 168 - 
160                         THE  GEOLOGY  OF  WEYMOUTH
Long,      long was fought that battle in the clouds,
And at the last the myrmidons of Frost,
The countless  icy hordes from out the north,
Had conquered,    and the vanquished hosts  of Fire
Had fled  far  south in desperate confusion,
Or sought  again the molten depths of earth.
All but the king and queen,                    too great for  flight
And born of fire  and granite on the earth,
The hidden fiery  depths were not for them -
Two royal  captives in their royal halls.
The hosts of Frost in savage mockery,
Fast  to  a frowning cliff  with mystic chains,
Enslaved the grand old king of fiery hosts.
Aprisoner  forever in those halls
Where he had ruled and revelled ages long.
And as he saw the fulness of his shame,
The glorious light  outfaded from his  eyes,
And all his face was passionless and cold,
Just as the granite that around him closed.
They shouted as they saw his  silent  woe.
See,   the triumphant standards of the snow
Still  to  this  day are waving on the heights,
And gone all  trace of halls  and hosts of Fire.
Cold are the  mountains now and called in truth
White Mountains,     and one sees the prisoned King
" The Old Man of the Mountains, "  named of men.
They shouted as they left  him in his woe.
They shouted as  they siezed his  noble queen ,
Who,    like her  lord,    was stricken  still  and cold,
And tore her fiercely  from his  lonely side.
Aloft  they bore her on their  myriad arms
Down the steep mountain paths and to the plains.
Withglittering spears of ice in triumph raised,
Onwith resistless  might and hoarsest  shouts,
They bore her,    captive in their icy arms ;
At last  they halted and encircling  round,
They loosed her,     and she rested,    great  and calm,
Here in the fertile  stretch of Weymouth fields
Here within hearing of the murmurous sea.
But now in the low surges  of the  sea,
They heard the deep defiance of new foes,
And leaving in the  fields  the royal  queen,
In captive chains of  mystic witchery,
Onward they rushed and all the countless host
Forever vanished in the engulfing  seas.
And here upon the lowly Weymouth Fields
She sits  in  exile ,    proud and nobly calm,
Agranite queen,   an elder  mightier Sphinx,
The mystic spell still  broods upon her brow
And never may she seek her mountain heights
Where mourns in solitude her royal lord.
But here  she sits  in  silent  wonderment :
A seer of the western  march of empire,
Aholder of the hopes,     of  sunrise born,
Aguardian,    not of deserts,     but of life,
And called of men,    " The Lady of the Fields .  "
OLIVER  HUCKEL.
Nov. 22,     1893.

THE STONE  SPHINX  AT  WEYMOUTH
Men call thee " The Sphinx! "  O,      bowlder gigantic!
Halfwoman,    half lion,  majestic and vast.
Wert thou wrought by some giant  in rage fierce and frantic
'Midst the ice and the floods  of the aeons long past?
Mencall thee "An Alien! " O wand'rer erratic!
Thy face and thy form,   they are  strange to  this  clime.
Perhaps from some mountain of grandeur emphatic
Far off thou wert brought,   in the dawning of time.
These scars on the face and these cuts and these seamings
Tell of tempests and storms when fierce lightnings were hurled
But patient forever in wonderful dreamings
Thy great eyes look out in the face of the world.
How strange was the world!    What marvellous changes !
From the ages of ice to the ages  of heat
Tillglacier-bound vales and ice-glittering  ranges
Transformed,    smiled with verdure,   -all  earth bright and sweet
Then the gay flowers were fragrant and blooming so fairily.
For the warmth of all  life  was as heavenly good
And the insects and bees and the birds sang so merrily
And the foxes and deer roamed free through the wood.
Then later the red man  -fantastic and savage.
Oft peered at thy still  face with half- frightened glance.
He held thee for  some dread mysterious image
And sought for  thy favor in wildest war- dance.
Still  later  the white men from far o'er the waters,
ThePilgrims and Puritans sought thy rich  fields;
And here 'neath thy shadow reared brave sons and daughters
And taught them the wisdom the storied past yields.
But thou speakest never -what e'er the world sayeth.
Mysterious still!     Grim Sphinx of grey stone,
No motion or word thy dark secret  betrayeth
Till the ages are past and thou standest alone.
EAST  BRAINTREE,      MASS.
HELEN H.  B.   HOBART.

THE  FIRST  INHABITANT
(An Erratic)
I.
While geologic cycles  rolled
And earth was ploughed by glaciers cold,
On mammoth ice- craft,    pond'rous load,
A mighty Sphinx to Weymouth rode.
Where Mastodon and Mégathère
Prowled hungry from each horrid  lair
Serene she sat nor deigned one look
To beast  or  reptile.         But the book
Of Fate and Prophecy she read
With steadfast  eye and upraised head.
And here she sat and here her face
Prefigured Adam's unborn race
Ere yet for  man the earth was fit.
II.
Grown gray with years  she watched alone,
A peerless  Sphinx of  bowlder stone,
Whilepunyman with drill  and wedge
Wrought sister- shape from Egypt's ledge.
The sunrise song of Memnon's lyre,
The blithesome trills  of feathered choir,
The war- whoop shrill  from ambush line,
She noted all  but gave no sign.
Still  undismayed she reigns,    a Queen,
While empires rock and thrones careen ;
Nor anarchist nor crank she  fears
Nor reason finds for smiles or tears
She simply sits  and waits.
-JOHN J.   LOUD.
HOW TO  FIND  AND  SEE  THE  SPHINX
Leave  the  Braintree  and East Weymouth electric  at the  corner
of  Essex  and  Broad  Streets ;        walk  along  Essex Street  toward  the
south and soon the top of the great boulder will be seen,    not unlike
the  roof  of  a house,    rising  from the  field  on the left.
Having  reached  the  site,     station  yourself  between  the  barbed
wire  fence  and the  rock,     opposite  the center  of the  latter  and  as
near to  the  fence as  the  trees  will conveniently allow.
Follow  along  the  fence  toward  the  east,     watching  the  easterly
end  of  the  great  boulder and you will  see  the profile growing  into
shape.
When the  breast  begins  to  detach itself  from the  neck you  will
see  a  bolder  face  perhaps  but a less  perfect  profile.        Generally  the
face  shown herewith  will be accepted  as  the  more satisfactory .

THE  FLORA  OF  WEYMOUTH
By SARAH  E.  BRASSILL
Shall  we say  at  once  that  the  flora  of  Weymouth is  that  of  a
New  England  coast  town,     and  so  smooth  the  way for  the  often
quoted  statement  that  every  old  resident  of  the  town  indorses :
' And when  I  had considered  more seriously  of  the  beuty  of  the
place with all  her  faire  endowment,     I  did think  in  all  the  knowne
world it  could not be parall'd.           For so many groves of planes,     sweete
crystall  fountaines  and  cleare  running  streams  that  twine  in  fine
meanders  through the meadows.  "
Tree and flower  and lichen  are  not less  interesting  because  they
grow  also  elsewhere.          Their  charm  lies  in  their  abundance  and
distribution  and grouping .
The plant  life  of a place is  closely connected with the geography
and the geology of that place.         A botanist includes  in his  marks
of  identification  of a species  the habitat.          Because the  surface  and
soil   of  Weymouth are  so  varied,    the plant  life  is  correspondingly
various .              Rocky ridge  and  swamp,    plain  and meadow,      riverbank
and  seashore,      barren  pasture  and  fertile   meadow  have  each  its
own forms  of  vegetation,     changing  with  the  changing  season,      re-
appearing  each year in  their  season.
Had the  surface  been  more uniform,    more readily  adaptable  to
any one form of exploitation,    much of  its  early charm would have
been long ago cultivated  away.          As it  is,    one has to go but a short
distance  back from  the  homes  that  border  the  old  roads  to  find
much the same scenery  that  the  early settlers  found.        Trees  such
as  sheltered  the  first  log  cabins,    fruits  the  same as  those  that  eked
out  the  settlers'     scanty  food  supply,    herbs  like  those  from which
simples  were then brewed,     all  still  abound.
The roads wind along  avoiding  the ledges  on the one hand and
the  too  wet footing  near  lake  or  river  on  the  other.         From  the
roadway one looks  off  to  a  horizon fringed with trees,    usually oaks .
Sometimes,      when  the  road  climbs  a  hill,      a wayside  elm  is   seen
overtopping  the  oaks;     and  again,    when it  dips  into  a  valley,     the
nearer  pines  are thrown into relief against the sky.        Woodland has
been  cut  over  and  wood  fires  have  done  their  part  in  destroying
the  primitive forests.             Level  stretches  had  been  cleared  for  farms
and  meadows.           A few pastures have grown up to  brush  and a new
growth  of  trees  has  replaced  what was  destroyed,     making it  true
now  (as  it  was  three  hundred years  ago)    that  the  place  is   " very
pleasant  and healthful,                               and  is   well  timbered and hath  good
store  of  hay ground. "
...
 - 172 - 
164                           THE  FLORA  OF  WEYMOUTH
Oaks  predominate  on  the  ledges,                  red  oak,       white  oak,      scrub
oak,    chestnut oak, -and seedlings that it would be hard to  identify.
On the plains  the pine  that bears  the  same name as  the  town is
abundant.             There were giant pines in the earlier days,   as old stumps
still  show.              There are  still  several pine groves carefully  tended and
increasing  in  beauty with  every year.             There are scattered  single
trees  that  somehow  escaped  when others  around  them were  cut,
and,       growing  in  the  open,    have  developed  into  handsome  speci-
mens.               There are  new growths  (chance sown or set  out)   that well
keep up the succession.
Formerly  wood- cutting  was  a regular  winter task.           Every  well-
equipped  farm  included  a  woodlot  from  which  the year's  supply
of  fuel  came.             The best  of  these lots  furnished  lumber,      and  the
winter cut of pine furnished spring  work for  several  mills .
The cut  is  smaller  now in  size  and quantity,   although  hauling
logs   to  the  mill  to  be  cut  into  box  boards  is   still   done  each
spring.
There  are  red  maples  bordering  the  meadows and white  cedars
in the swamps.           There are red cedars in the upland pastures mingled
with white birch  and pitch  pine.        There are elms  along  the main
highways.                  Norway  and  white  maples  and  ash  trees  shade  the
newer  streets.           Some of  the  old  trees  have been  cut  away in  the
interest  of  safe  travel.         Shorter- lived  trees  have been set  where a
growing  population  has resulted  in the breaking up of large  land
holdings into smaller properties.       Still, one can judge approximately
the age of a street by its  overhanging foliage.
There are  hillsides  grown up to  beech.            There are willows  along
the  river  and by the lakes.            There is  at  least one hemlock-covered
hill .                 There  are  stray  tupelos  and  numerous  aspens  and  button-
woods  and  hickories,    yellow  and  gray  birches  and  wild  cherries
and all  the  long  list  of  native  bushes  and shrubs  that  make the
New England woods so lovely .
Wherever  homes  have  been  long  established,     trees  other  than
native  are  sure  to  be found,  -   Norway spruce and  arbor vitae  set
to  break the force of the  north winds ;     apple and pear  orchards ;           a
tulip  tree ;          a  copper beech ;        a row of  Lombardy poplars.
On the  newer  " house lots "  trees  are now left  in the  process  of
clearing,     and new trees  are set,    doing away entirely with the " land
boom" effect.
These  trees  shade  home grounds  individual  in  their  treatment
and harmonious in their expression  of order and thrift  and love  of
growing things.              Tiny grass  plots  alternate  with  larger  ones  edged
with  barberry or privet hedges.          Woodbine and honeysuckle shade
porches.             Grape  vines,      with  main  stems  thick  as  the  trunks   of
small trees,     cover arbors ;        trumpet vines hold out big blossoms from
old  trees  and fences,   inviting all the humming birds in the neighbor-
hood.             Trim  flower beds  edge  trim  walks.        Shrubs  border   the
grounds and frame the houses ;        hollyhocks grow against the fences.
Everywhere  are  signs  that  the  people " love  not only the  love  of
 - 173 - 
THE  FLORA  OF   WEYMOUTH                   165
flowers  and the  sight  of  them and  the growing  of  them and the
picking of them and  the  arranging of them,    but also  inherit  from
Father  Adam a natural  relish  for  tilling  the ground  from  which
they are taken and to which they shall return.
a
There  are  grounds  that  merit  special  mention:         a  lovely  rose
garden  on  Commercial  Street,      and  another  at  North  Weymouth ;
an  informal  garden  shielded  from  wind  and dust  by  tall  shrubs
which  enclose  a  wide,     tree-shaded  lawn  and  form  a  background,
for  a charming  succession  of  blooming  things  new  and  old,
garden always  fragrant,     always  colorful  and a source  of delight  to
owner and  to  those  who  are  fortunate  enough  to  be  among  her
many friends ;       a garden  in  which  a rock  ledge  meets  one side  of
the lawn and protects  the  early  bulbs  that  creep  up in  its  warm
shadow;     a garden in which a wistaria clothes the long front  porch
and drapes  the house to the top of the  second  story  windows ;          a
lovely colonial  garden  around a colonial  cottage  where  the  walks
are  box-bordered  and  the  green  and  white  gateway  sets  one  to
imagining the beauties beyond it .
A garden  now  largely  a  memory was  that  tended  by  Abigail
(Smith)  Adams,    whose name has been chosen for the new women's
dormitory  at  M.  A.  C.  as  being  that  of  the woman most  closely
associated  with  the  early  agriculture of  Massachusetts .
There are many of these little gems of gardens scattered  all  over
the town.         There are many more beginning  to be,    and there are  in
places  of  older  gardens,    outlasting  the homes of  which  they  were
once a part,     clumps of lilac  spreading  and flourishing,    inviting  by
their   fragrance  the  childish   pruning  that  renews   their   youth;
bouncing Bets along  the  roadside,    descendants  of the  plants  whose
leaves were so  useful  to  the early  housewives in  scouring the deal
tables;      cinnamon roses  and clove pinks,   spicy forerunners  of more
modern varieties .
lavender
There are  " old-fashioned "  flowers  in many gardens,
and  honesty  and mullein  pink.         There  are  several  " old-fashioned
gardens "   in  the  making,     and  the  pleasant  neighborly  custom  of
exchanging seeds  and cuttings  and roots of this  and of that abides
still  with us.
Florists  find  the town a good one to  locate  in.           One nursery  is
taxed to its  full capacity.        One dahlia and two gladiolus  specialists
are here,   and our peony specialist,   the late George Hollis,   known and
honored by his neighbors for his  charming personality,    was known
everywhere among growers of  that flower for  his  skill  as  a grower
and as an originator of  new varieties.
In  a  town  of  permanent  homes,     the  home  vegetable  garden
flourishes,     large  or small according  to  the  amount of land  and time
available for  it,    but always a matter of  pride  and a source of much
satisfaction.
There are  a  few larger  gardens,    business  propositions  for  whose
output  there  is   a good  market  locally  and  in  near-by cities   and
summer colonies..
 - 174 - 
166                           THE  FLORA  OF   WEYMOUTH
Land not  so  well  adapted  to farming is  ideal for fruit  growing.
Small  orchards,    largely  apple  orchards,     are  an established  part  of
the  homesteads.            There  is  one  seedling  apple,    the  property  of  a
Weymouth man,      which  has  associated  with its  name " Penelope,"
a bit  of  local  folklore.          Larger  orchards  just  coming into  bearing
are  ready  to  take the places of some of the picturesque gnarled old
patriarchs  that  still  make apple-blossom  time  here  a  thing  to  be
remembered.                Small  fruits,      especially  strawberries,     are  grown,     re-
placing the wild  ones whose hiding places  are  known to  a favored
few.
Interest  culminates  in  the  annual fair  in  September.        That this
fair  has  outlived  all  other  fairs  in  the  county tells  its  own story,
and proves,      if  proof be needed,    that  our townspeople " sette  great
stoore by theyr gardiens.  "
The overflow  of  interest  results  in the pretty  parks  and greens
and squares in town;       in  the  well- kept grounds of public buildings ;
and in  the  attractive  school  and church  grounds.
The  strips  and  plots  of  land lying  between  the  home grounds
and the  woods  or  the  water are  rich  in  plant life.          On the  ledges
lichens   paint   colorful   impressionist   pictures,       and  saxifrage   and
columbine and corydalis  find foothold in the cracks and crowd the
tough  little  polypody fronds.          Near by are the  upland  pastures,
home of the early everlasting and the sturdy little  cinquefoil,     later
fragrant  with  bayberry  and  sweetfern.            Here,     too,    grow  the  low
goldenrod  and the  stiff- leaved  aster,     covering the  fields  in  fall  with
cloth- of- gold  embroidered  in blue.       If the  underlying  rock is  near
enough  to  the  surface  to  make healthy  pockets  of soil  here,   these
pastures  are  overgrown  by berry  bushes  and known to  pickers  for
miles  around.              Once  " free  for  all "  these  berry  pastures  are  now
becoming  valuable  private  property  from  which  trespassers   are
warned by  the  rather  gruesome  sign,      " Private  Berrying  Ground.
Keep Out.   "     Down in the swamps cat- tail  rushes shelter a variety
of   orchids   and  orchid- like   plants.             Under  the  pines  the  lady's
slipper   blooms  with   Indian   pipes   and  wintergreen.                On  well-
drained woody hillsides the arbutus hides,    and in sunny open spots
hepatica  grows.
The meadows are wonderful hunting grounds.       Spite of care,    the
best  ones  are  sprinkled  with  buttercups  and  daisies.                 The  fresh
meadows  are  gemmed with  marsh  marigold  in  spring;     then  pale
blue  with  violets  and  iris ;       yellow  with  loosestrife  and  seneca  in
summer,      and bordered with joe-pye weed and thoroughwort in  the
fall.           The salt  marshes gleam red with samphire in autumn.          Along
the river  cress  and forget-me-not thrive  and the lily-pond  is  white
and  fragrant  in  June,       blue  and  white  with  pickerel   weed  and
arrowhead  in  August,    and  framed  in  the  lavender and old lace  of
aster  and wild carrot  in September.
Along  the  shore,     seaside  golden  rod  lifts   heavy  plumes,      and
marsh  rosemary  creeps  toward  the  beach.           Off  shore,    seaweeds
wave as  the tides come and go.
 - 175 - 
THE  FLORA  OF   WEYMOUTH                   167
The  stone  walls  that  still   separate  many of  the  pastures  are
overgrown and concealed by sumach and June berry and shadbush,
and these  in  turn  have been seized  upon by climbing  bittersweet
and  clematis  and  woodbine  and  wild  smilax,       to  the  joy  of  the
birds who find a refuge there.
A little  way out  from  the  centers  of  the  villages,      the  broad
thoroughfares narrow to country roads.
Earliest  spring  finds   the  spicebush  blossoming  there,      and  late
October  is   welcomed  by the  witch-hazel.            In  the  interval   have
appeared   successively   anemones   and   ferns,         early    buttercups
and white  violets,     star  flower   and  blue- eyed  grass   and  yarrow,
wild  rose  and  elderberry  and  black  alder,   -everything  that  the
books  list   as  common in  New England,    and some blooms  not  so
common.
There is  one locality where the yellow violet grows,    and at  least
one  place  where the fringed  gentian  is  found.          There  are  several
stretches  blue  with  the  wild  iris,    some specimens  of  which  show
color  markings  not yet  recorded.           There are long  lines  of cardinal
flower  by the  river.             The rare  and lovely  sabbatia,     both  the  pink
and the white variety,    grows  by the pond.             One spot  is  known as
"the  place  where  the  maiden- hair  grows" ;       perhaps  its   hollow  is
where the  fallen  plaster  of  an  old  home furnished  the  lime  that
made possible the germination of  some wind- sown spores.
There is   always  color  here,    the white of meadow- rue  and daisy,
the  green  of  fern,    the  purple  of  blossoming  grasses,     the yellow  of
dandelion.              There  is  fragrance  from  blossoming  maple  and  wild
bean and clethra.          There are sounds of wind in the beech and pine
and poplar  trees  overhead,     and of  bees in  the blossoms  underfoot.
There  are  things  to  nibble,     many of  them  if   one  turns  aside  to
follow   footpaths,   -checkerberry  leaves,       and  sassafras   root  and
sweet  cherry  bark,      elderberry  and  barberry,      mint  and  sweet  flag
and hazel nuts.
There are pictures  for  an  artist -of the river
You could trace (it)   through the valley,
By the rushing in the spring time,
By the alders in the summer,
By the white fog in the autumn,
By the black line in the winter -
of the cottage  roofs  peeping  out among pines on a hillside;        of  the
church  spires  rising  above  the  tree  tops;     of  loaded  hay  wagons
moving slowly toward home in  the late  afternoon.
One knowing  the  New England  writers  and  knowing  also  the
scenery  in  Weymouth could  find  here  illustrative  material  for  the
choicest   passages   of   our   poets,        for   whole   poems,                  Holmes'

for couplets or  stanzas

Whole chapters  from  Bradford Torrey's books could  have been
written about Weymouth,   as,   indeed,    many of them were:       " Flowers
and Folks;   "    "A November Chronicle; "    " In  Praise of Weymouth
Pine; "   "An Old  Road "  (known to all  old  residents) ;     " My Real
Estate",(a bit of land still  taxed to his  heirs) .
One could quote from his writings  endlessly,   and to get the best
descriptions  of Weymouth bird and plant life  one must read Brad-
ford Torrey.
Two there are who sense the full  beauty of a place, -he who sees
it  for  the  first  time,    as did Thomas Morton,   and he who has grown
up in  intimate sympathy with it,    as did  Bradford Torrey.
Just  a New England coast  town,    but " in all  the knowne world
it  could not be parall'd.  "
