Jan.  26,       1911 ,      and  the  parish  transferred  its  property  and  duties
to  the church Jan.  9,    1922,    just one hundred and ninety- nine years
after  the parish  was established  as  the  First  Precinct.
The  old- fashioned  big  stoves  in  the  meeting- house  and  chapel
have  recently been replaced with a modern heating  plant,    and the
Ladies'          Benevolent  Society  have  had  a new  kitchen  and  parlor
finished  off in their annex.         The interior of the meeting-house is   to
be  renovated  at  considerable expense,     for  which funds  are  already
pledged.
In addition to  the Joseph Loud Fund,    the church has received  a
number  of  small  funds  from  various  donors,      the  income  of  most
of which has  by vote  of  the  church  been  made available  for  the
benefit  of needy persons in  the parish .
All  the old  records  of  the  church  and  also  of  the  parish  have
been placed in  the care  of  Tufts  Library.
THE SECOND  Church,     OLD  SOUTH
Before the close of the seventeenth century settlers had established
their  homes here  and there  in  the  south  part  of the  town.                The
long distances from the  meeting-house,    in  some instances  five  and
six  miles,      and the  rough,    ungraded ways,    scarcely  better  than  the
aboriginal  trails,     made it  a wearisome journey  for  those  who  at-
tended  church  services,      and well-nigh  impossible  for  women and
children.             When  Rev.   Peter  Thacher  left  the  pastorate  in  1718,
amidst  great  disaffection,     it   seemed  to   these  South  Weymouth
people  that  they  were  numerous  enough  and  ought  to  withdraw
and  form  a  separate  church  that  would  be  more  accessible  and
more harmonious.
A year  or  two later  some of the leading  citizens  agreed  together
to  secure  a central location  and erect  a  meeting- house.            The place
selected  was  at  Great  Plain,    now  called   Columbian  Square,       on
land of Jacob  Turner.         Here  they  erected  the  first  meeting-house
in  South Weymouth.
During the years  1722 and 1723,    it  seems that preaching services
were held in  the  new house with more or less  regularity,     according
as  arrangements  could  be  made by the  proprietors  for  preachers
and for  necessary  expenses ;       but there  was  no  regular  organization
that would have been legally  sustained  or  recognized.
To establish  a  church  and  be responsible  for  the  support  of  a
minister,     it  was  necessary  to  secure  a  special  act  of  the  General
Court.            A petition  was prepared  by John Vining  and thirty- eight
others  and brought before  the  May session  of  the  General  Court
in  1722,    praying  that a precinct  might be set  off  with  the line  of
division two miles northward from their  new meeting- house.             This
incurred  the  opposition  of  the  north  part  of  the  town,     where  a
committee was chosen  to  use  every  proper  means  to  prevent  the
division.              The General  Court  sent  a special  committee to  investi-
gate  the   situation.          This  committee  reported  favorably   at   the
 - 242 - 
234              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
August Session,     but  final  action was not taken  until June 5,     1723,
and then  the  Second,     or  South,       Precinct  was set  off.         On June 21
the  first  meeting  was  held  and  the  necessary  officers  were  chosen.
At a  meeting  in  July,      Mr.  James  Bayley  of  Roxbury was given  a
First meeting-house in South Weymouth.          Built in 1723
(From an engraving in an old punch bowl,  brought from England by D. Rogers)
call  to  the  " ministerial  office "   at  a  salary  of  £76.             One  hundred
and  thirty  pounds were allowed him for  a settlement.
But  a  church  had  not  yet  been  formed.           The Second  Precinct
having  now  become  an  established  fact,     the  people  remaining  in
 - 243 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          235
the  First  Church ceased their  opposition  and graciously  assisted  in
forming the new Second Church.          The pastor,     Rev.  Thomas Paine,
prepared  a  church  covenant  that  was  acceptable   and  took  the
leading part in the work of organizing.           This was on Sept.  18,     1723.
There  were  ten  members  besides   Mr.  Bayley,      to  whom  they
voted  to  extend  a call  as  the  precinct  had  already  done.               The
ordination  took  place  September  26,     and  a  month  later  the  first
deacons  were chosen,                     Samuel Whitman and Jacob Turner.
Mr.  Bayley must have provided his  own parsonage,     and several
of  his  successors  must  have  done  likewise,     for  there  is   no  record
that  the  precinct,    or  parish,     ever  owned  a  parsonage  or  had  any
interest in one until 1851 .
Mr.  Bayley continued  as  pastor  until  his  death in  1766,       almost
forty- three years.         It was his  privilege  to receive  two hundred and
seven  persons  into  membership  in  the  church,     and  at  his  death
there  were  ninety-four  still  remaining.          In  the  year  1742  sixty-
seven joined the church on confession of faith,    a record  not equaled
since.            He was greatly  beloved by the people,    but the question  of
salary  was  always  a  matter of  worriment.           The precinct  insisted
upon regulating it from year to year,   partly because it was customary
and partly  because  of  the  fluctuating  values  of  money occasioned
by the  scarcity  of  " hard money, "  or  coin,       and  the  abundance  of
paper  money,    known  as  " old  tenor "   or  " lawful  money."    Some
years  the  salary  was  voted  as  " hard  money "  and some  years  as
"old  tenor, "  and in varying  amounts.
In  1729 he was voted  £10 in  wood,     and at least  twelve cords  of
wood were delivered at  the  parsonage annually after that.          During
the last nine years of his life,   Mr. Bayley suffered much from failing
health,    and the  pulpit  was often  supplied  by  others,      so  that  the
precinct  felt  obliged  to modify his  salary  accordingly,    paying  him
in full  only when he preached.           He died Aug.  22,     1766,    at  the  age
of  sixty- eight  years.
In  1738  the  meeting-house  was  repaired  and a  new  floor  laid ,
but the ownership of the building  remained with  the  original  pro-
prietors  until  1741.    That  year  the  following  record  was  entered
in the precinct book:
October  12,       1741.    At a meeting  of the  Second  Precinct  in  Weymouth legally
warned and convened,     Doctor  Nathaniel  White was chosen  Moderator.
Themajor part of the proprietors of the meeting house and land being present
at the meeting consented to give up their rights  of the meeting  house  and land
belonging to it  to  the  Precinct.
Entered by me,    John Pool,     Precinct  Clerk.
This  is   all  the  known documentary  evidence  of  the  passing  of
the title  of the greater  part ofwhat is  to-day called Bayley Green,
and the  street about it.
The same year  more  extensive  repairs  were  made at  a  cost  of
£109.          The following winter it  was voted " to sell places for pews.  "
For  these  over  £100 was received.          In  1752  it  was  voted  to  sell
 - 244 - 
236               ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
more places  for  pews,     to  be paid for in lumber within six  months,
or  after  that,    in  money.            Twenty- two places  were sold  at  auction
at  prices  ranging  from  £10  to  £62.              Thus  private  ownership  of
pews in the meeting- house  was established.
To  secure  a  successor  to   Mr.  Bayley,      ten  or  twelve  different
ministers  were  asked  to  supply  the  pulpit  during  the  next  two
years,       each  for  several  Sundays.         Finally  a call was given  to  Mr.
Simeon Williams  of  Raynham at  a salary  of  £73,     6s. ,     8d.  ,       and a
settlement  of  £133,      6s.      8d.
As he seemed not to be quite satisfied  with the call,   he was invited
to  an  adjourned meeting of the precinct  " to  see  what his  request
was. "     It  was  then  voted  to  add twelve  cords  of  wood yearly  to
his  salary,      " when he shall  marry and have a family. "
Mr.  Williams  answered  as  follows :
To the  Second  Parish  in  Weymouth,
GENTLEMEN:   - I    accept  your  invitation  to  the  work  of  the  ministry  and
expect a maintenance.
From your humble servant,
SIMEON  WILLIAMS.
He was ordained  Oct.  26,     1768.    The expense of  providing  and
entertaining  at  the  ordination was bid  off  at  auction for  £14,    13s.
6d.          by  Capt.         William   Holbrook.              The  ordination   sermon  was
preached by Rev.  Mr.  Smith of  the  First  Church.            Mr.  Williams
was  born  in  Easton,     and was graduated from New Jersey  College
in 1765.
Thus began the longest  pastorate yet recorded  in  the history  of
the  town,         and  one  of  the  most eventful.         The troublous  times  of
the Revolution and the years  of adjustment to  the new conditions
that followed it  brought difficulties,     vexations,    trials  and solicitude
to the church and its  pastor,    as well as spiritual blessings and growth
in  membership.             The question  of  maintaining  an adequate  salary
was  a  frequent  cause  of  unpleasant  discussion  and  perplexity  be-
cause  of great  and  frequent  fluctuations  in  money values  and the
inconstant  ratio  between coin  and paper currency.
In 1777  Mr. Williams felt the need of an increase  in salary,    but
did not get it.             The next year he presented  two or three different
plans  for  adjusting  the  payment  of  his  salary,     so  that  he  might
receive  the  equivalent  of the salary  received  at  his  settlement.               A
committee was chosen to  investigate  and recommend.
It  was decided  after  long  consideration,     that  £45 of  the salary
should be regulated by a comparison of the prices of labor in summer,
of beef and  pork in  November,      of  cheese  in  August,       of  corn  and
rye the first  of May,    and of wool and flax  the fifteenth of June,    the
year  he came,    with the going  prices  year by year.         A calculation
reported  in  December,       1779,      made the  salary  amount to  £1,439 ,
18s.   ,           1d.  ,            " lawful  money"   (paper) .            In  December,      1780,      it   was
£6,190,       19s.  ,     4d.            This  arrangement proved so  unsatisfactory  that
in  March,      1781,      it  was decided  to give  up regulating  the salary in
 - 245 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          237
that  way,     and  to  have  stand for  the  future  as  at  his  settlement ,
£73,       6s.   ,       8d.   ,       " hard  money, "  and this  agreed to  by  Mr.  Williams .
On account of " bodily infirmities, "  Mr.  Williams  asked in  1811
to  be relieved  of the work of the ministry,    to  be on half  pay and
to  have a colleague.         The parish,     however,      was  not  ready for  that
action,    but directed  that,    in case of his failure  to supply the pulpit,
a meeting of the parish be called  to  take  such  action  as  should  be
thought proper.          He kept on heroically,    contending with increasing
feebleness  of  body,   and persevered  through  the  cares  and  troubles
incident  to  the  War of  1812  until  1818,    and then he was provided
with  a colleague,   but not very long.        On May 31,     1819,     the  good
man passed  away.       He had been pastor for  nearly  fifty- one years.
Notwithstanding  all  the  trials  and  adverse  circumstances  of  that
of a long term,    a hundred and five  members were received into the
church.
Among the  many events of interest during  the  pastorate  of  Mr.
Williams,       there  should  be  noted  the  formation  and  development
of the church choir.          On Nov. 4,   1778,      a committee was chosen  to
consider  the  seating  of  the  singers  together.            The committee  re-
ported  that they " thought the front gallery was the most suitable
place. "    Thereupon it  was voted that the  singers  should  sit  there
for  a month,     " and if  it  makes no disturbance in the parish,     then to
continue. "    In  1788  Dea.       Samuel  Blanchard,       John  White  and
Thomas  Blanchard  were chosen " to  be choristers  with  the  liberty
of choosing as  many more as  the  singers  think  proper. "
It was decided in 1780 to have the constable warn parish meetings
by " setting  up notification  at the meeting house, "  and in 1795 the
fall   meetings  of  the  parish  were  ended  and  all  business  done  in
them referred  to  the  annual meetings held in  March or April.
For  the  purpose  of  procuring  a bell  for  the  meeting-house,       $70
was voted Oct.  21,    1788,    and Mr. John Tirrell,     Col.  Thomas Vinson
and Capt.       Eliphalet  Loud were chosen to  procure it.          The bell  was
brought from London by Capt.      Reuben Loud,     who is  said  to have
had $100 worth of silver cast  in it.           This was the noted silver- toned
bell that was in  use until  1865,   when it  became cracked while being
tolled  for the death of President  Lincoln.
But  the  most important  event  in  Mr.  Williams'      pastorate  was
the  building  of  a new meeting- house  in  1785.    In  March,       1783,      a
committee was  chosen  " to  draw  a  plan  of  a  meeting  house  and
agree on some method they think most proper and lay it  before the
parish at an adjourned meeting. "    In April the committee reported,
recommending  to  build  a house  eighty-eight  feet  long  and forty-
four feet wide,    and that a building  committee of  seven  be chosen
by written  ballot  to  have  full  charge  and  be  accountable  to  the
parish  for  the  whole  cost.        A sale  of  pews was  to  provide for  the
cost of  the house.
The report with accompanying plans was accepted and a building
committee chosen.       The new house was to  stand where the old  one
stood,     but  to extend back to  the boundary line  of the lot.           Against
 - 246 - 
238              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
the protest of one of the leading citizens,   it  was voted to pull down
the old  house  as  soon  as  may be,    and also  to  use  the  serviceable
material in  the  new one and to  sell  at  auction whatever remained.
The  new  house  was  completed  in  1785.     The  whole  cost  was
£780.                             Elaborate  specifications  that  are  on  record  show  that  the
new meeting-house  must  have been quite  a  notable  structure  for
those  times,      with  its  forty-four  windows  of forty  squares  each  of
seven-by- nine  glass,      and  its   outside  doors  with  eight  panels  and
Old South (Second Congregational)    Church.        Built in 1785
cased  according  to  the  Doric  order  of  architecture.            Pulpit  and
pews were  fitted  with  leaning  benches,      and  seats  and doors  were
hung with iron  hinges.         Six  turned pillars  with  capitals  supported
the  galleries .          The  building  was  used  without  material  change
until 1825.
About  the  year  1813  an  important  change  took  place  in  the
method of supporting the church.          Up to that time the whole pre-
cinct  had been  subject  to  taxation  for  the support of  the  Second
 - 247 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          239
Church;    but  thereafter  citizens  were  excused  from  that  support
upon  presenting  a  proper certificate  of  membership in  some other
religious  society.       During the next twenty years,    quite a number of
such   certificates   were  recorded,     especially  of  residents   who  for
some  reason  preferred  to  be connected with  the  old  First  Church,
the   Union  Society  of  Weymouth  and  Braintree,       the  Methodist
Church in  Scituate,      the  Baptist  Church in  Randolph,     or  the  new
Methodist  Church in East Weymouth.
Rev.  William Tyler of Attleboro,    a graduate of  Brown University
in  1809,     who had accepted  a colleague,     or junior  pastor,     with  Mr.
Williams  in  December,     1818,     was ordained  Feb.  24,      1819,      and  on
the  death  of  Mr.  Williams,      in  May,     became  the  regular  pastor.
His  parsonage was the house now standing  next south of Highland
Cemetery,     but it  was built by Mr. Tyler in  the shade of  the  great
elm  opposite Odd Fellows'     Hall,     and stood  there until  about  1860,
when it  was moved to its  present location.            It is  still  known as  the
" Old Parsonage. "
Mr. Tyler continued as pastor over twelve years,   and appears to
have  been  a  man  of  decision  and  energy.            During  his  ministry
forty- two  were  added  to  the  church.            In  1819  he  organized  the
Sunday school,      of which Noah Torrey,     Esq.  ,    was the  first  superin-
tendent.         He preached  a  centennial discourse  in  observance  of  the
first  hundred years  of  the  church.         He also  started  the  first  total
abstinence  society in Weymouth.          Through his  influence  the church
had a copy of  the original  church  covenant  prepared  and  passed
about for  the members to  make copies  for  themselves.
In 1824 the singers were requested to use occasionally the " Watts'
and Select  Hymns "  of  Dr.  Worcester,    and this book was in  use for
the  next  fifty years.           The singers  were also  allowed $50 with which
to  purchase instruments.
But it  is  not  to  be  assumed  that  Mr.  Tyler's  efforts  were  all
unanimously  endorsed  by the  church.           There  is   evidence  of  con-
siderable  opposition  to  him  during  a  large  part  of  his  ministry.
Not  only did  quite  a number transfer  their  membership to  other
parishes,     but  in  1826,      and again  in  1827,      votes  were  taken with
reference  to  asking  his  dismission  that  showed  quite  a  movement
against  him,     although far from successful.
In April,       1831,      the  church  asked  the  concurrence  of  the  parish
in calling a mutual council to consider the  expediency of dissolving
the pastoral relation.          The parish asked Mr. Tyler for  an explana-
tion  of  this request,     and then by a small majority voted to  concur
with the church.
Whether the  council  was  called  is  not  recorded,      but  in  October
Mr.  Tyler  asked  to  be released,    and after  hearing  his  reasons,     the
parish voted to comply.
In  1819  the  parish  chose  a committee  of  twelve  " to  invite  a
physician  to  settle with  us."     This  resulted  in  a formal call  being
extended to  Dr. Appleton  Howe,  who had just  completed his  pro-
fessional  studies and was not yet married.
 - 248 - 
240              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
An interesting event of lesser moment was the placing  of a stove
in  the meeting-house in January,    1822,    after a " heated "  argument.
That it  caused some disturbance,     was indicated by the calling  of a
special  meeting by request,   within  a month,    " to place a stove  and
funnel  in  the  gallery  and  wood for  the  season  and  a  person  to
tend it."
The purchase  of a hearse and also  a shed to put it in was voted
in 1825.
In spite of the loss of members and other untoward circumstances ,
a large  committee was chosen in  1822  to  consider  the  enlargement
of  the  meeting-house.          After  various  votes  taken during  the  next
two  or  three  years,     among them one  to  change the  pews  to  long
pews,      it   was decided  to  cut open the meeting-house and build  in
twenty feet,    making the width of the house  sixty-four  feet.                This
was done at  an expense of  $7,560,     of  which $5,918  came from the
sale  of  pews,      and the balance was assessed upon the parish.
In 1830 the  sexton's  duties  were put  up  at  auction  and bid  off
at  $10,        " attendance  or  service  at  funerals  and the scouring  of the
railing  in  front of the singers  not to  be included. "
By petition  of the singers  in April,    1832,     they were empowered
to  organize  themselves  into  a  society  and to  fill   vacancies  in  the
position of chorister.
The parish  also  provided  a lamp and lanterns  for  the  meeting-
house.
A successor to  Mr. Tyler was not secured for over a year,      though
several  candidates  preached  a number  of  Sundays  each.           In No-
vember,       1832,    a call was given to Rev. Charles J.  Warren of Boston,
at  a salary  of  $700.               He accepted  and was installed  Jan.  1,     1833.
He was educated at  Brown University  and was ordained at Attle-
boro in  1828.    His stay was very brief,    only a year and a half.             At
his  own request,    and much to  the regret of the people,     he was dis-
missed Aug.  13,    1834.
He was a strong advocate of temperance,    and was later employed
by the American Temperance Union for twenty years.          During this
pastorate  the  church adopted the following  resolution :
Resolved,      That  this  Church  will  use  in their  future  sacramental   occasions
such wine and such only,   if  such can be obtained,     as  is  believed to be the pure
juice of the grape,   in which no alcoholic liquor or other intoxicating and poisonous
substance has been infused.
In July,    1834,   the parish voted to  have a committee of one from
each  school district  to collect funds for  the  support of the gospel,
no one to  be held to pay his  subscription  unless  $550 be  so  raised.
This  appears  to  have  been  the  first  attempt  to  raise  money for
ordinary parish  expenses  otherwise  than by taxation.
It was nearly four years before another pastor was obtained,    and
they  were  years  of  serious   trial   and  division.          The first   trouble
came in connection with supplying the pulpit.      In accordance with
 - 249 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          241
custom,      when there was not  a settled  pastor  it  devolved upon the
parish  to  see that the pulpit was supplied.
The parish committee at the time was composed of men of strong
personal  views  quite  at  variance  with  the  prevailing  orthodoxy,
and they did not hesitate  to  declare that if  they had to supply  the
pulpit they would hire men more agreeable to their way of thinking.
Thereupon,     from February to April,    1835,    this committee employed
Rev.  Sylvanus Cobb,     a  noted Universalist minister of those days.
Nearly the whole church resented this  action and withdrew from
the  meeting-house  and  worshipped  in  Rogers'        Hall.              There  they
adopted the  name of  " Edwards Society "  and hired  preachers inde-
pendently  of  parish.             Over a hundred and twenty,    most  of  them
church  members,    withdrew their connection with the parish during
the  next fifteen  months.
A very few of the church members,    however,   continued to worship
in  the  meeting-house  and  to conduct the  Sunday school,     realizing
that   otherwise  the  parish  might  secure  the  formation  of  another
church  and so deprive those in  the Edwards Society of their prop-
erty  and rights.          For this  conduct the Edwards Society disciplined
them as  recreant to their church obligations,    but afterward forgave
them.
Meanwhile,       the  parish  committee having  been changed,      a  more
orthodox  supply was provided for the pulpit.         In April,   1836,     Rev.
Thomas C.  Biscoe was hired for  a year,     and in  February,    1837,     he
was invited  to become their  minister.          This  was the  action  of  the
parish  only.                   The parish  committee were instructed  to  use  all  fair
and  honorable  means  to  secure  Mr.  Biscoe,      and  if  it  was  found
strictly  necessary to  form a new church,    then the church members
still   worshipping  with  them were to  be  requested  to  take  proper
measures  to  bring it about.
Accordingly on March 25,     1837,   four church members requested
dismission  from  the  Edwards  Society   (the   church)     and  recom-
mendation  to  a  council  to  be called  by them  to  form  a  distinct
church to be connected with the Second Parish.          This  request was
declined.          Then they requested the church to join them in a mutual
council  to consider  the  question,    and this  they  agreed  to  do.             The
council  met April  17,     1837,     and recommended a delay  of  ten days
to  await  the  result  of  a  movement for  the  reunion  of  the  church
and parish.            If  nothing was done in  that time,     then  the request  of
the  petitioners  should  be  granted.         This  had a favorable  effect.
On April  21  the  church voted to  return  to  the meeting-house  as  a .
place of worship,   and on April 24 the parish voted approval of the
doings of the council.
Mr.  Biscoe declined  to  accept his  call  because  of  its  irregularity
in procedure and because  its  acceptance would be  apt  to  continue
" difficulties,    hard thoughts and feelings " and prevent the possibility
of uniting  on some other candidate.         A committee on pulpit supply
was instructed to  procure a  minister “ approbated after  the  Calvin-
 - 250 - 
242               ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
istic  order,  "   and the  next April  (1838)   Rev.  Jonas  Perkins,       Rev.
Lucius  Alden  and Rev.  Lyman Matthews were chosen to  be  that
committee.                Meanwhile over eighty men had rejoined  the  parish.
But now there was another serious  division.        Those in the parish
who held  liberal  views  were no longer  content  or willing  to  listen
to such strict  orthodoxy.          Within about a year after the reunion of
church  and  parish,      a  hundred  and  forty-eight  persons  withdrew
from  the  parish,    and most of them joined the Universalist  society
that had been formed.
The committee on pulpit supply soon recommended Rev.  Wales
Lewis,      and he was invited to become pastor.        He came from Maine
where  he  had been  educated and ordained,    and was  settled  Sept.
12,       1838.    He was a man of firm convictions  and was earnest in his
work.         He won the unshaken confidence of many,   and also acquired
the  cordial  dislike  of  others  through his  rigid  insistence  upon the
observance of church duties and unswerving devotion to  Calvinistic
doctrine.            So almost from the beginning of his nine-year pastorate
there  was  criticism,     opposition  and  serious  division.        Even  his
character  was  aspersed,      and it  became necessary  to  call  a church
council  to  investigate  charges.        Although  the  council  exonerated
him,       the  stigma  of  accusation  remained  to  the  detriment  of  his
influence  and the injury of the church.          The real  source of trouble
appears  to  have been  the widespread  spirit  of controversy of that
period,      and  the  refusal  of people who held to the right of freedom
in  belief to submit to the stultifying discipline imposed by a rigidly
Orthodox church.
At length,      in June,    1842,     a number of men who felt particularly
aggrieved,       held  a meeting  in  Rogers'      Hall and formed a religious
society for  the support of a new church.            Then they sent a request
to the Second Church to grant letters of transfer to certain members,
in  order that they might assist  in  forming a new church.
The  Second  Church  refused  to  do  this,     believing  that  such  a
movement  was  irregular,      not  called  for,    and harmful.        The new
society  and  the  aggrieved  church  members  then  sought  to  call  a
mutual council to consider the situation ;      but the church protested
vigorously  and refused  to  join  in  such  a council  or  to  respect  its
findings .              So an ex parte council was held and resulted in the forma-
tion  of  the  Union  Church  of  South  Weymouth,     Nov.  1,     1842 .
During the  next  two or  three years a  number of councils  were held
to  settle  matters  in  controversy,    but the Second Church kept aloof
as  much  as  possible,       and  would  neither  accept  the  overtures  of
ex  parte  councils  nor  enter  into  any  fellowship  with  the  Union
Church.
This trying condition continued for  several years,    until at length
those  considered  by  the  Second  Church  as  deserving  discipline
wrote  a joint  letter  of  acknowledgment of  their  irregular  conduct
toward  the  Church,     disclaiming  any wrong intent  and asking  for
forgiveness .               This  was accepted by the Second Church,    and there-
after there was due recognition and fellowship,  though it  has always
 - 251 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          243
been felt to be unfortunate that two churches so nearly alike should
be so near each other as to  offer a great opportunity and temptation
to  jealousy,     prejudice,   disparaging criticism and petty competition.
It  gradually  became  evident  that  the  interests  of  the  church
would be promoted by a change in the pastorate,    and on Nov.  1 ,
1847,        Mr.  Lewis was formally dismissed.          The parish  thanked him
for " the pungent and lucid manner in which he had uniformly dis-
coursed on the truths  of the gospel,"  and " bore willing  testimony
to  his  uprightness  of character as  a christian  and citizen.  ”
Notwithstanding  the  unfortunate  conditions  of  his   pastorate,
forty persons had joined the church.        Mr.  Lewis removed to Maine
where he served  as  a  pastor for  many years.
For a few months,     Rev. Joshua  Leavitt was employed to  supply
the pulpit,      and in  February,      1848,      an  attempt was  made to  give
him  a call,     but  it  was defeated,    and was followed  by a great de-
pression   regarding  the  future  of  the  church.            Soon,     however,       a
better state of feeling appeared,   for in the latter part of April thirty-
six men joined the parish,    and two weeks later the parish concurred
unanimously  with  the  church  in  giving  a  call  to  Rev.  James  P.
Terry.               Evidently Mr. Terry's  candidacy revived their  hopes.               He
accepted  and was installed July 6,   1848.    He was graduated  from
Amherst  College  in  1834 and was  ordained  at  Somers,      Conn. ,     in
1839.     His  genial  manner,     dignified   bearing,     tactful  labors   and
sound  preaching won the good-will  and  support  of  all,    and  a  new
period of prosperity followed.
To provide  parsonage for  Mr.  Terry,      nearly  forty  people  asso-
ciated  themselves,    under the name of the South Weymouth Parson-
age  Company,    in August,    1848,     and subscribed  cash  and  notes  in
$25  shares.                 With the  proceeds  a  parsonage was built  on land  of
Dr. Appleton Howe,     northwest of the meeting-house on Columbian
Street.
In April,    1851,   this  company donated their whole stock,   including
the  parsonage  and land,    to  the parish,   in  the form of  a parsonage
fund,      stipulating that the income only was to be used in the support
of  a " sound  orthodox  ministry"   of  the  type  of  Pres.      Jonathan
Edwards,        Dr.   Samuel  Hopkins,      Dr.  Bellamy  and  Dr.  Nathaniel
Emmons.           If  perverted  to  the  support of other doctrines,     then  the
whole fund should be forfeited and revert to the heirs of the donors,
or  to  a  new society that should support the required doctrines .
In  connection  with  Mr.  Terry's  call  it  had been voted  that  he
be allowed " one  or  two  Sabbaths  each  year for  needful  rest  and
relaxation,     on condition  that he supply the pulpit at  the  expense
of  the  Society,    and also  that he be allowed to consult his  health in
relation   to  a  third  service  on  the  Sabbath."    This  was  the  first
movement for  an  annual vacation  for  the  pastor,    but not  for  the
congregation.
During the  next  five  years,     nearly  sixty  men joined  the parish.
In  1850 a clock was placed in  the meeting-house for  the  first  time,
near  the  middle of one of the  galleries .
 - 252 - 
244             ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
The meeting- house  was again needing extensive  repairs,       and  in
April,       1853,      a committee was chosen to  consider  necessary  repairs
and also  the expediency of building  a new house.         In September it
was voted  unanimously to  build a new house.
The year  1854 was  nearly  all  occupied  in taking down the  old
house  and  building  the  new  one.            By  invitation  of  the  Union
Society,      the church worshipped in their house,   holding the Sabbath
services  at  9  o'clock in the morning and 4 o'clock in the afternoon .
The new house was located  as  far  north  and east of the old one
as  the  lot  would  permit,     and  some  additional  land  was  bought.
The building  was set  high  enough  to  admit of  a cellar  under the
whole  structure,     and  also  with  a view  to  a  more  pleasing  archi-
tectural  effect.             Furnaces in which to burn coal were placed in the
cellar.        The roof  was covered  with  slate.        Through the  efforts  of
Mr.  Terry  in  securing  special  contributions,    and  aided  by  gifts
from people in other parishes,    a clock was placed in the  tower.
The new edifice had a seating capacity of five hundred.           Through-
out  there is  evident the  finest  proportion and artistic detail,    and it
is  still  one of the noblest and most beautiful structures of its  type.
The total cost was about $15.500,   of which over $12,400 was realized
from the sale of pews,    and $973 was contributed by the  Ladies'     Aid
Society.              The new house was occupied in  1855.   The Union Society,
now having  occasion  to  repair their  house of worship,    was in turn
invited  to  worship meanwhile in the  new meeting-house.
In  1856 measures were taken to introduce congregational singing,
and in  1858  all  business  relating  to  singing and to  an organist was
referred  to  the parish  committee.         The next year the parish  com-
mittee  were instructed  to  hire  an organ  harmonium,   and to pay an
organist  not  over  $50.              For  the  congregational  singing,      Nason's
Congregational  Hymn and Tune Book was selected.          In August of
that year the ladies,    under the  leadership of Miss Florinda Grover,
secured  a  Holbrook church organ and placed it in the gallery at an
expense of about $ 1,500.          The first organist was Miss Alzira Packard,
and she  served most faithfully and satisfactorily for many years .
The bell having become cracked at the time of President Lincoln's
death,     in  1865,     it  was broken in  pieces  and incorporated in  a new
and larger  bell,     for  which $500 was expended.
Acommittee was chosen in  1866 to confer with the Union Society
with reference to uniting the two societies,   but no practical result was
accomplished.         Asimilar committee in  1868 succeeded no better.
Up to this  time,    the annual parish expenses had been met for the
most part  by taxation  of property,    and assessors  had been  chosen
annually  to  levy  the  parish  tax.           This  had been done  ever  since
the Second Precinct was established.          But now the ease with which
citizens  could  withdraw  from  the  parish  and  refuse  to  share  its
burdens  made it  more and more difficult  to  collect  enough for  the
needs  of  the  parish,    and frequent  arrears had to be met by special
voluntary efforts .
In  1866 it  was voted to tax the pews 10 per cent of their original
 - 253 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          245
valuation.                 This,     however,    was soon found to be impracticable,    and
in  1868 a committee was chosen to  solicit  $1,250  by subscription,
and  assessors  were  not  chosen.          This  change  proved  to  be  much
more  satisfactory  and was continued  for  many years.
In the spring of 1868  Mr. Terry was taken ill  and was granted a
six  months'         leave  of  absence;      but  he did  not  recover  his   health
sufficiently  to  return to  his  pastoral duties,    and in April,      1869,      his
resignation   was  reluctantly  accepted.           He had  served  faithfully
for  twenty years,   had received one hundred and fourteen into church
membership,      and  had  sustained  the  good-will  and  respect  of  the
church and the community.
A most cordial  invitation  of the Union Church to  worship with
them,    under the ministration of Rev.  Mr. Hayes,    during the illness
of Mr. Terry,      was accepted.
After Mr. Terry's resignation,  a committee on supply was chosen
and the church returned to worship in its own house.           Rev. Benjamin
Labaree,    a retired  clergyman,    was engaged to supply the pulpit for
about a year.
Meanwhile  resolutions  were  adopted  as  to  the  expediency  of  a
union  of the two churches,    and a committee was appointed  to meet
with  a similar committee of the Union  Church  and report  on  the
matter.              This  brought about a number of meetings and the formu-
lation of acceptable plans,   and a  union would have been effected if  a
misunderstanding had not developed which prevented further action .
Up to the end of Mr. Terry's pastorate there had been no regular
church clerks.               The church  records,     as  far  as  any were kept,    were
made by the ministers.
When there was  no  pastor,      a  clerk pro  tem.     was chosen  at  each
church meeting,  and he made record on loose  sheets  of  paper,     very
few  of  which have been preserved.          In June,      1869,      at  one  of  the
meetings  to  consider  the  union  of  the churches,      Henry  Dyer was
regularly chosen clerk,   and he continued to serve  until June,      1883,
when he declined  further service  and Edward Lewis  was  chosen  to
succeed him.
In  the summer of  1870  a  unanimous  call  was  extended  to  Rev.
George F. Stanton,    at a salary of $1,200 and the use of the parsonage.
A settlement  of  $200  was also  given  him.            He accepted  and  was
installed Oct.  27,      1870.   He was a graduate of Amherst College and
Bangor Seminary,    and had been  pastor  of  a  church  in  Gardner,
Mass.          He was most positive in his  opinions,   a clear,     forcible  and
ready  speaker,    and a self-denying,   faithful  worker.        His pastorate
extended  through  fifteen   years,     during  which  much  was  accom-
plished  to develop and strengthen the interests of the church.            One
hundred and ten became members of the church.
In June,     1872,     it  was decided to  build  a vestry at the rear of  the
meeting-house,    if   $4,000  could  be  raised  for  the purpose.       That
sum was  pledged within  two  weeks.        A building  committee  was
chosen,    and the next April a commodious  vestry  stood  completed
and  fully  furnished  at  an expense  of  about $4,800.
 - 254 - 
246              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
In  September,      1873,     there was  a  notable  observance of  the one
hundred and fifteenth anniversary of the organization of the church,
at which Mr. Stanton preached a historical  sermon,    and there were
addresses  by former  pastors  of  this  and of  neighboring  churches.
Aplan for making weekly payments of pledges for parish  expenses
was introduced in 1877 .
The parish  recommended a change of name in  1880 to  Old South
Congregational Society.
A row of  horse  sheds  was built in 1882 along the northerly  side
of  the  meeting-house,    and were used for  nearly forty  years.
About  1885  the Young People's  Society  of  Christian  Endeavor
was organized  as  a union  society by the young people of both the
Old South and the Union Churches.         Their meetings  were held  in
Clapp's  Hall.         After  a few years  it  was deemed  best  to  separate
into  two societies,     one to  be connected with each church .
In  1884  ladies  began  to  be appointed  upon the soliciting  com-
mittee  for  parish  expenses.              This  year  also  the  hiring  of  a solo
singer  for  the choir was begun.            Miss Lydia A. Torrey was engaged
at  a  salary  of  $150 a year,      and served  most acceptably for  a num-
ber of years.
Mr.  Stanton resigned  from the  pastorate in October,        1885.    He
removed  to  Boston  and  became a valued  member of  Park Street
Church.                 A successor  was  not  found  until  the  following  spring,
when a call  was extended  to  Rev.  Henry C.  Alvord,   then pastor of
the church in  Montague,    Mass.         He began his labors  in July and
was duly  installed  Sept.  15,    1886.    Mr. Alvord was a graduate of
Hartford  Seminary,      and  had  been  ordained  in  1879.    He was  a
man of  singular  devotion and quiet but strong  personal influence.
He made no enemies and won many friends,    though staunch in his
convictions  and  fearless  and faithful  in  the  performance  of duty.
His  pastorate proved to be long  and eventful.
In  1892 largely  through his  efforts,    the  church was incorporated
as   " The  Old  South Church of Weymouth. "     The next year  there
was a similar change in the  name of the parish .
Mr.  Alvord,      as  chairman of a committee,    carefully  wrote  out  a
revised  constitution  and by- laws  for  the  church,    which were pub-
lished in a church manual in 1913.   On the occasion of the twentieth,
twenty- fifth  and thirtieth  anniversaries  of his  installation,      he was
honored with receptions  by the church and his  many friends .
Twice during  his  pastorate  unsuccessful  attempts were made to
reunite  the Old South and Union Churches,   once in  1892 and again
in  1902 ;       but the movements were inauspicious  and had a repellant
effect,       injurious  to  both churches for many years.
The one hundred and  seventy- fifth  anniversary  of the organiza-
tion of the church was observed in  September,    1898,   with historical
services  on the Sabbath,    the fall meeting of Norfolk Conference on
the following  Tuesday,    and a reunion  gathering and reception  on
Wednesday.
In  1903  a  beautiful  Hastings  organ was presented to  the church
 - 255 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          247
and  society by Mrs. Josephine  L.  Dyer as  a memorial of  her late
husband,        William Dyer,    who for  many years had been the faithful
leader  of  the  choir,     superintendent  of  the  Sunday  school,       and  a
deacon.             The same year electric lights were installed in  the meeting-
house.
In 1904 a salt  marsh on the easterly side  of  Back River,    that had
been owned by the parish  for  many years,     although there  appears
to  be  no  record  of  its  acquirement,     was  transferred  to  the  United
States  government  to  become  a  part  of  the  Magazine  Station  at
Hingham.
Two  bequests  were  received  in  1905,    - a  fund  of  $2,000  from
Mrs.  Josephine  L.  Dyer,    and from Mrs.  Harriet  H.  Matson a  lot  of
land  lying between the  meeting- house and the parsonage.            Smaller
bequests were received  in  1908 from Miss Elizabeth Dyer and Mrs.
Caroline T.  Whitcomb,   and in 1909 from Miss Florinda Grover.
In 1908 the pastor was bereft of his wife and the whole community
mourned with him.          He married again in  1911 ,     and from that time
ceased  to  live in the parsonage.
As  the  house  was  getting  old  and  not  well  adapted  to  more
modern needs and improvements without a large outlay,    it  seemed
best to sell  it.         This was done,    and it  was voted that the  proceeds
of the  sale should be invested  as  a  Parsonage Fund,    " the  same to
be left  to accrue until such time as the Society or its  successors may
vote  to  build  a new parsonage,"  and that  the proceeds,      together
with  the  earnings  from investment,    be  used for  that  purpose  and
" for  that  purpose  only."    This  practically  restored   the  original
Parsonage Fund of 1851 .
The  active  membership  of  the  society  had  now become  very
small through deaths  and removals,    and there had been no earnest
effort   to  secure  new  members  for  many years.             Because  of  this
condition  and  because  the  church  was  now duly  incorporated,      it
was deemed best to  transfer  all property and vested interests  from
the society  to the church.
The transfer  was  made  May  1,      1912,      and  since  that  date  no
meetings  of  the society have been held.
In August,      1917,     the  spire  of  the  meeting- house  was  struck  by
lightning and the little room containing the tower clock was set  on
fire.          The clock was ruined and house would have been destroyed
but for  the timely and strenuous efforts  of the fire  department.           A
new clock was  procured  and  extensive  repairs  were  made to  the
building,     including  a steel  ceiling  in  the auditorium.
When the house was ready for  the resumption of church services ,
an invitation was extended to the Union Church to combine services
during  the coming winter.        This  was  done  to  conserve  fuel  and
other  expenses   in   accordance  with   the   President's   request   for
stringent economy to  meet the stress of the country in carrying  on
the Great War.
Aplan was adopted and put in force in December.        A few weeks
later,      the  Universalist  Church  was  also  invited,      and for  the  next
 - 256 - 
248              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
three months the three churches worshiped together.        In the spring
the  Universalist  Church returned  to  its  own edifice,  but the  other
churches  were  led  to  consider  a plan  for  permanent union.         The
combined service  was continued through the summer and fall,      and
then a carefully developed plan of merger was unanimously adopted.
It  was  practically  a  reorganization  of  the  Union  Congregational
Society  as  a legal measure,    but to be known historically and other-
wise  as  the  Old  South  Union  Church.              Both  pastors  were  to  be
continued,     services were to be held in the Old South Meeting-house,
and  the  Union  edifice  was  to  be  removed  and  converted  into  a
parish  house  as  soon  as  practicable.         The merger went into  effect
Nov. 30,       1918.
In January,     1919,    Rev.  Mr. Price,   the pastor of the former Union
Church,     was released from duty for a year in  order to  take up war
work with  the  Y.  M.  C.  A.  in  France.         During  his  absence  Mr.
Alvord conducted the  pastor's  work alone,   but only  a few weeks.
In the midst of a Sunday evening discourse,    Feb. 9,   1919,   he suddenly
dropped to  the  floor  and passed away.      He had been pastor nearly
thirty- three  years,     and held  the love  and esteem  of  his  people  to
the  end.            He had received two hundred and twenty into  the mem-
bership  of  the  church,     a number not equaled in any previous  pas-
torate .                     A beautiful  memorial  window  has  been  placed  in  the
meeting- house,  the gift  of Mrs.  Alvord.
Mr.  Price was unable to return until June,   and he then resumed
his  pastoral  duties.         He continued  until  the summer of  1921 ,       and
then resigned to accept a call  to  the church in Leominster,    Mass.
In  December,            1921 ,          a   unanimous  call   was  extended  to  Rev.
Francis A.  Poole,     Ph.D. of St. Johnsbury,   Vt.          He began his service
Feb.  1 ,     1922,      and was duly installed  the following June.
UNION  CONGREGATIONAL  CHURCH  OF  SOUTH  WEYMOUTH˙
As has  already been stated in the history of the  Second Church,
a  number  of  its  members  withdrew  in  1842  and  formed  a  new
society.               In  response  to  a  petition  of seven men to a justice of the
peace,     a meeting was called and held in the hall of John G. Rogers
on the 20th of June.          It was voted to take the name of South Wey-
mouth Union Society.
After vainly  endeavoring  to  secure  the  transfer  of  certain  mem-
bers   of   the   Second  Church  to   the   proposed   new  church.       the
disaffected  members  were led  to  ask  for  a  council  of  churches  to
consider their case and advise them.            The council could not be made
mutual,     as  the Second  Church bitterly protested against the whole
movement.                   The ex parte council,    however,    advised favorably,   and
accordingly,    on the first of November of that year,   the Union Church
was organized  with  fourteen  members,    and duly recognized.            The
new church expressly disclaimed any intention to injure the Second
Church and society.
The next July a unanimous call was given to Rev. George Denham
 - 257 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          249
to  become their  pastor,    at a salary  of $550.            During 1843 a church
building was erected on Pleasant Street,    nearly opposite the Second
Universalist  Church,     and  November 1  it  was dedicated  and  Mr.
Denham installed .
Within three years  the membership of the church became  about
thirty,     and of the society  about  a hundred and twenty.
In  April,       1847,       Mr.  Denham resigned  because  of  a disturbing
influence  to  which he would  not  yield.           He was given  a  vote  of
confidence  and upheld in his  independence.
Union Congregational Church,  South Weymouth,   1843
In  July a call  was given  to  Rev.  William  M.  Harding  and he
accepted.          He continued in the pastorate for  nearly ten years and
received  over seventy  into  the  church.          The  state  of his  health
became such in 1856 that he was granted leave of absence until the
next year,    and then he resigned.      His resignation was accepted by
a majority of one vote.
In March,    1858,      a call was given Rev.  Stephen H. Hayes.          He
had been a pastor  for  nearly  fifteen  years at Frankfort,   Me.         He
 - 258 - 
250              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
was installed April 8 and remained in the pastorate until  1870,
twelve years.
In  1859  it   was  voted  to  rely  on voluntary  collections  for  the
necessary  expenses of the society,     and in 1860 the pastor began to
be allowed  an annual vacation  of four Sabbaths.            About this  time
a small  chapel,   called the " vestry,"  was erected  nearly in the  rear
of  the church,     and was used for  evening  meetings,     and social  and
other public gatherings.         For several years the Mutual Library,     so
called,      was  kept in  it,    for  two  or  three  seasons  lyceum  meetings
were held  there,     and  for  two  years  it  was  occupied  by the  South
High School.
From  1866  to  1870  the  question  of  reuniting with the  Second
Church  was  actively  considered  three  times,     and  in  1870 it  came
near  being  accomplished,      but  was  defeated  through  a misunder-
standing,       as  already  stated  in the history of the Second Church.
Mr.  Hayes  presented  his  resignation  in  April,      1870,    but  it  did
not go into effect for many months.         He seems to have been actuated
by a desire to remove any hindrance his stay might be to the union
of  the  churches.         But at  length  he accepted  a call  to  the  Salem
Street  Church in  Boston,     and continued  there  a number of years,
until  advancing  years  caused  him to  retire  from  active  pastoral
duties.               His  pastorate  here  was  the  longest  in  the  history  of  the
church,      and was notably successful.          Nearly ninety were added to
the  church.                 He was  highly  respected,      also,      as  a  public- spirited
citizen,      and had great influence with young people.
In  the year 1866  there  was an extended season  of  revival,     and
this  was  followed  by  the  formation  of  a Young Men's  Christian
Association ,             which  developed   much  religious   interest   in   both
churches  for  the  next  two  or  three  years.          Afterward  a  lack  in
competent leadership  caused the  association  to disappear.
From  February  to   October,     1871,      the  pulpit  was  supplied  by
Rev.  Henry E.  Cooley,    a young man who was well liked.           The state
of his  health,      however,      made it  inadvisable for him  to  accept  the
pastorate.               He died within a year.
Rev.   James  McLean  was  called  in  December,      1871 ,         and  was
settled  the  next February.
During  1871  and  1872 a new and commodious church edifice was
erected  on Columbian Street,    nearly opposite the Old South Meet-
ing- House,         at  an  expense  of  over  $30,000,       largely  through  the
efforts and gifts  of John S.  Fogg and Josiah Reed.         It was dedicated
in  1872.    A parsonage was also  built  close by the church.
Mr.  McLean  continued  as  pastor  until  May,      1876,        and  then
resigned  to  accept  a  call  north  of  Boston.            He was  followed  by
Rev.  George  N.  Marden who came in  February,      1877,        and  served
as  acting  pastor  until  the  summer of  1881.    He then  resigned  to
accept  a professorship  in  Colorado  College,  where he labored with
great  success  for  many years.
In  September,        1881 ,     Rev.  William  H.  Bolster  of  the church in
Everett,       Mass. ,   received  a  unanimous call.            He was installed April
 - 259 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          251
12,     1882,     and served  most acceptably for  ten years,     resigning April
14,     1892,       to  accept  a call  to  a church  in  Dorchester.           During  his
pastorate  one hundred members were added to  the church.
Until 1884 it  had been the custom to have two preaching services
on the Sabbath.             In April that year it  was voted to  dispense  with
the afternoon service,   and it was never restored.
At this  time a legacy was received from the estate  of  Dea.       John
S.  Cobb  in  the  form  of  a  fund chiefly  invested  in  real  estate  in
Boston,     the income of which was to be "applied towards the main-
tenance  of  public  worship,"  on  condition  that  the  society  cease
not  " to  exist  or to maintain orthodox preaching  of substantially
the  same theological  sentiments  as  it  has  heretofore  maintained. "
In  November,     1892,      the  society  voted  unanimously  " that  it  is
the sense of the meeting that this society and the Old South Congre-
gational  Society of Weymouth unite and form one common society
and church, "  and a committee was appointed to  co- operate to  that
end.
Aplan of union was proposed,    but the details and method proved
to be unacceptable,    and there  the  matter ended.
On Dec. 23,    1892,    a call was extended to  Rev. Judson Van Clancy.
His installation  took place May 23,      1893.    He remained only until
Oct. 15,  1895,   and then accepted a call to the church in Beverly,   Mass.
Through the will of John S.  Fogg,    the society had now come into
possession  of  a fund  of  $25,000,      the  income  of  which  was  to  be
used in keeping the church edifice  in good repair and fully  insured
against fire,    for  the salary of an organist,    and to beautify and adorn
the  grounds  around  the  edifice.         The church  must remain  of  the
same denomination,      but if  the  building  be  removed  or  destroyed
and the society unites with another of the same denomination within
the limits ofWard 5,   the new society must adopt the name " Union
Congregational Society of Weymouth "  in order to  retain the fund.
On May 29,       1896,   a call was extended to  Rev.  Frank E.  Butler
to become acting pastor.          His service began June 14 and continued
until Jan. 31,    1903,  when he accepted a call to the church in South
Hadley,    Mass.
The question of uniting the two churches was again actively con-
sidered in  1902.    This led to  a series  of  communications between
the  two  churches  which  unfortunately  awakened much personal
feeling,    misunderstanding  and  distrust.       At length  the church re-
sorted to an ex  parte council,   to consider the situation  and recom-
mend a course of action.
After thorough investigation  and careful deliberation,  the council
reported about four months later,   advising  " to labor for  the  things
that make for peace,"  and that " all present agitation of the subject
ofunion be dropped. "    In this  the church acquiesced.
The next November a call was given  Rev.  Harry W. Kimball to
serve as acting pastor.    He served acceptably until April,    1910,   and
then resigned,  that  he might advocate the cause of savings  bank
life  insurance.

In 1907  the  room over the  vestry was fitted  for  a gymnasium,
and for  the next ten years was of  great use to young people.
A church manual was  prepared  and issued  in  1909.
On Jan.  29,       1911,    a call  was accepted  by Rev. Albert  V.  House
of  Worcester,        Mass. ,    and he served  as  acting  pastor  until  Oct.  1,
1914.    He then accepted a call  to  Danvers,      Mass.
In the winter of  1912,    extensive repairs were made to  the church
edifice,      and the furnaces  were replaced with a steam-heating plant.
A unanimous call was given in April,    1915,     to  Rev. Ora A.  Price
of  West  Gloucester,        Mass. ,      and  he  was  duly  installed.             In  the
summer  of  1916  the  church  became  incorporated  as  the  Union
Congregation  Society  of  Weymouth,     and all  parish  property  was
conveyed to it .
As already stated in the history of the Second Church,     the course
of events in  1917 and 1918 opened the way to more cordial  relations
with the Old South Church,   and resulted in the unanimous decision
of the two churches to come together as the Old South Union Church,
through the reorganization of the Union Congregational Society.
UNION CONGREGATIONAL  CHURCH OF  WEYMOUTH AND  BRAINTREE
At the beginning of the nineteenth century,     Weymouth Landing
and East  Braintree  were growing into  some importance as villages ,
or  rather  as  one  village,     though  lying  in  two  towns.             Because  of
this  and the  distance  to  the  Weymouth and  Braintree  churches,
the members of those churches who resided in this  village were led
to  consider  the  advisability  of withdrawing from  their  respective
churches  and forming a new church  nearer  their  homes.       Finding
that  they  could  support  a  church,     they  soon  took  measures  to
bring  about  its   formation.            A society  was  organized  March  13,
1810,       and  immediately  undertook  to  provide  a house of worship.
In this  they were  favored  with  an exceptional  opportunity.         The
Hollis  Street  Church in  Boston  was  about  to  be taken down and
replaced  with  a  larger  building.        The  new  society   secured  the
edifice at a low figure,   had it  taken apart with care,   and transported
the material by water to  a place close by the Fore River,    just over
the  Braintree  line.       Here they rebuilt  the house with  such  altera-
tions  as were necessary.            They soon had a notable edifice  that was
to  accommodate them for  nearly ninety years .
On Feb.  21 ,       1811,     the  society  was  incorporated and on Aug. 14
a church  was  organized  as  the  Union  Church  of  Weymouth  and
Braintree.
Acall was extended to  Mr. John Frost  to  become pastor,   but he
declined.               Another call  was given in November to  Mr.  Daniel A.
Clark,        and he  responded favorably.         He was  ordained on the last
day of the year.            His stay,     however,     was brief.          A few members of
the church  and  of  the  congregation  soon  became disaffected,     and
this  made it  difficult  to  raise  his  full  salary.         He resigned  and was
dismissed Oct.  20,      1813.
 - 261 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          253
For more than a year there was financial distress,    and the supply
of the pulpit was from Sabbath to  Sabbath.             By January,       1815,      a
better  feeling  began to  prevail  and the  society became sufficiently
interested  and united to engage Mr. Jonas  Perkins  of  Bridgewater
to  preach for  three months.           He served  so  acceptably that  he was
soon  given  a  call ,      and  he  was  ordained  on the  14th of June.                For
almost  forty- six years  he ministered  unto his  people with devoted
zeal  and  held  their  love  and  esteem.            The  church  increased  and
became  strong  and  influential  in  the  vicinity.        It  was  his   only
pastorate.             At the  age  of  seventy  years,      in  accordance  with  his
own  wishes,      his  resignation  was  accepted,   and  the  long  pastorate
was  ended.              This was in October,     1860.    But his home had become
established  here.    and here  he continued  to  live  and to  be actively
interested   in  the  welfare  of  the  church,     until  he  passed  away,
June 26,     1874.
After his resignation,   an attempt was made to secure Rev. E.  Porter
Dyer of Hingham to succeed him,   but this was not successful .
In December,      1860,    a  call  was given  Rev.  Lysander  Dickerman
of Gloucester,      and he was installed  Jan.  17,      1861.    This  pastorate
continued for about six  and a half years and proved to  be very un-
fortunate.           A bitter difference of opinion arose between the pastor
and nearly half  of the  congregation,    and continued until the close
of his  official  connection with them in July,    1867.    For over a year
the  very  existence  of  the  church  and  society  had been  seriously
threatened,     and many withdrew their connection.          Not until  1868
did  it  become practicable to invite a successor to  the pastorate.
In  April,      1868,    Rev.  Alfred A.  Ellsworth  of  Milford was secured
to supply the pulpit.       This he did very acceptably for  about  three
years.        After  that  a  better  spirit   prevailed  and  after  extensive
alterations  had been made in  the church edifice,     a hearty call  was
extended  to  Rev.  Lucien H. Frary of Middleton.          He was installed
April  13,      1875.    Under him the people were gradually  united  into
a strong  and  prosperous  society,    and the  heavy debt  incurred  in
remodeling  the house of worship was happily discharged.
During  the  summer  of  1886  Mr.  Frary's  daughter  became  so
critically  ill  that her physician could give no hope of  her recovery
except by a removal to  California,     so  Mr.  Frary tendered his  resig-
nation  and  was  dismissed  by  Council  in  October  of  that  year.
During the eleven  and a half years of his  ministry he had,    by tact
and faithful  service,  not only won the respect  and affection  of  his
own people,    but was highly esteemed by the whole community.
In  December,     1887,     the  Rev.  Eddy T.  Pitts  of  Plymouth was
called  to  the  pastorate,     which he accepted  with  the  proviso  that
he  serve  for  a  time  as  " Acting  Pastor.  "     He  resigned  in  April,
1889.
On June 1,   1890,   Oliver Huckel,    a graduate of Boston University,
was  engaged to  supply  the pulpit  for  the  ensuing  year.             He was
ordained  to the gospel ministry Sept.  10,    1910.    In June,    1891,    he
was  installed  to the full  pastorate.            Greatly to  the sorrow  and  re
 - 262 - 
254               ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
gret of his  church and society,  his decision  to take up a course  of
study in Europe led to his  resignation,     to  take effect  Sept.  1,     1893.
In  December,      1893,     the  Rev.  W.  H.  Alexander  was  engaged  as
acting pastor for the succeeding year,    and was continued in service
until  the end of 1896.    In April,    1897,    the  Rev.  Henry S.  Snyder
was called to the pastorate and remained until April 1,      1901 .
On the 19th of June,   1897,   the old meeting- house erected in  1810
was  totally  destroyed  by fire  which  caught  from  sparks  from  a
passing  locomotive,    thereby  removing  an  old  historic  landmark,
which  was  greatly  regretted  and  missed  by  everybody.             It  was
deemed wise not to  rebuild  on the old  site,    and a new lot of land
was  purchased  on  Commercial  Street,     where  the  present  church
edifice  was  erected  and dedicated  Dec.  13,      1898.
On  Sept.   1 ,        1901,        the  Rev.   Robert  H.  Cochrane  became  the
pastor  and  remained  until  July,    1913.     On Aug.  13,       1911,       the
church celebrated its  one hundredth anniversary  with  appropriate
exercises  and  a sermon by its  former  pastor,       Dr.  Oliver  Huckel.
On March 1 ,     1914,    Rev. Albert P.  Watson became the pastor  and
remained  until  Feb.  1,    1919.    On  Dec.  1 ,     1919,     the  Rev. J.  Caleb
Justice  became  the  acting  pastor,     and  on  Dec.  9,     1920,     he  was
installed  into  the full  pastorate by the council.
EAST  WEYMOUTH  CONGREGATIONAL  CHURCH
The  early  history  of  the  Congregational  Church  is   so  closely
linked  with  that  of  the  Methodist  Church  that  at  the beginning
the  two  seem to  overlap each other.
In  1822,       through the  efforts  of  Urban Rice,   a preaching  service
was  established in the house of his  father,     David Rice.             ( This  was
the  gambrel- roofed  house still  standing at the foot of the hill  near
the site of the old "White Church.")     This service resulted in the
formation  of  a  Methodist  Episcopal  Church,     the  first   Methodist
organization in town.
Early  in  1825  the  society  resolved  to  build  a house of  worship,
and land was purchased by Alvah Raymond and William  Rice for
the society .              This house was completed and dedicated in 1825,     and
cost  $1,144.68 .               This  structure was enlarged in  1828.
The society  continued  in  its  original  form and place of worship
until  1842,      when,      some  dissatisfaction   arising  as  to  the  form  of
church  government,     a  meeting  was  called  in  February,      1843,     for
the  purpose  of  forming  another  religious  society.           John  Tirrell,
Josiah E.  Rice and Nathaniel T. Shaw were chosen as  the standing
committee of the new society,   George Bates,   treasurer,   Amos Tirrell ,
collector,       and Eben Tirrell,    John Tirrell  and Josiah  E. Rice minis-
terial  committee.
The society  organized in 1843 under the name of the First Evan-
gelical   Methodist  Society.             Rev.  Stephen  Lovell  was  the  first
minister.             He received a salary of $500,    and the provision was made
that his  house rent  should  not exceed  $60.
 - 263 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          255
From  the  society  a  committee,      consisting  of  Josiah  E.   Rice,
Daniel  Bates,      Jr. ,      Urban  Rice,      Z.   L.  Bicknell  and  Nathaniel  T.
Shaw,      was appointed to  secure a building site  and draft a plan  for
a meeting-house.         The chapel  of  the  Methodist Episcopal  Society
which stood on the site of the " White Church"  was purchased,    and
plans  for  rebuilding were immediately formed.           These  plans  were
perfected,       and during  the summer and autumn of  1843  the  work
went rapidly on,   the new edifice being formally dedicated in Decem-
ber of that year.
The dissenting  members  then  formed  the  Methodist  Episcopal
Society and built a house of worship near the house of Bela French.
Congregational Church,   East Weymouth,   1843
In  1846  Rev.  Mr.  Lovell,    feeling  that  the church should  have
more of his time than he could give on account of his growing literary
work,   resigned  the pastorate.        He was succeeded by Rev.  Jotham
Horton of New York,   who received a salary  of  $500.         Mr. Horton
remained as pastor two years and was succeeded by Rev.  Edmund
S. Potter.
The church had received  into  its  membership several  from  the
Old North Church.        These members brought with them a strong
congregational sentiment,    and the new pastor holding similar beliefs
it  was decided that a change in the form of government and name
 - 264 - 
256              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
should be made.        A new covenant and articles of faith were adopted.
and the  name of  the  organization  changed to  " The First  Congre-
gational  Church of  East Weymouth. "
Under the  new name and form  of  government the  first   officers
were Nathan  Canterbury,    treasurer ;        George  Bates,      clerk ;          Albert
Humphrey,        Joseph  Totman  and  John  P.   Lovell,      standing  com-
mittee.             Although  Congregational  in  name,    the  church  sustained
an independent relation  to the other churches of that denomination
until May,     1859,    when it asked for admission to the Norfolk Confer-
ence  of  Churches,    and in  February,      1860,    became Congregational
in all its  affiliations .
In  May,       1860,      Mr.  Potter  resigned  and  was  followed  by Rev.
James P.  Lane.             In  February,     1861,    the  first  deacons,     Alvah Ray-
mond,       Jairus  Sprague and  David Burrell,     were elected  and conse-
crated  to  that service.
In  1864  it   became  necessary  to  alter  and  enlarge  the  church
building.             An organ  was  also  purchased  to take the  place  of  the
orchestra  which  had been the  accompaniment of the choir.            Mr.
Lane resigned in  1865,    leaving the church in  a somewhat unsettled
condition.
The coming  of  Rev.   Daniel  W.  Waldron  quickly  dispelled  all
clouds and healed all differences .              His zeal and enthusiasm resulted
in increased  activities,    and five years of remarkable prosperity and
harmony  prevailed.              Mr.  Waldron  resigned  in  1871  to  become
pastor  of  the  Maverick Church of  East Boston,      and was later  city
missionary  of  Boston;      but he continued to be the beloved friend
of  the  church  until his death.
Mr.  Waldron was succeeded by Rev.  Elbridge  P.  McElroy,      who
remained  until  1875,    and was followed  by Rev. John A.  Cruzan,
who,         after  a  single  year's  pastorate,      resigned  to  accept  a  call   to
Portland,      Ore.            The pastorates  of  Rev.  Henry W. Eldridge  ( 1877-
80) ,           Rev.   John  W.  Malcolm  ( 1880-81) ,       Rev.  Frank  J.   Mundy
(1881-83) ,         Rev.  William  A.  Depew  (1883-86)    and  Rev.   Merrill
Blanchard  ( 1887-90)   covered  the period from 1877 to  1890.
In  May,         1891 ,       Rev.  Daniel Evans,     a young man just  graduated
from  Andover  Theological  Seminary,      was  ordained  and  installed
as  pastor.               A very  happy pastorate of eight  years followed.        The
church edifice was again renovated  and  beautified,     and all  depart-
ments  of  church life  quickened  and  strengthened.             Mr.  Evans  re-
signed  to  accept  a call  to  Cambridge,      Mass. ,    and was followed by
Rev.  Francis  A.  Poole.          Although  Mr.  Poole's  pastorate  was not  a
long  one  on  account  of  ill  health,     it  will  always  be  remembered
by  the  strong  bond  of  love  and  sympathy  between  pastor  and
people.
In July,    1902,    Rev.  Emery L.  Bradford was installed  as  pastor.
The pastorate began under very auspicious  conditions,     and pastor
and people  looked  forward  with  great  expectations  in the new re-
lation.               But on Sunday evening,     Feb.  9,   1903,    the church building
was  completely  destroyed  by  fire,       and  the  " White  Church,  "   so
 - 265 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          257
linked  to  the  life  of its  members with  its  many associations,       was
but a fond memory.
Stunned but  not crushed  by the loss,    the  society  rallied  imme-
diately  and plans for  rebuilding were made at once.           The location
of the church building  had for some time been considered  unsatis-
factory,     as  the  parish  had grown up in  other  directions.               Accord-
ingly   the  estate  of Albert  Humphrey,    near  Jackson  Square,       was
purchased,     the  Unitarian Church  building  on Cottage Street  being
used  for  worship during the building  of the new edifice.
The corner stone of the new church building was laid with appro-
priate services  in June,     1904.    The building was formally dedicated
in  May,      1905,     with elaborate and impressive  ceremonies.
Mr. Bradford remained with the church until  1911.    Rev. Walter
Commons'     pastorate  of  two  years  followed.        In  1914  the  church
called  Rev.  Edward Torrey Ford of  Tacoma,     Wash. ,    to  become its
pastor.            Mr.  Ford resigned  in  1920  to  accept  a call  to  a church  in
Vermont.
The church chose for its  next minister a young man just graduated
from  the  theological  seminary,      Rev.  Karnek A.  Handanian,     who
is  now serving  the church  and community with all  the  ardor  and
enthusiasm of his young manhood.
PILGRIM  CHURCH  OF  NORTH  WEYMOUTH
The  year  1850 found  the  old  First  Church  outgrowing  its  ac-
commodations,   and the population of  that part of the parish  called
Old Spain  increasing  in  numbers  and  prosperity.          Instead  of  en-
larging the meeting-house,    or building a new one in the old location,
it  seemed wiser  to  establish  a new church  in  Old  Spain.            Accord-
ingly an ecclesiastical society was formed May 14,    1851,     and began
at once  to  secure  plans  and funds  for  a  new meeting-house  to  be
erected  about a mile north  of  the First  Meeting- House.
Some of  the women had already  anticipated this  by forming  a
Ladies'     Sewing Circle about ten days before,   to assist  the enterprise.
The frame of  the  new building  began  to  rise  the  latter  part  of
August,      and  by Christmas  the  bell  was hung  and  ready  for  use.
The structure was valued at  $7,000.
Fifty- one  members of  the  First  Church were granted  letters  to
form a new church,     and  on  March 11,     1852,    a council  of ministers
and delegates  from  neighboring  churches  met  and  recognized  the
Pilgrim  Church and dedicated their  meeting- house.          The venerable
Dr.  R.  S.  Storrs  of  Braintree  preached  a masterly  sermon  on  the
occasion.              The new church  adopted the  Confession  and  Covenant
of the First  Church.
Rev.   Calvin  Terry  was  called  to  be  the  first   pastor  and  was
installed  May 18,     1852.    David Pratt,     3d,     and James Torrey,      were
chosen  to be the first  deacons.
Mr.  Terry remained until  Dec.  25,     1856,     and was then dismissed
because  of  great differences  with the church.       The next  fall  a  call

was  extended  to  Rev.  Charles  E.  Reed of Taunton,    but was not
accepted,     and a  pastor was not secured until the early part of 1858.
Then  Rev.  Samuel  L.  Rockwood was  called  and  he was  installed
March 12.    He continued until July 31,   1871,   and then resigned on
account of failing health.            He was soon succeeded by Rev.  Louis B.
Voorhees,       who was ordained  December 6 the  same year.
During  the  pastorate  of  Mr.  Voorhees  there  was  an  extensive
religious  revival,    which resulted in eighty- one new members received
into the church on confession of faith.           But his work was interrupted
in  1876 by a call  to  service  elsewhere,     and his  resignation  was ac-
cepted July 1 .

Rev.  Amory H.  Tyler became acting  pastor  May 17,     1880,      and

The year  after  Mr.  Vincent left,    Rev.  Frederick  G.  Merrill  was

1919   Rev.   Thomas  Bruce  Bitler  was  called  and  is   the  present

The  following  organizations  are  connected  with  the  church  as
