FIRST  METHODIST  EPISCOPAL  CHURCH
During  the  early  part  of  the  nineteenth   century  Methodist
ministers   had  occasionally  visited   the  town,      but  without  any
definite  result.
Some of  the  people  in  the  First  Parish  (Old  North) ,     however,
were  becoming restive  under  the  Puritanic  methods  and  severe
Calvinistic  preaching which they had to  help  support;          and when,
a few years after the formation of the Union Church at Weymouth
Landing,      the residents  at East Weymouth felt  that they also  ought
 - 268 - 
260              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
to  have  a  church  nearer  their  homes,     it  was  not  strange  that  a
different  style  of  preaching  and of  church government appealed  to
them as desirable.        In the autumn of 1822 Mr. Urban Rice,    a young
man,      while visiting friends in Springfield,   attended some Methodist
meetings  and became a convert.          Upon his return he immediately
began to work as  an evangelist.
Not  long  after,      Joseph  Dunbar  of   Hingham,       another  young
Methodist convert,     announced at  the close  of a Sunday afternoon
service  in  the old First  Church that  " God willing,   there  will  be a
religious   meeting  in  the  Back  River  schoolhouse  this  evening. "
This was the first  Methodist service in the town,   and led to others
on succeeding Sunday evenings.
Soon  regular preaching  services  were established  by Rev. Aaron
D.  Sargent,      preacher- in-charge  of  the  Scituate  Circuit,       which  in-
cluded  the  entire South Shore.        These were held in  Urban Rice's
home,        the  house of his father,      David  Rice,    which  still  stands  on
Pleasant Street,   just at the foot of the little hill  where the meeting-
house was afterward  built.        In 1823 a class  of eleven members was
organized with Joseph Dunbar as  leader.
During the next two years,    there were several different preachers.
In  1825  a building  lot  was  secured  on the  hill  mentioned  above
and a plain  chapel  was  erected  and  dedicated  June  22,     with a
sermon  by  Rev.  Isaac Bonney.         Three years  later  the  attendance
had  increased  so  much  that  it  became  necessary  to  enlarge  the
chapel.
Within  ten years  nearly a hundred members withdrew from the
First   Church  and joined  this  Methodist  Church.             Nevertheless,
many of  them soon became weary of discipline  and domination of
presiding  elders  and bishops,    and desired  to be independent in  the
choice  of  their  pastors.          Some returned  to  the  fellowship  of  the
First   Church  within  a  few  years,      but  the  greater  remained  on
account  of  the  distance  to  the old  meeting-house.       At length,     in
1842 feeling  ran so high  that  a majority of the members voted to
organize  as  the  Evangelical  Methodist Church in  name,    but with
a  Congregational  form  of  government.           They secured  the  church
property,     took down the  chapel in  1843,    and erected  on the  same
site  the  house so  widely known afterward as the " White Church .  "
Eventually the name of the church was changed to East Weymouth
Congregational  Church.
But a  sizable  minority of the members remained steadfast to  the
Methodist polity,  withdrew from the new movement,    and renewed
the original  organization.          Their meetings were held in the village
schoolhouse  until  1844.     Meanwhile  they  secured  a  lot  in  the
rear  of  the  late  Bela  French's  house on  Commercial Street,     and  a
church edifice was erected  there,   with  Mr.  Cyrus Washburn as the
builder.
It  was dedicated Oct.  30,    1844,    when Rev.  Henry Mayo was the
pastor.                Rev.  George  Landon  preached  the  dedicatory  sermon.
 - 269 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          261
Six years  later,    in  the pastorate of  Rev. John B. Gould,    it  was con-
siderably  enlarged  and was rededicated  Oct.  23,     1850.    Rev.  Abel
Stevens ,        D.D.,    preached  the dedicatory  sermon.              But a  little  over
a year from that  time it  was destroyed  by  fire.
Another house was erected  on the same spot by the same builder,
in  the  first  year of  the pastorate of  Rev.  Charles  H. Titus,    and was
dedicated   Oct.   12,       1852,         with   Rev.   Daniel  Wise,         D.D.,       as   the
preacher.             This  house  also  was  enlarged  in  1864,    while  Rev.  John
Howson  was  pastor.              It  was  reopened  October  27  with  a sermon
by  Rev.  J.  A.  M.  Chapman,      D.D.
On  the   afternoon  of   Feb.   23,       1870,        a  fire   which  started   in
an  adjacent  stable  spread  to  the  church building  and burned it  to
the   ground.                     The loss  was  estimated  at  $12,000  and it  was  only
partially  covered by insurance.
GAGrant
First Methodist Church,   East Weymouth
It  was decided to rebuild  at  once and a  new site  was selected  on
Broad  Street  where  the  church  now  stands.             Through  the  efforts
of  the  pastor,     Rev.  William V.  Morrison,    during  the last  weeks of
his  service,    the  necessary  funds  were  raised.           His  successor,    Rev.
Francis J.  Wagner,   was also a vigorous leader in the work.
Much of  the work was gratuitously  performed by members  of
the parish,    and the bell was the  gift  of the  Sunday school.             This
house also was  built  by  Mr.  Cyrus  Washburn.          It  was dedicated
Dec.  23,     1870.    Rev.  W. F.  Warren,     D.D.,      afterward  president  of
Boston University,   preached the  sermon.
This building has several times been in danger from lightning  or
 - 270 - 
262              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
fire.            The most serious occasion was in 1879,   when lightning wrecked
the structure and partially demolished the  steeple.
A new spire was built,    and other extensive alterations and repairs
were  made at  various  times  up to  1909.     While  the  church  was
being  built,       a fine  large  three-manual organ was  acquired,     which
was originally constructed for the Hanover Street Church in Boston.
It was entirely  rebuilt  in  1909.
Of  the  various  organizations  connected  with  the  church,     the
oldest  is  the Wesleyan Singing Society,   now the choir of the church.
It was organized in  1826 by Mr. Charles Bates,    and he was chorister
for  many years.            The  Sunday  school  was  organized  in  1831  and
Mr.  Cotton  Bates  was the  first  superintendent.
The Ladies'      Social  Circle  was in  existence before 1848,       and the
Epworth League dates from 1889.
Seven different houses have served as parsonages,    the present one
having  been erected in  1915,    in the pastorate of  Rev.  William M.
Newton.
The  fiftieth   anniversary  of  the  erection  of  the  present  church
edifice  was  fittingly  observed in  1920.
The history of this church has been marked by revival seasons of
great  power.              The  pastorate  of  Rev.  Henry  H.  Smith,      1848  to
1850,     became memorable for  an extensive  revival,    and that of Rev.
Henry D.  Robinson,     1865  to  1867,     was similarly  notable;      but the
one  of  greatest  interest   occurred  during  the  pastorate  of  Rev.
William V.  Morrison,     1867 to 1870,   and the Congregational Church
was equally involved in it .
In the list  of ministers  who have served  this  church  as  pastors
in   accordance  with  the  practice  of  the  denomination,      there  are
fifty-nine  names.              In  addition  to  those  already  mentioned,        Rev.
Walter  Ela,         Rev.  Samuel  L.  Gracey,      Rev.  George  C.  King,      Rev.
Albert A.  Kidder,    Rev. William I.  Ward,    Rev. George G. Scrivener,
Rev.  George  A.  Grant  and  Rev.  Frank  Kingdon  are  perhaps  as
well  remembered as  any,     and are worthy of special  mention.            The
present  pastor  is   Rev.  Earl  E.  Story.

PORTER  METHODIST  EPISCOPAL  CHURCH
In  the spring of 1864 six  women living at or near Lovell's  Corner
formed  a " union  female  prayer  meeting. "    They held  meetings
weekly for  nearly  three years.             On a  Sunday in  September,     1866,
through  the efforts  of these women,    a  service  was held  in  the  hall
over  the grocery store,     and Rev.  Daniel  W. Waldron preached.
Mr.  Waldron had recently  begun his  first  pastorate  at  the  Con-
gregational  Church  in  East  Weymouth,     only a mile  or so distant.
It  was  decided to  continue services  and organize  as  a mission  for
that purpose.
Mr.  Waldron conducted the mission,    preaching regularly  until he
left  East Weymouth in  1871 .
In 1867 the ladies formed the Union Social  Circle,    which became
the working  and  financial  support  of  the mission ;       and associated
with  them for  some time was an organization  of young men who
made it  their  special  work to  secure  the fitting  and furnishing  of
the hall,     and to  assist  the  Social  Circle.
After the departure of Mr. Waldron,   preachers were sent out from
the  Congregational  Bureau  in  Boston.          This  continued  for  about
fifteen  months,    when it  became  evident that  the  mission  needed
a leader who could be among the people and do pastoral work.
After due consideration,     it  was decided  to seek the advice of a
council of neighboring  churches,   and if  found  expedient  to  ask its
assistance in forming and recognizing  a church.      The council  met
Oct.  29,       1872,       and was composed of delegations  from five  Congre-
gational  churches  of  Weymouth,     the  First  Methodist  Church  of
East Weymouth and the Maverick Congregational  Church of East
Boston,    of which Mr.  Waldron was then pastor.        The council were
unanimous in favoring the project,   and the " Puritan Congregational
Church  of  Lovell's  Corner"  was  duly  organized  and  recognized.
The churches represented in the council afterward presented the new
church with a communion service,    which was highly appreciated.
There were twenty members.       In November a call was extended
to  Rev.  J.  C.  Halliday of  Northbridge to  become  pastor for  a  year
at  a salary  of  $1,000 and he accepted .
 - 272 - 
264             ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
At this  time  Lovell's   Corner  was  a  prosperous,      growing  com-
munity,     but soon  there  came  changes  in  business  interests  which
made it  more  and  more difficult  for  the  young church  to  sustain
the  new burden of  a pastor's  salary.         At length,   in 1877,      the pastor
felt  compelled to leave,    and the church was very soon in danger of
dissolution.                 In  their  extremity  they  appealed  to  the  Methodist
presiding elder.
Rev.  Dr.  W. V.  Morrison came and arranged to have the pulpit
supplied  by  Rev.  Henry  P.  Haylett  until  April,     1879.    Then the
church was reorganized as  the  Porter Methodist Episcopal Church
with  Mr.  Haylett  as  its  first  pastor.          At first  the church  was in-
cluded in  the  New Bedford  Conference,   but in  1882 it  was trans-
ferred  to   the  New  England  Southern  Conference  of  Methodist
Churches.
The  name  " Porter "  was  given  as  a  memorial  to  Miss  Eunice
Porter,     who had bequeathed a legacy of about $600 " for the building
of  the first  Methodist church in South Weymouth."   This,     together
with a lot  of land given by Mr. Joseph  Holbrook,    and liberal  sub-
scriptions  from  the  residents  about  Lovell's   Corner,     enabled  the
church to  erect  a house of  worship in  1886 on the easterly side  of
Pleasant  Street,    a little  way south  of the Corner.
This was during  the  pastorate of Rev. Julian S.  Wadsworth,    and
he  labored  earnestly  for  the  success  of  the  enterprise.        Sept.  16,
1886,       was  the  day of  dedication  of  the  new edifice.         It  was  the
twentieth  anniversary  of  the  first  sermon  preached at the  Corner
by  Rev.  D.  W. Waldron,    and he was present to  assist  in the exer-
cises.             During  the  exercises   Bishop  John  W.  Hamilton,      at  that
time  pastor  of  a  church  in  Boston,      with  consummate  tact  and
eloquent  appeal,    induced people in the crowded auditorium to sub-
scribe  many hundreds of dollars  to provide sufficient  funds  to com-
plete  the  building  and its  furnishing without recourse to  borrowing
money.               Thus with much rejoicing  the house was dedicated free of
all debt.
During  the  forty- four  years  of  its   existence  as  a  Methodist
Church it  has  received  the  ministrations  of  twenty-eight  different
pastors,    in accordance with the practice of the denomination to make
frequent  changes.         Nearly  all  of  these have been young men who
were  still   pursuing  theological  studies  at  Boston  University.               A
number of them have become widely known and honored preachers ,
perhaps  no  one  more so  than  Rev.  Dallas  Lore  Sharp,      who  was
pastor in the years 1896 to  1898,    and who has since become a promi-
nent  professor  at  Boston  University  and a popular public lecturer
and writer.
In  July,       1920,      Mrs. Arthur S.  Emig,    whose husband  was  then
pastor  of  the  church,     was granted  a  license  to  preach.              She  was
among the first women in this  Conference to  receive such a license.
She was  thus  able  to  supplement  the  labors  of her husband at  a
time  when the  state  of  his  health  forbade  his  rendering  efficient
service.            The present pastor is   Rev.  A.  E.  Greenler.

UNITARIAN  CHURCH
The first  attempt to introduce Unitarian preaching in Weymouth
was  made in  1833.    A society  was formed  and  a committee  con-
sisting   of  James  Whittemore,      Whitcomb  Porter  and  Amos  W.
Stetson  was authorized  to  enter into  a written  agreement with  the
Overseers  of  the  Weymouth  and  Braintree  Academy for  the  use
of the lower room of the Academy building  at Weymouth Landing,
except when needed by the school then kept there.            The rent  was
to be $75 a year.
The first  meeting was held Jan.  19,    1833.    In  March the society
was incorporated as the First Unitarian Religious Society of Brain-
tree  and  Weymouth.         Services  were  held  on  succeeding  Sundays
with  preaching  by different  clergymen.           Among them were  Rev.
Increase  S.  Smith,   preceptor  of  Derby Academy,     Hingham,     Rev.
George Whitney,   son of Rev.  Peter Whitney of Quincy,      Rev.  Dr.
Henry W.  Bellows  and  Rev.  Dr.  Ezra  S.  Gannett.
Sufficient   interest,     however,       to  sustain  the  movement did  not
develop,      and in July the room at the Academy was given up,    and
meetings were discontinued.
The  next  movement was  not  until  about  1872  or  1873  when
meetings  were begun at the home of Mrs. James  Lovell  on  Broad
Street,         East  Weymouth,    probably with the hope of establishing  a
Universalist organization.
The services  were conducted by Rev.  Elmer  Hewitt,     Rev.  B.  F.
Eaton,        Rev.  Jacob  Baker  and others,     most of  them of  the  Uni-
versalist  belief.         These services  were continued for several years,    a
lot  of  land  on  Cottage  Street  was  bought  (where  the  Unitarian
Church  now stands) ,    and  a fund  of  $700  was  accumulated;         and
then,    for  some reason not recorded,    the enterprise was abandoned.
About 1885 another society was formed and held meetings in  the
Masonic Hall building  on Broad Street.            To this  society the fund
and building lot of the former society was given.       The new society
was  induced to  take the  name Unitarian  by an  agreement  of  the
Unitarian  Association  of  Boston to provide funds for the building
 - 274 - 
266              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
of a church edifice.       The building was begun in 1887 and was com-
pleted and dedicated April  18,      1889.
The society prospered for  nearly twenty years,    eventually paying
for  their  edifice  besides  supporting  all  other expenses.           The older
members,        however,     were  passing  away and  some were  removing
from town,      and younger people did not come to take their  places.
At length  it  became  necessary  to  give  up regular  services   and,
finally,       to  close  the  house of  worship.
The Universalist  Conference  of  Boston  undertook  negotiations,
with the  result that the property was sold  to the State Universalist
Conference in  1909.
An attempt  was  made  to  hold  Universalist  services,      but  there
was so  little  encouragement  that  they were discontinued  in  Sep-
tember,       1910.    The church  building  has  been unoccupied  most  of
the time since.
FIRST  UNIVERSALIST  SOCIETY  OF  WEYMOUTH
On July 11.  1836,   the following  notice was posted :
To Fisher A.  Kingsbury,        Esquire,     one of the Justices of the Peace within and
for the County of Norfolk:
We the  subscribers,    members of  the  First  Universalist  Society  in  Weymouth
in  said  County  of  Norfolk respectfully  request  you to  issue  a  warrant  in  due
form  of  law,       for calling  and notifying  the first  meeting thereof and organizing
the same;      requiring  the  qualified  voters  of  said  society  to  meet at the Hall of
Asa  B.  Wales  in  said  Weymouth,      on  Thursday,     the  twenty-first  day  of  July
instant,     at  seven of the clock  in the afternoon,    for  the following purpose,    viz.:
1.   To organize said society  agreeably to  the Laws of this  Commonwealth.
2.  To choose a moderator  for said meeting.
3.   To choose  all  officers  required  by Law in Parishes and Religious Societies.
4.  To hear the report of the  Com.    chosen at the last  meeting.
5.  To adopt a code of  By-Laws for  the government of said society,     calling
and notifying  all future meetings of said society,    and to transact  all other busi-
ness that may be legally  brought before  them.
ASA B.  WALES.
ENOCH LATHROP.
HIRAM  CUSHING.
HENRY B.   COWING.
HENRY F.   THOMAS.
On July  21 ,      1836,     this  meeting was held and Jacob Allen  was
elected  moderator.           The committee  appointed  to  prepare by-laws
read  them  and  they  were  unanimously  adopted.        The  preamble
was as follows :
We the subscribers,     feeling  desirous  to  grow in grace and in the knowledge of
our Lord and Saviour Jesus  Christ,    do hereby form ourselves  into  a Society that
we may be helps  to  each  other,    and that by our united energies  we may better
serve the purposes  of religions  and truth,    and we cheerfully adopt and subscribe
to  the  Constitution as the basis  of  our government.
After adopting the constitution,     Asa B.  Wales was chosen  treas-
urer,     and Asa  B.  Wales,    Jonathan Hunt and  Enoch Lathrop were
 - 275 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          267
chosen  a standing committee.       Addison Chessman was chosen col-
lector.            Henry B.  Cowing was chosen  clerk.
The standing committee were instructed to secure a preacher,    and
they made arrangements with Rev. Matthew Hale Smith to preach
each fortnight.
At a meeting of the parish,    held  Oct.  17,      1836,    it  was voted  to
choose a committee  to  ascertain  how much money could be raised
toward building a meeting- house,   Jonathan Hunt and Hiram Cush-
ing  being chosen on this  committee.
In the fall of 1838 subscription of stock was started in  Weymouth
and  Braintree,    and a meeting of  the  stockholders  was held  at the
First Universalist Church,   Weymouth
Hall  of  the  Hotel  in  Weymouth,      Dec.  27,      1838.     Maj.    John  W.
Loud was chosen moderator and John A.  Hobart clerk,  and it  was
voted on motion  of  Asa  B.  Wales,    " That  we proceed  to  build  a
meeting  house for  Religious  Worship. "    The building  committee
chosen  were Asa  B.  Wales,     Ira  Curtis,     Adoram  Clapp,   John  W.
Loud and John A.  Hobart.
The committee were instructed to select and purchase a site,    and
they  purchased  the  lot  where  the  church  now stands  on  Wash-
ington Street  of  Mr.  Asa  Webb.           Stephen  S.  Foye was  the  con-
tractor  and John A.  Hobart the  draftsman .

268               ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
The committee reported  the meeting-house ready the  next  Sep-
tember.          Including  land,    bell and furnishings,    the cost was $6,400.
Friday,       the  thirteenth  day  of  September,       1839,     was  appointed
by the  society  to  dedicate  the  house to  the worship of  the  only
living  and  true  God.           It  was a  fine  day and a large  concourse  of
people attended.       The following was the  order  of dedicatory  serv-
ice:
Reading Scripture:     Rev. M. B.  Ballou of Stoughton.
Introductory  Prayer :        Rev.  Elmer Hewitt of Scituate;     anthem.
Dedicatory Prayer:       Rev.  A.  A. Folsom of Hingham.
Sermon:        Rev.  O.  A.  Skinner of Boston,   from Heb.   10:    25;    hymn.
Concluding Prayer :      Rev. I.  Gregory of Quincy.
Sermon in the afternoon by Rev. A. B. Grash of Utica,    N. Y.
The sale  of  pews took place on the  next day,    and Sunday,      the
fifteenth day of September,  1839,   was the first Sabbath that meetings
were held in  the new house,    a thing  long desired and highly prized
by the true lovers of Zion.            Rev.  Calvin Gardner was the preacher
on this  and the three following Sabbaths.
On Nov.  25,      1839,     a call was extended to Rev. John S.  Barry for
six  months,         and  this  call  was  renewed  at  the  annual  meeting  in
April,   1840.
Rev.  John  M.  Spear was chosen as  minister in April,      1841,      re-
maining until  April,      1845.
He was followed by Rev.  Mr. Coffin until  November of the same
year.         At the  annual meeting  held  in  1843  it  was voted that  the
parish committee confer with a committee from South Weymouth
in regard to preaching,   but there seems to have been no report from
this  committee.
The next permanent minister was Rev. Mr. Dennis,  his  pastorate
beginning in  1846.
Rev.  John S.  Barry was again extended a call in April,   1847,     and
this  was repeated in  1848,    and he remained until Jan.  1,     1850.    In
April,      1850,     Rev.  Mr. Hemphill was chosen pastor and he remained
until April,     1852.   Then Rev. D. P.  Livermore was called as minister
and  remained as  pastor until  April,     1854,     at which time Rev. Mr.
Davenport accepted a call  and served  as minister until he resigned
at the annual parish  meeting in March,       1855.
Rev.  Mr.  Mellen was called during the year 1855 and remained
as pastor  until  April 1,   1860.
In  May,       1860,      Rev.  D.  F.  Goddard was called as pastor,   and he
resigned Nov. 30,    1861.
From November,    1861,    to April,    1864,   supplies were employed to
fill   the  pulpit,     and  then  Rev.  Miss  Olympia  P.  Brown,     the  first
woman preacher,    was called  to  be pastor.          At last  accounts  Miss
Brown was still  alive  and was one of the women prominent at  the
convention held  shortly  before  woman suffrage  was  adopted,       she
being then ninety- three  years  old.           Her pastorate continued until
September,      1869.
 - 277 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          269
In the fall  of 1866 the vestry of the church was remodeled  and
dedicated as  Lincoln  Hall.        During the year 1867 a new organ  was
purchased  and installed  in the church.
In October,      1870,     Rev.  Benjamin H.  Davis became pastor of the
church  and  remained  with  the  church  until  April  1,      1873.    Rev.
L.  W. Crossley became pastor April 1,   1877,   and closed  his  service
in  March,      1878.    At the  March meeting of  1879,     a committee was
appointed by the parish to take up the matter of having one minister
for  two parishes,    this  and the  Third  Universalist  Society at North
Weymouth.
After  hearing  several   candidates,       Rev.  Anson  Titus   became
pastor  of  the  two  societies.     This  arrangement  continued  until
April ,     1921 ,     when each society resumed having a minister by itself.
Rev.  Mr.  Titus  served  in  the  double  pastorate  from  1879  to
April,       1883,    when Rev.  B.  F.  Eaton was chosen minister and began
his  service in  December of that year.          He was also  acting  minister
of the church at West Scituate.           He remained until April,       1893.
Rev.  Ira  Morrison  was called  as  minister in  August,       1893,       and
served   the  two  churches  for  a  year  and  a  half.              The following
ministers  served during  the remainder of  the arrangement with  the
Third  Society :
Rev. Edward Morris,  from 1895 to  1898,
Rev.  Melvin S.  Nash,    from 1900 to  1909,
Rev.  Rufus H.  Dix,    from 1910 to  1914,
Rev. Arthur Mercer,   from 1915 to  1916,
Rev.  Charles C. Earle,   from 1917 to  1918,
Rev.  Elbert  W. Whippen,    from 1918  to  1920,
Rev.  Roger L.  Marble,  from 1920 to 1921.
The present pastor of the First Universalist  Church is  Rev. J.  L.
Dowson,     who was called  Oct.  1 ,     1922.
Second  UNIVERSALIST  SOCIETY,        SOUTH  WEYMOUTH
The first  preaching of the Universalist interpretation of the Bible
in  South Weymouth was heard some time in  the year 1835 .
This way of  explaining the  " Word"  had occasioned  much com-
ment,     being comparatively  new,     and had  also  caused  considerable
argument among the families of this  part of the town.           The parish
committee  of  the  Second  Parish,    consisting  of  Benjamin  Tirrell ,
Charles Pratt and Amos Merritt,    all  Universalists,    had been author-
ized  to supply the pulpit  (there being  a vacancy in the pastorate) .
They warned the society that they would get ministers of their own
faith,   but the warning was not heeded.          Charles  Pratt was selected
to furnish the first supply.         He engaged the services of Rev. Sylvanus
Cobb,     and so it was brought about that " Father Cobb, "  as  he was
known,     preached the first  Universalist  sermon in South Weymouth.
For about six  months this  committee supplied ministers  of  their
faith,   and the services were held in the Second Church (Old South) ,
there being at that time no other  church in  this  part of the town.
 - 278 - 
270              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
After the six  months those who believed in the liberal faith with-
drew from the society and held services  in  Rogers'    Hall.            From this
time  until  the  chapel  was  built  services  were  held   more  or  less
regularly,     as  they could be arranged,    in  Rogers'     Hall for some time,
in  John Reed's  Hall,    and in  the schoolhouse standing  at that time
on Pond Street,    then again in  Rogers'     Hall  and finally in the chapel
in  the present  location.
In the services  in  the chapel  Father Cobb was the  first  to preach,
Rev.  Thomas Whittemore the second,      and others  heard were Rev.
Otis A. Skinner,    Rev. John G. Adams,    Rev.  Hosea Ballou,   generally
known as  " Father Ballou, " and Rev. A. A.  Miner,     D.D.;    but those
oftenest  heard were  Father Cobb and Rev. Thomas Whittemore.
Among the  supplies  before  any  one  was  called  as  pastor  were
Rev.  Albert  A.  Folsom of  Hingham,    who used occasionally  to hold
a  5  o'clock  meeting,   as  it  was then  called,    Rev.  Columbus  Lake,
Second Universalist Church,  South Weymouth,   Mass.  ,    1850
Rev.   Charles  S.   Gifford,        Mr.  Berea,        Mr.  Preston,     J.   S.   Dennis,
Abram Norton,      Charles  Crocker,      C.  H.  Canfield  and  Dr.  Dodds.
These occupied  the time up to about  1848,     Mr. Crocker being here
in 1841  and  Mr.  Canfield in  1847 .
A conference  was  held  here  in  1841  or  1842,      and  among other
notable  speakers  was  Rev.  Thomas  Starr  King.        In  speaking  of
this  conference,    a lady who was present  recalled  the circumstance
that  she for  the first  time heard a woman speak in public.           Father
Cobb's wife attended the conference,    and,    feeling desirous of adding
her  word,      stepped  out  into  the  aisle  and said  her say,    and at the
close  started the hymn,   " When I  can read my title clear, "  and first
the ministers joined in,     and then the people,    till  all were singing.
The seats  in  those earlier  days were not especially comfortable,
sometimes being  cheap wooden chairs,    sometimes  benches without
backs,    but when the chapel was built they had arrived at the dignity
of settees.
 - 279 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          271
In the course of the years  1848 and 1849,   Rev. John N.  Parker
preached  here  quite  frequently,    and was finally  engaged  to  preach
regularly,     either  in  1849  or  1850,     thus  becoming  the  first  settled
pastor,     and he  soon  set  about  raising  money to  build  a place  of
worship.
The society when first  organized at about this time,   1848 or 1850,
was  known as  the  "Washington  Corporation,  "   and  the  members
of  that  corporation  were  stockholders  in  the building,      the  money
for which was raised largely through the efforts of Mr. Parker.           The
lot  upon which the building stands was given by Mr. Minot Tirrell .
The foundation for the chapel was begun on May 28,       1850,    with
appropriate  ceremonies,     for  which  occasion  Mr.  Parker  wrote  an
original  hymn;      the  frame was raised June 15,   and the house was
dedicated  on September 26.   The original  chapel was a small  rec-
tangular  building  without  a tower,    with two doors  on the  street,
and   the  words  " Universalist  Church"   and  the  date  " 1850 "   in
large  raised  and gilded  letters  over  them.
In  the afternoon of the day of dedication,     Bro.    J.  N.  Parker was
installed  to  the  care of the Universalist Society of this  place.
The women of the society had all  along been efficient helpers,    but
now  took  up  the  work in  a  new  direction  by forming  a  Ladies'
Circle.
They held their  first  fair  some time in  1851,   and the first  May
party  in  1852 or  1853,      and these have been annual events  and are
still  continued.
The  Sunday  school  was  organized  in  1849,      and  was  held  in
Rogers'      Hall,      with David S.  Murray as superintendent,    which office
he held until  1859  or  1860.    The number of  scholars  was between
forty and fifty.
In 1853 an entertainment was given,   at that time called  a Sabbath
school  exhibition.       The printed  program shows an arrangement  of
the exercises  in  two parts,   with twenty- two numbers in  each part.
In  1854  another  exhibition  was given  with  a like  arrangement  of
the program but with fewer numbers.
Mr.  Parker was succeeded in 1855 by Rev. Elmer Hewitt,    whose
installation  took place July 8 of that year.        An original hymn was
written for this occasion by D. S.  Murray,    a member of the Society ;
and among the  clergymen  present  and officiating  were  Dr.  A.  A.
Miner  and  Dr.   Wm.        H.   Ryder.             During  the  pastorate  of  Mr.
Hewitt the chapel was remodeled  raised and the tower added,    and
a basement,    or vestry,   put in for use as a Sunday school room about
1858,       and as  nearly as can be found the  Washington  Corporation
ceased to  exist,   and the  Second Universalist  Society  of  Weymouth
was formed at this time.
Mr.  Hewitt stayed with  the  parish  until  the  summer  of  1868,
then  Rev.  Jacob  Baker  preached  as  a  candidate  with  others  for
some months,    and in January,     1869,   was engaged  as  pastor.
The Church of Christ connected with the  society was organized
by  Mr.  Baker  in  July,     1869,    with  a  roll  of  fifty-nine  members,
 - 280 - 
272             ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
others being added from year to year until at the fiftieth anniversary
the  roll  numbered  one  hundred  and  twenty-two,    of  whom only
eighty were then living.
In 1870 the chapel was enlarged to its  present dimensions  at  an
expense of nearly or quite $3,000,   which,   by the efforts of the various
organizations   of  the  parish,       was  gradually  reduced  and  finally
cancelled at  the fiftieth  anniversary in 1900.
In the spring  of 1871  the  parish  decided that a new organ was
needed,      and J.  M. Whitcomb,    C.  Loring Stetson and  Capt.     C.  W.
Hastings were appointed  a committee to  procure one.
The organ  was  set  up in  the  church,      and  paid  for,     before  the
expiration of the time specified  in the contract,    and on September
23 the builder,       Dr.  J.  H.  Wilcox,    gave an organ concert to demon-
strate its  quality.
Mr.  Baker  resigned  the  pastorate  in  1878.    In  February,       1879,
Rev.  E.  A.  Perry was engaged and preached for the society a year,
living  at  the time in Scituate and being pastor of the church there
also.
In  May,       1880,      Rev.  A.  P.  Rein was engaged for  a year in  con-
nection  with  the  Scituate  parish,      as  was  Mr.  Perry.        He did  not
stay  the year,     as  he resigned  to  accept a call  in New Hampshire.
In  March,         1881,      Rev.  Anson Titus  was engaged as  pastor,     and
he stayed with the parish until March,   1883.    He was succeeded in
June,     1883,     by Rev.  Benj.     F.  Bowles,     who came also  to the parish
in  Abington where he made his  home.
In the spring of 1889 the by- laws of the society were so amended
as  to allow women to  become members and vote at the parish meet-
ings ,    and at the regular sessions  members have been added until the
names of the men and women are very nearly equal in number.
On Oct.  26,       1890,       Mr.  Bowles  preached  his  last  sermon  in  the
chapel.               From then until  March,    1891,    the pulpit was supplied by
his  wife,      Rev.  Ada C.  Bowles,  a large  part of the time  speaking
herself.              At this  later date,    on account of continued ill  health,    Mr.
Bowles resigned the pastorate.
In  June  of  the  same  year  Rev.  L.   Weston Attwood  came  as
pastor,      immediately  after  his  graduation  from Tufts  College.           A
service  in  recognition  of  the beginning  of  his  pastorate  was  held
Oct.  28,        1891 ,       Dr.   C.   H.  Leonard,     Dean  of  Tufts  College,    being
present and taking part in the services.
In  1896  Mr. Attwood was given a vacation of a year,   beginning
July 1,    for rest and a visit  to his friend Rev. I.  Wallace Cate,    D.D.,
in Japan,     and the pulpit  was supplied by different  clergymen,     but
the larger part of the time by Rev.  Flint  M.  Bissell.
A memorable occasion in the history of the society was the cele-
bration  of  its  fiftieth  anniversary,     Oct.  3,     1900.    The reading of a
paper  on  the  " History  of  the  Church"  by  Mrs.  Curtis  proved  a
most interesting feature of the afternoon exercises ;       also an original
poem by Mrs.  Brown.           The address  by Rev.  Dr.  F.  W. Hamilton
of  Boston  on " The Religious  Changes of a Half Century"  was  of
 - 281 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          273
exceeding  interest  and  greatly  enjoyed.       At 6  P.M. ,      supper  was
served  by the ladies  of the Social  Circle,     and  more than  one hun-
dred  guests  enjoyed  the  hospitality  of  the  happy  people  of  the
parish.               The evening  exercises  included  fine  music and  a stirring
address  by  Rev.  F.  O.  Hall  of  Cambridge,   on " Fifty  Years  as  a
Christian  Church.         Does it  Pay? "    At the  close  of  the  exercises
Mr.  Howard  H. Joy,   superintendent of  the  Sunday school,     invited
the  audience  to  rejoice  with  the  members  of  the  church  in  the
burning  of the mortgage which had so long  been a burden to  the
society,     thus  leaving the church free from debt.
On the 27th of June,    1902,     a special  parish  meeting was held  to
consider  renovating  the interior  of the auditorium  and putting  in
new pews.             Considerable money was pledged that evening,     and  in
the  course of a few weeks  enough  to  complete  the  work.                 Work
was begun the last of July or the first  of August and completed in
October.           The change consists of a metal ceiling  and cornice painted
in pale blue,    pink and white,   the walls painted in terra  cotta,       new
pews  of dark oak and the  wainscoting  of  the  room to  match,       an
enlargement  of  the platform,     new drapery  for  the  choir  rail,      up-
holstery of the platform  furniture,     a new carpet and electric  lights .
In  the  autumn of  1904,    the  Jane  T.  Clark  Mission  Circle  was
formed  and has done much good work.          At the annual meeting of
the  parish  in  May,      1905,      Capt.       C.  W. Hastings  as  executor  gave
into  the  hands  of  the  Prudential  Committee  a  deed  of  the  estate
of Mrs.  Joseph  Harding.           Mrs.  Pauline  P.   Hollis,     at  her  death,
Nov. 10,     1904,    gave her estate to  the society.          The society received
by bequest,     August,    1908,     $100 from the estate of James A. Reed.
In  the  fall  of  1911  the  health  of  Mr.  Attwood being  impaired
he sent in his resignation,   but was prevailed upon to finish  the year
if  possible  with such assistance as he might need.
Mr.  William  Wallace  Rose was engaged as  assistant  pastor.            At
the  close  of  the  year  in  the  spring  of  1912,      after  his  graduation
from Tufts College,    Mr. Rose was engaged as pastor,     Mr. Attwood's
resignation  having been accepted.
On June 21,     1912,   a reception was given by the parish to Mr. and
Mrs.  Attwood,     in  recognition  of his  twenty- one  years  pastorate,
and  was  largely  attended by the people  of  the  town,     irrespective
of denominational  lines.             Mr.  Gordon  Willis  for  the  parish  pre-
sented  to  Mr. Attwood twenty-one gold  pieces,    one for  each  year
of  his  pastorate.         The various  speakers  emphasized the  sympathy
and tenderness of Mr. Attwood in his  bearing toward all  with whom
he came in contact,   and the value of his life  as an example of citizen-
ship and the doctrine he preached  and represented.
A service of ordination  and installation  of  William Wallace Rose
to the Universalist ministry and pastorate of the Second Universalist
Church of Weymouth was held  Nov. 6,     1912.
In the spring of  1914  a  reception  was given  to  Rev.  and  Mrs.
Rose,   who were married in the previous December,    and was largely
attended  by friends  from  the  other societies  in the village.
 - 282 - 
274            ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
In June,     1915,    Mr.  Rose resigned  to accept a call  to  Bridgeport,
Conn. ,    and in November was succeeded by Rev. Fred A. Line.
During  his  pastorate  Mr.  Line  gave  a  yearly  report  at  each
parish meeting of the way his  time had been occupied in the busi-
ness  of the church.
A service  of  installation   to  the  pastorate  of  the  Universalist
churches of South Weymouth and Assinippi was held in this church
Sunday evening,     Dec.  5,     1915 .
During  the  winter  of  1915  Sunday  evening  illustrated  lectures
were given  and were  very  well  liked  and well attended,   and have
been since continued.
The concerts  at Easter,    Children's Sunday and Christmas,    given
by the children of the Sunday school,   have been of fine quality,    and
have been held  since the school was begun.
During the year  1917 a new organ was assured by subscriptions
from  the  parish,     almost  every  member being on the  list,       and an
Austin organ was set  up in the church in the autumn.     Also during
the summer a memorial window to  Mrs.  Lucy Allen Vining,     who
was for  many years  a  worshipper  and worker in the  church,    was
given by her son,    Mr. Andrew J.  Vining of San Francisco,     Cal.
In the  drive for  world  service during  the years  1918  and  1919,
the  subscriptions  conducted  by  the  pastor  in  cash  and  pledges
went over  the top,   and three  new memorial windows  were placed
and dedicated at  a regular morning service in the autumn of  1918.
On July 1,     1919,    Mr. Line tendered his  resignation to  take effect
October  1,        feeling  that duty called him to a parish  in great need.
The wording  was  such  that  the  parish  felt  the  request  must be
granted,     though it  was exceedingly regretted.     During his  pastorate
he had been busy with work for other organizations  in  addition  to
his  work for  the  church.           He held  many special  services  for  Odd
Fellows,      Knights Templars,    Firemen's Relief,    G. A. R.,     Boy Scouts,
Old  Colony  Women's  Club,    and gave addresses  to  business  men's
associations  and on other special  occasions .
A very pleasant reception was given to him and his family Tues-
day,     September 16,    in the vestry of the church.       Fully one hundred
and fifty  friends were escorted by the ushers  to meet Mr. Line and
his  family.             Mr.  Gordon Willis,   in behalf of the South Weymouth
parish,     presented  Mr.  and Mrs.  Line with a purse of gold.
At a special meeting of the parish in November,    1919,    it  was de-
cided  to  call  Rev. James H.  Peardon to minister to this  parish.
This was done and the pastorate was accepted,  to begin in Decem-
ber.               In January,     1921,     Mr.  Peardon resigned  to  accept a call to  a
church  in  South  Hingham.           He was followed  by Rev.  Charles  H.
Murch,        D.D.,     in  March,    1921,   but he remained only until October
of the same year.
Rev.  Barton  Watson came to  the parish in January,      1922,      and
concluded his  pastorate in  May,     1923.
William  D.  Veazie,    a  student at Tufts,    assumed charge in Sep-
tember,      1923 .

ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF   WEYMOUTH          275
THIRD  UNIVERSALIST  SOCIETY,            NORTH  WEYMOUTH  ( CHURCH  OF
GLAD  TIDINGS)
In order to improve an opportunity to secure a lot of land suitable
for  the  location  of  a church edifice,     and desiring  to  form a society
of  the  Universalist faith,    between twenty and thirty men attended
a legally  called  meeting in  the  First  District  schoolhouse,     Nov.  19,
1853,          and  organized  as  the  Third  Universalist  Society  in  Wey-
mouth.             Prominent among them were  Henry  Cleverly,    George W.
Cleverly,      Wilmot  Cleverly,      Samuel  Cleverly,      John  W.  Bartlett,
L. Q. Spear,    Seth Pratt,    Elisha  Pratt,    William Pratt,    E. M. Manson,
Elias  S.  Beals  and Noble Morse.          At a meeting held in  Harmonial
Third Universalist  Church,    North Weymouth
Hall the next March,   it was voted to have weekly lectures if sufficient
funds  were  obtained,     and  also  to  meet  on  Fast  Day  to  form  a
Sunday school.
The first  minister was Rev.  R.  L.  Killam of Scituate.          He began
April  1 ,       1855,   and preached in  Harmonial  Hall for three years.            For
this  he was paid  $6  a  Sabbath .
The deed of a lot  of  land at the corner of  Sea and Bridge  Streets
was  received  by the  society,     under  date  of  May 16,      1855.    This
same  year  a  Ladies'      Sewing  Circle   appears  to   have  come  into
existence,     and the  next year it  made a donation to the society.
In  1856,       also,    contributions were solicited  for  the formation  and
support  of  a choir.          A melodeon was probably rented for  the  use of
the choir,      for in  1858 it  was voted to  pay $25  upon it,     and also  to
 - 284 - 
276              ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
buy a melodeon.          This year preaching services  were conducted by
various  ministers  every other Sabbath evening.
In  August,        1858,      the  Norfolk  County  Universalist  Convention
was held in Harmonial Hall.
At the  annual  meeting  in  March,      1859,       Augustus  Beals  was
chosen clerk,     and he held the office  for  thirty-four years,      until  his
death  in  1893.    Beginning  May 1,     1859,       Rev.  E.  H.  Hawes  of
Stoughton  preached  on  alternate  Sabbaths  for  a  year,       and  was
followed the summer after by Rev.  Mr.  Killam .
For the next ten years the pulpit was supplied by various minis-
ters,      though mainly by the pastors  of neighboring churches .
During the  period  of the  Civil  War it  was difficult  to maintain
services ,      and  there  is  no record  of  regular  meetings,    although  the
Sunday school  was held part of the time.         In 1864 there began to
be a brighter  outlook.          The Sunday school was fully  organized,     or
reorganized,       and  was held  every Sabbath.           Webster  Hall  was en-
gaged  for  the  use  of  the  society,    and  meetings  were  held  nearly
every  Sabbath,     either  in  the  afternoon  or  the  evening.              In  1867
the  treasurer was able to  report all  bills  paid,     and a balance of $40
on hand.         At this time the pulpit was occupied by Rev.  Mr. Hewitt,
Rev.  Mr. Aldrich,    Rev.  Mrs.  Hanaford  and Rev. Miss Brown,     in
rotation,      and the meetings  were well attended.
At the  annual meeting in  1870 a committee was chosen  to con-
sider  the  expediency of erecting  a house of  worship.             Their  report
in 1871 led to  the adoption of plans,    the securing of funds and the
building  of  a chapel.         It was begun in September,     1872,       and was
dedicated  Jan.  16,      1873.    It  was furnished  with  settees  and  pro-
vided with  an organ.          The total  cost was nearly  $4,000,     to which
the  Ladies'        Sewing Circle contributed a very large  share.
On April  1,       1871,      Rev.  G.  W.  Skinner  of  Quincy became  the
regular  preacher  for  a year,    and he was followed  by  Rev.  G.  W.
Whitney  of  Quincy,       who  continued  as  pastor  until  July,       1878.
During his  pastorate  a church of twenty- two members was formed
in  June,      1874.    In 1878 an addition  was made to the chapel and a
vestry was finished  at  an expense of more than  $1,100,     by Elias  S.
Beals,   Esq.
Rev.  Anson Titus,    Jr.,     of the First Universalist  Church at Wey-
mouth Landing,    also  preached in the chapel from September,     1878,
to July,      1880,    and Rev. E. A.  Perry of Quincy succeeded him until
April 1 ,    1882.
In  1879  the  time of service was changed from evening  to  after-
noon.               From  1882  to   1884,      Rev.   R.  T.  Sawyer  of  Quincy  was
pastor.          Rev.  B.  F.  Eaton  became pastor  in  1885  and remained
until  the latter  part  of  1893,    - nearly  nine years .
In  1886,      with the help  of the  Ladies'    Sewing Circle,  the chapel
was carpeted,    pews were put in,   and the walls  were repainted  and
other  repairs  made at  a  cost  of about $700.
Rev.  I.   D.  Morrison succeeded Rev.  Mr.  Eaton in 1894,   and he
was followed by Rev. Edward Morris.
 - 285 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          277
In 1896 electric lights were installed in the chapel by the Ladies'
Sewing  Circle.            A trust fund was received  in  1897,     under the will
of Elias  S.  Beals,     Esq.
In January,     1898,   the twenty- fifth  anniversary of the dedication
of the chapel was fittingly  observed.          Rev.  Mr.  Morris resigned  this
year  and Rev. Judson P.  Marvin succeeded him,    and Mr.  Marvin
was followed  in  1900 by Rev.  Melvin S.  Nash.
An organ was  presented  to  the church  in  1902 by the children
of Elias S.  and Betsy T. Beals as a memorial of their parents.           This
brought about  an expense  of  about  $800 for enlarging  the chapel,
carpeting  the  floor  and retinting the walls and ceiling.      The organ
was dedicated Jan.  29,    1903.
The fiftieth  anniversary  of the society  was celebrated  the  week
beginning Nov. 15,   1903,   with special services,    including a historical
sermon  by Mr.  Nash,   addresses  by Rev.  Chester  G.  Miller,      Rev.
Dr.  James F. Albion,   Rev. Charles Conklin and Rev.  W. H.  Morri-
son,     and two historical  sketches,     one of the society by Mr.  Russell
H.  Whiting,      and one of the church by Mrs.  Wilmot Cleverly.
Anotable feature of the celebration was a reception  tendered to
Dea.      and Mrs. Wilmot Cleverly on the sixtieth  anniversary of their
marriage.
Rev. Mr. Nash was released from the pastorate in  1909 to become
the head of the Universalist Publishing House in Boston.          A farewell
reception  was tendered  him  December  1.      During his  pastorate  a
Men's  Club was organized which still  continues.
Rev.  Rufus H. Dix became pastor in  1910,     and he was followed
by Rev. Arthur Mercer in 1914.    Then came Dr.  Charles  C.  Earle,
and,    after him,   in 1918,    Rev.  Elbert  W. Whippen.          In  1920 he was
succeeded by Rev.  Roger S.  Marble.
In  1921  it  was  voted  to  sever  the  pleasant  relations  by which
the society had shared for  many years with the First Universalist
Society,    the  services  of  the same pastor.          It  is  now known as  the
Church of Glad Tidings .
In addition to the Beals Fund,    two other funds have been received
since,  one given by Lewis A.  Beals in  1904,     and one by William T.
Shaw.
The Sunday school has always been prominent in the service of
the society,     and has been fortunate in its  leaders.             Mr.  Augustus
Beals was superintendent for many years  until his death.         He was
succeeded  by  Mr.  Edwin  R.  Sampson,     who  also  served  a  long
term and was then  followed  by Mrs.  Sampson,    the  present  super-
intendent.
In November,     1922,     church and society were suddenly bereft by
the  death  of  their  pastor,     Rev.  Roger  L.   Marble,      after  a  brief
illness.          He was a young man of marked  ability  and  earnest  de-
votion.

FIRST  BAPTIST  CHURCH
Late in  the  autumn  of  1851  a little  prayer  meeting  of  Baptist
people was held at the home of Mrs. Samuel Gove on Broad Street.
Only four  or  five  were present.
It  led  immediately  to  the holding  of other  meetings  on  nearly
every evening  for  five  or  six  weeks  at  the  same place.           The at-
tendance  increased  so  that  it  was  necessary  to  remove  to  larger
accommodations.          Torrey's  Hall,   at the corner of  Washington and
Broad Streets ,     was secured and the meetings were continued.
During  the  winter  and  spring  following  occasional  preaching
services  were  held  by the pastors  of  neighboring  Baptist  churches
and by students from the Newton Theological  Institute.
In  June,       1852,        regular  Sabbath  services  were begun.          To help
defray expenses a Women's Sewing Society was formed and became
a  devoted  and permanent  source  of  aid.          Its  members  not  only
made articles  to sell,    but also  took in family sewing and lined shoes
and bound boots.
A Sunday school  was organized in  March,    1853,    and on Feb. 7,
1854,      the  First  Baptist  Church was formally organized.             Five men
and  fifteen   women  presented  letters  from  various  churches  and
banded  themselves  together  and  adopted  Articles  of  Faith  after
the Baptist order.         The pastors of the Baptist churches in Braintree
and Hingham assisted .
The  only  other  business  of  the  day  was  the  appointment  of
February  14  as  a  day  of  fasting  and  prayer  for  God's  blessing.
Besides  Rev.  George  Deland  of  Braintree  prominent  leaders  in
this  whole movement were  Rev. Jonathan Tilson of Hingham and
Dea.       Elias  Vining .
At a business  meeting held  March  13  Elias  Vining  and George
Graves  were  elected  deacons  to  serve  during  life,   and  two  com-
mittees  were chosen,   one to look after  the spiritual  interests  of the
church,       and  the  other  to  take measures for  a church building.         A
lot  on the  southeast  corner of  Washington and Broad Streets  was
soon  bought.                Rev.  H.  C.  Coombs of  Middleborough was  engaged
to supply the pulpit and to collect  money for a house of worship.
In October he  was succeeded by Rev.  Hervey Fitz .
Acouncil was assembled Aug.  17,    1854,   for the recognition of the
church.               The recognition  service  was held by special invitation  in
the Union Church,    and  Rev.  Jonas  Perkins took part in it.
The  new  church  was  admitted  to  membership  in  the  Boston
South  Association,      which  appointed  a  committee  of  its   own  to
assist  in  securing  money for  the desired  house of  worship.           They
secured an appropriation of $1,500 from the Baptist State Conven-
tion.
In December Rev. Andrew Dunn of  Bridgewater was invited  to
succeed Mr. Fitz.         After two months he was invited to the pastorate
and became the first  settled pastor March 18,   1855.    Twenty mem
 - 287 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          279
bers had already been added to the church,   and during this pastorate
of a little  over  three  years,     fifty  more were received  into  member-
ship.
Ahouse of worship known as the " chapel,"  a plain building with
no  steeple  and containing only one room,   but large  enough to  seat
three hundred people,   was erected on the building  lot  of the  church
and dedicated July 12,   1855.    The total  cost was $3,200,       a part  of
which continued  as  a  burdensome debt for  some years.
Mr.  Dunn closed his  labors Jan.  31,     1858,      and removed to  West
Randolph.
Without  a  pastor  the  church  quickly  became divided  into  two
parties,    and would soon have fallen  into  a more serious  condition
but for  the  timely  agreement  upon  a  new pastor.          Rev.  Levi  A.
Abbot was called from Milford and came May 1,     1858.    He proved
to be a peacemaker and was beloved by all .
During  a pastorate  of  five  years  forty- three  were  received  into
the church.              Mr. Abbot was also interested and influential in public
affairs .               He as  well  as  other  Weymouth  pastors  served  on  the
school  committee  of the  town,   and became chairman.      He also
served  a  term in the State  Legislature.          He left  to  accept a call  to
Middleborough,    in  May,    1863.
In  December,     1858,     the  Boston South  Association  held  a three
days'    meeting with the church.
Mr.  Abbot was succeeded Nov. 1,    1863,   by Rev. Gideon Cole of
Sheldonville.            The next summer,    because of the increased  needs  of
the church,     it  was decided  to  build  a larger  house.        Accordingly,
the present location was purchased and measures adopted to  secure
the necessary funds.      It was a great task.         The pastor by energetic
appeals outside the parish obtained upward of $2,000 of the desired
amount,     " from all  over the country. "   At length the building  was
erected and was dedicated Feb. 1,   1866,   the total cost being $14,500.
The " chapel "  had been sold  a short  time before,     whereupon the
Union Church sent  a cordial  invitation  to  occupy their  house  of
worship until the new house was completed.       The vestry  was  so
nearly  ready  to  use,   however,     that  it  was deemed inexpedient  to
accept the offer,    and it  was declined with appreciation of the kindly
spirit  shown.
Mr.  Cole continued  until Jan.  1,     1871,     when,      on  account  of  ill
health  in his family which required  removal to  a different  climate,
the church with deep regret granted him dismission  to  a church in
Minnesota.              During  his  pastorate  one  hundred  and  sixteen  were
added to the church.
The  next  pastor  was  Rev.  Charles  H.  Rowe,     who  came  from
Dorchester April  1,    1871,    and  remained  three  years.       Thirty  had
been  received into  the  church  when he  was  granted  dismission,
April  30,       1874,    to become pastor of  the  church in Wollaston.            The
people were attached to him and were reluctant  to  let  him go.
Rev.  William  C.  Wright of  Pawtucket,     R.  I. ,     accepted  a call  to
become pastor,   and began his labors Oct.  1,    1874.   He also remained

three  years .                     Through his  interest  and influence  as  a musician,     a
fine pipe organ  was placed in the  church.        He was followed March
1,       1878,      by  Rev.  Philip  A.  Nordell of Arlington,  who served  until
December,      1882.   He then became pastor of the First  Church,    New
London,         Conn. ,     and  ten  years  later  became  a  professor  in   the
University  of  Chicago.          In May,    1882,    the Articles of Faith of this
church were printed.
Next came Rev.  Seth J.  Axtell,   Jan. 1,   1883.    He had letters  of
dismission  from  the  church  in  West  Medway,    but the  service  he
had just closed was that of president of Leland University,    a school
for freedmen in New Orleans,   where he had been for four years.          He
remained until  June  1,     1888,     and  then  left  to take the presidency
of  Pella  University in  Iowa,     and  a year later  became professor  of
Greek in  Kalamazoo College  in  Michigan.
On Oct.  1,      1888,     Rev. Wesley L. Smith,    from Providence,     R.  I. ,
began  a  pastorate  that  closed  May 1,     1894.    In  1889  the  church
voted  unanimously to  become incorporated,   and thus  the  society
that had hitherto held all  property was no longer a necessity.
In 1892,     about thirty Baptist people in Braintree,    who desired to
form  a church  to  succeed  the one that had ceased  to  exist  many
years  before,       were  welcomed into  the  fellowship  of  this  church as
a  branch  church.          The  next  year  twenty-two  members  of  this
branch  church  were  given  letters   of  dismission  that  they  might
organize  a  separate church.            The Braintree church was recognized
May 12,         1893.    At the  close  of  Mr.  Smith's  pastorate  there  had
been  seventy  additions  to  the  church  membership.        He went to
the  pastorate  of the  Baptist  Church at  Fells,     Mass.
Rev.  C.  F.   Clarke  of  Swanzey,     N.  H.,     came Feb.  1,     1895,     but
continued  only  two years  and  three  months,                     the  shortest  pas-
torate since  the formation of the church.      He was particularly  un-
fortunate in that his son fell  sick and died soon after he came.
On May 15,     1897,    Rev. Frank B.  Cressey,   who had been a pastor
in San Francisco,    but was then residing in Boston,   began to supply
the pulpit,      and received  a formal call  the next August.
The church  began  in  1902  the  practice  of electing  deacons  to
serve  for  three years instead  of for  life.
On Feb. 7 and 8,    1904,   the church observed its fiftieth  anniversary.
There was  an  historical  sermon  by  the  pastor,     Mr.  Cressey,      and
other  parts  were taken  by  most of  the  Protestant  pastors  of  the
town,    and there was also an address by the venerable Rev. Jonathan
Tilson,       who had  been  prominent at  the formation  of  the church.
These exercises were followed the next evening by a reunion supper
and roll  call.
Mr.  Cressey  closed  his  labors  with this  church in August,     1908.
He was  succeeded  in  December  by  Rev.  Robert  H.  Carey.     who
served  until  September,     1910.
Rev.  Philip  A.  Nordell  was acting  pastor during the  remainder
of 1910 and the next year.           Then followed Rev. Chester J.  Underhill
as  pastor  from  February,     1912,    to June,     1916,    and Rev. James W.

Tingley  from  December,      1916,     to  April  27,     1919.    Rev.  Charles
W. Allen came Nov. 2,    1919,     and is  the present  pastor.
The  Ladies'           Missionary  Society  was  organized  in  1894.    Mrs.
Nellie  M. Fox,    daughter of  William B.  and Abigail Hollis,     and wife
of  Rev.  Earl  M. Fox,    was engaged with her husband in  missionary
service  in  Assam for  seven  years,    from September,     1911,     to  1918.
In September.      1922,     Miss  Fanny Hollis,    daughter of  Otis J.  Hollis,
began service at a Baptist school  in  Porto  Rico.
In  1905  the  choir  was organized  as  a  Choral Society.             In  1909
the  Farther  Lights  Society  was formed,     and in  1913  the  Ladies'
Sewing  Circle was newly organized.
BRIEF  OUTLINE  OF  THE  CATHOLIC  CHURCH  IN  WEYMOUTH
The Parish  of St.  Francis Xavier was the  first  parish  of  this  de-
nomination,     and embraced territorially  the whole town.        The first
priests  of  the  parish  were  Rev.  Fathers  Roddan and  Lynch,     who
came to the town in  1851,   and the first  services  were held in East
Weymouth that same year in private houses.         After a few months
the place of worship was changed,   and services were held in Tirrell's
Hall  at  Weymouth  Landing.        In  1854  Rev.  Father  Roche took
charge of the parish,   but it  was not until  1859 that the  first  church
was erected,      which was located  on Gravel  Hill,    which is  now the
Catholic Cemetery,   Middle and Washington Streets.          From 1858 to
1866  this  church was a mission  of the  Abington  Parish,       and  was
cared for by Father Roche.          Weymouth's first  pastor,    in  1866,    was
Father  Timothy Hannigan,    who remained  here  until  the summer
of  1869.     He  was  succeeded  by  Rev.  Hugh  P.   Smyth.                 About
Thanksgiving  time,    1869,   the church building  was burned  down.
For a period of one year the Catholics held services in the old Town
House on  Washington Street,    opposite  the  cemetery.           Meanwhile
the South Weymouth church had been built  by Father Smyth and
dedicated  to  Saint  Francis  Xavier.        Here all  the  Catholics  of Wey-
mouth worshipped for the period of a year or  more.          The year fol-
lowing the Catholics  of  East Weymouth held  religious  services  in
Randall's Hall in the rear of  Canterbury's  shoe shop.        In 1872 the
foundation  for  the  East  Weymouth  Catholic  Church  was  built.
The corner  stone was laid in August,     1873,    the present  church  of
the  Immaculate Conception.           At a later  period land in the  rear  of
the church was bought of John P.  Lovell,     and an old- style  cottage
on the  new land  was  made  over  into  a  parish  house  for  Father
Jeremiah Millerick,    who succeeded  Father Hugh P. Smyth.           Sacred
Heart Church at  Weymouth Landing was nearing  completion,    and
Father   Smyth  took  up  his  permanent  residence   at  Weymouth.
The Sacred Heart Church was on Washington Street,    and the parish
house was  the  old  Wales  Hotel made over.          Until  the  new church
building  was completed,      the  Catholics  worshipped  in  the  hall  in
the rear  of the hotel,  which was formerly used for dancing parties
during the cattle  shows.           The former rectory  is  now the  Convent
 - 290 - 
282           ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
for  the  Sisters  of  the  Sacred  Heart  Parish.          Father  Smyth  next
built  Saint  Jerome's  chapel  at  North  Weymouth.          Father  Hugh
P.  Smyth,      who is  known as the " man of the seven churches,"  also
built  the  churches  at  Hingham,      Cohasset,    Scituate  and Kingston.
In  East Weymouth  Father  Millerick  was  succeeded  by  Father
Daniel  Healy.            Rev.  Michael  Begley     1892- succeeded  Father
Healy.           He was succeeded by Father James Allison,    who was fol-
lowed  by  the  present  pastor,       Rev.   Cornelius   I.    Riordan.             The
South Weymouth church  remained a mission of  the Sacred  Heart
Church at Weymouth until  1907,    when Rev. John A. Butler became
the  first  pastor.         Father  Hugh P.  Smyth went to  Boston  in  1883
and was succeeded by Rev. John J.  Murphy,    who in turn was suc-
ceeded by Rev. John B. Holland,   pastor of the Sacred Heart Church.
About 1914 Father Butler at  South Weymouth was promoted to
the  pastorate  of a large  Cambridge parish.         He was succeeded by
Rev.  D.  P.  Crimmins,   the present incumbent.
At  North  Weymouth  the  small  wooden  building  erected  by
Father Smyth has been replaced by a beautiful  stone church.
At  Weymouth  the  new  rectory   is   the  beautiful  old  colonial
Cowing House,     recently purchased.
TRINITY  PROTESTANT  EPISCOPAL  CHURCH
At the  time  of  beginning  service  of  the  Protestant  Episcopal
Church in  Weymouth there were a number of people,   members of
that  Church,    living  in  the  town  but  connected  with  the  other
churches.            Some of these were members of Christ  Church,   Quincy,
and  Emmanuel  Church,       Boston,      and  some  had  relatives  in  the
ministry of  the Episcopal Church,     or,    for instance,    Ralph Haskins ,
whose  brother,     Rev.  David  Green  Haskins,     was  a  rector  in  the
Episcopal  Church.              The question  of  starting  regular  services  had
been  talked  of,      and  Bishop  Eastburn  consulted,    but  he did  not
give  much  encouragement.        Occasional  services  had  been  held in
houses,       but finally,   in  1867,     at a meeting of those interested,     it  was
decided  to  try  and hold  services  in  Williams  Hall on the corner of
Washington  and  Front  Streets .              Mrs.  Ebenezer  Hunt was chosen
to  procure  the  hall,     which  she  did,     and  on  July  7,        1867,         was
held  the  first   service  in  the  hall.           The  Rev.  Henry  Burroughs,
rector  of  Christ  Church,    Quincy,    officiated at the service,     and was
assisted  by  Rev.  David  Green Haskins.          Messrs.      Ebenezer  Hunt
and Edward Avery were appointed to  arrange for the continuance
of the services,    and they were held in Williams Hall.        The hall being
found too small to accommodate the congregation,    Messrs.     Edward
Avery,       Ebenezer  M.  Hunt,       Lewis  M.  Pratt and  Charles  C.  Jewett
were chosen a committee to  arrange for a larger  place.            Mr. Jewett
was  senior  warden of  Christ  Church,     Quincy.         The  result  of the
work of this committee was the purchase,  on Sept.  10,    1867,     of the
homestead  of the late  Atherton  W.  Tilden  on  Front  Street,     and
the  alteration  of  this  house  so  that  it  might serve  for  a church.
 - 291 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          283
Messrs .          E.  M. Hunt and Edward Avery were chosen as  a  building
committee,     and the alterations  were  completed  Dec.  7,      1867,      the
first  service being held in the church Dec.  8,      1867 .
The parish  was organized  as a free  church  Nov.  11,    1867,      under
the name of Trinity  Church,     Weymouth,    and the following  officers
elected :         senior  warden,        Edward  Avery;       junior  warden,       E.   P.
Butler ;         vestrymen,     Ralph  Haskins,    John  M. Walsh,    E.  M.  Hunt,
Wm.     J.  Hunt and Wm.    S.  Wallace.
The opening service in the church Dec. 8,   1867,    was held by the
Rev. Henry Burroughs of Christ Church,   Quincy,   who also preached
the  sermon.            During the  time from July  7,   to  December  8,     1867,
regular   services   had  been   held   in   the   hall   by  the  following
clergymen :            Rev.   Henry  Burroughs,       Rev.   Dr.   Nicholson  of  St.
Paul's,         Boston,       Rev. F. Gardiner and the  Rev.  S.  R.  Slack.           The
following  clergymen  also  officiated  in  the  hall  and in  the church :
E.   M.  P.   Wells,      F.   Huntington,     Rev.   Mr.  Coolidge,       Rev.  Mr.
Mills,        Rev.  Mr.  Converse and  Rev.  Mr. Gifford.       A call was  ex-
tended  to  the  Rev.  Henry  Burroughs  to  become  the  rector  at  a
salary  of  $ 1,000  a year.
The first  Episcopal visitation to the parish was made by the Rt.
Rev.  Manton Eastburn,     D.D.,     Bishop  of  Massachusetts,    May 24,
1868,      when a class  of ten was confirmed,   and on July 4,     1869,     the
same bishop confirmed a class  of  twelve persons.            The church was
consecrated  by  Rt.      Rev.  Benjamin  H.  Paddock,      D.D.,       Bishop  of
Massachusetts,      May 21,     1874,     and  the  following  clergymen  have
served  as  rectors :          Rev.  Samuel  R.  Slack,    Rev.  Henry  Burroughs,
Rev.  T.  W. Street,      Rev.  F.  O.  Barstow,    Rev.  W.  F.  Lloyd,    Rev.
W.  C.  Winslow,    Rev.  John A.  Jerome,     Rev.  Charles  Luke Wells
and Rev. William Hyde,  the present rector.          During the rectorship
of  Rev.  Wm.       Hyde the church has been repaired  and improved so
that the interior has been largely changed.          The chancel and altar
have been improved  and enlarged,    and  a vested  choir  organized,
besides other improvements of great importance in carrying on the
services .
THE  CHURCH  OF  THE  HOLY  NATIVITY
In the latter part of 1915 a movement was started looking toward
the  establishment  of  an  Episcopal  Church  in  South  Weymouth.
Mr.  Robert  Pierce  Casey  of  Boston,     then  a student  at  Harvard
College preparing for the ministry,   saw in this village a field for his
chosen  work,    and  set  about  actively  canvassing  the  community.
He found a number of families  anxious for the establishment of an
Episcopal  Church,    and the matter was brought to  the attention  of
the  Eastern  Diocese,    through  a  series  of  conferences  between  the
Bishop,       the  Rt.      Rev.  Samuel G.  Babcock,     and  a voluntary  com-
mittee of interested people.
Colonel Cornman,   a retired army officer and ardent  Episcopalian ,
offered  his  drawing  room,    in which to  hold  services,      if  a sufficient
number of people were found to make it  advisable  to go  on.
 - 292 - 
284               ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
Mr.  Casey worked  persistently,    and it  was decided  to hold  the
first   services  on  Christmas  Day,      1915.    The twenty-eight  people
present at the first  service were exceedingly pleased with Mr. Casey
in his capacity as lay reader,    and most enthusiastic over what they
could now feel  was a  real  beginning of an Episcopal  Mission .
The  Church  of  the  Holy  Nativity was the  name decided  upon
as  appropriate,     and each Sunday saw an increased attendance  and
great  enthusiasm.            The Diocese  assigned  the  Rev.  Wm.        Love of
Cambridge to  be priest in charge of the mission,    and the first  com-
munion  service  was  held  in  February,    with  the  Rev.  Dr.  Patten
as  celebrant,    with sixteen  communicants.
A little  later  a Sunday school was started and a large number of
children  enrolled.        On Dec.  13,     1916,    the first  confirmation service
was held,      when four  members were  received  into  the  church,       and
thirty- two more have been  added since.
Toward the end of  1918  it  became apparent that the growth  of
the  Mission  warranted  a larger  meeting  place,     and  a committee
consisting  of  W.  Carleton  Barnes,    Geo.    N.  Eck and Wm.    J.  Hol-
brook was named to take charge of the whole matter of  providing
for  a  church  building.           Mrs.  Edward  B.  Nevin  very  generously
offered  a lot  from  her  estate  on  Columbian  Street,    and an active
canvass  was  made for  funds with  which to  build  a church.               This
appeal  met a  most ready response,    and it became possible to start
construction in the summer of  1919.
The building is of Weymouth seam-face granite,   and the architect ,
Mr.  John Vining,    designed a church charming in its  simplicity and
beauty,    which,    though small,    is of the most approved ecclesiastical
architecture.            The interior woodwork is  of black walnut with deep
cream- tinted  walls.         The altar  was the gift  of  Christ  Church,    in
Oswego,       N.  Y.
The  building  was  formally  dedicated  by  Bishop  Babcock  on
Easter  Sunday,   April 4,    1920.    There has been a steady and most
satisfactory  growth in  the parish,    which at this  time numbers  ap-
proximately one hundred people,   with  nearly fifty  children in  the
Sunday school and sixty-nine communicants.
Mr. Casey has continued as lay reader,    with the Rev. Wm.     Love
in  attendance  at  least  one Sunday in  each  month.
In  1921  Rev.  Frank L.  Luce became rector  of this  church.
FAITH  MISSION  CHURCH
Some thirty years ago a  prayer meeting was held in the home of
Mr. John Bean on School Street,     East Weymouth,   for the purpose
of  interesting  people who were not  disposed  to  attend  any church
services .           Other  meetings  followed,    and after  two  or  three  years,
the attendance  outgrew the place of meeting,    and a hall known as
Temperance Hall,     in  Commercial Square,    was hired.          The interest
continued to increase  and a  mission was organized about five years
after  the  first  meeting.          The work of  the  mission was especially
 - 293 - 
ECCLESIASTICAL  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH          285
directed  to  the  help  of the  poorest  people,    drunkards,      and down-
and-outs;      and they were encouraged to sober and industrious living.
Their families were looked after,   the home life  was made pleasanter,
and many were brought under the gracious influence of the simple
gospel.
After the death of Mr. Bean,   in 1905,   his grocery store was made
over  into  a gospel  hall,   which was dedicated  on Labor Day,     1907 ,
and  regular  Sabbath services  were instituted.
In June,      1915,    an independent church was organized with thirty
members,      under the  name of  Faith  Mission  Church.             The church
is   supported  entirely  by the free-will  offerings  of  the  people,      and
without  recourse  to  suppers  or  entertainments  of any sort.             Mrs.
George H.  Loud was appointed pastor,    and is  still  serving  in  that
capacity.
The so-called "fourfold gospel"  is  taught,               " Christ our Savior,
our  Sanctifier,      our Healer,    and our coming  Lord.   "
Many people have been helped who stay in  the  community only
a short  time,      and have then  gone  to  other  parts  of  the  country,
some even  to  Canada and  across  the ocean.               So the  little  mission
is  gratefully  remembered far  and wide,   while its  local membership
increases  slowly,   being only about forty at the present time.
The  church   is   affiliated   with  the   Christian   and  Missionary
Alliance founded by Rev. A.  B.  Simpson and having headquarters
in New York.          It has educated and sent out the first foreign mission-
ary from Weymouth,    Rev.  Merrill  E.  Barter,    who went to  Congo,
West Africa,     in  1917 .
CONCLUSION
To-day  there  are  eighteen  churches  in  the  town,    representing
seven denominations .
While differing  in forms,   methods,    polity and doctrine,    they  are
all  earnestly  and peaceably  engaged  in  promoting  the  moral  and
civic uplift  and the  spiritual  welfare  of  the people of the  town.
As one,    they have always stood for loyalty to the town,    the State
and the Nation,    for the advancement of mankind,   and for the peace
of the world.
Taken together  they  are  a glorious  sisterhood  vitally  interested
in  advocating and exemplifying the profound sentiment with which
these  pages  began,    and  with  which  they  may  fittingly  close -
"In the name of God.             Amen!  "

ORIGIN OF THE EARLY ROADS OF WEYMOUTH,
AND THE EARLY SETTLEMENTS
Apaper read before the Weymouth Historical Society,    Jan. 29,   1890,    by
Quincy L.  Reed,   Esq. ,   of South Weymouth.
Previous  to  the  settlement  of  New England by the whites,      the
Indians  in  their  travel  and communication from different  points,
instead  of  roads,    had their  trails.         These trails,    from evidences  of
their  settlements,   and other evidences,    instead of changing,   as one
would naturally  suppose,    appear to  have been permanently estab-
lished.       The ponds and rivers were their landmarks;     their places of
settlement,       usually on the easterly incline  of the hills  or high land,
either  near  the  seashore  or  the  ponds  and  rivers.       Among these
different  trails  throughout  New England,    several  of them appear
to  have intersected  Weymouth at  different  points,    some of  them
as principal,    or through,    trails,    the others as intermediates.       Among
the  through  trails,     one  of  them  leading  from  Plymouth  through
Duxbury,      Marshfield  and Scituate,    which  I  shall designate as  the
Plymouth  or  Duxbury  Trail,      intersected  at  a point  near Accord
Pond  in  Hingham,    thence  along  the  westerly  point of Hingham,
through the Tuttle neighborhood to East Weymouth,   thence follow-
ing  Commercial Street,   around King Oak Hill to Monatiquot River
or  tidewater.             Until the period  of  turnpikes,     this  was the  line  of
travel  and communication between  Plymouth and Boston.        Fine
specimens  of  Indian  relics  have  been found  along  this  trail.             At
this   period,           Middleborough,      which  was  a central  point  between
Plymouth and  Mount Hope,    the home of  Massasoit,  had a large
Indian  population,   and another  important  trail  was the  Middle-
borough,       Bridgewater  and Abington,    which intersected  the  Plym-
outh and Duxbury at Accord Pond,    thence to East Weymouth and
Monatiquot River,     and until the period of turnpikes,   or until " the
way"  from  Weymouth to  Abington  was laid  out,   was the  line of
travel  from  Middleborough  to  Boston.           This  " way"  was what is
now known as  Front  Street  and  Pond Street,    known as  " the  old
road "  after  the period of turnpikes.       Another move of ashore trail
was the  Cohasset  and Hingham,    which intersected  the Plymouth
and  Duxbury at  East Weymouth.       But the most important trail,
and one that has certain  facts  connected with it,   that  to one un-
acquainted would appear almost a  mystery,   was the trail  that con-
nected  the  northern  and southern  bays of  New England,     Massa-
chusetts  and  Narragansett  Bays,    which  I  shall  designate  as  the
Bay Trail,       and  in  describing  its  location  shall  commence at  the
termination of the  Plymouth and Duxbury,     at  Monatiquot  River
or  tidewater;        passing  along  Front Street,    through Summer Street
to the junction of West and Summer Streets,    thence around partly
