352                    MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
At a town meeting held  on November 17,     an  appropriation  of
$4,000  was  voted  to  defray  the  expense  of  recruiting.             A com-
mittee  of  twenty was appointed to  aid in this  work,    and secured
so favorable  results  that the town was enabled to fill  its  quota.
This  committee  consisted  of  the  following:       James  Humphrey,
L.  L.  Bicknell,    Atherton  N.  Hunt,      Elias  S.  Beals,    William  White,
John W. Loud,   Abner Holbrook,    David S.  Murray,   Samuel Lincoln,
Nelson  Blanchard,     Jacob  N.  Baker,       Bela  Vining,    John S.   Fogg,
Stephin S.  Foye,    Henry Newton,   James Tirrell,   Benjamin F.  White,
Stephen  W.  Nash,     Josiah  Reed,    Isaac  N.  Hollis,    John  O.   Foye
and John  P.  Lovell.
During the late fall and early winter of 1863,   the government,
realizing  that  in  all  probability  the war was to  continue  another
year,       experienced  a  good  deal  of  uneasiness  as  to  what  would
occur when the time of the  three- year troops who enlisted  in 1861
and the early part of 1862 should expire.        To lose all these seasoned
troops  and  have  them  replaced  with  new and  untried  men,      even
if   the  numbers  could  be  made  good,     was  not  encouraging,       es-
pecially  as  the  strenuous  regulations  in  regard  to physical  exami-
nations  which were rigidly  enforced  in  the  earlier  years  had  been
much modified,     and  much of  the  material  which  was  now being
sent  into  the  army was notoriously unfit  for  military  service.            It
was  not  at  all   uncommon for  new recruits  to  break down with a
few  months'       service  necessitating  their  discharge.         To  meet  this
prospect  the  government  resorted  to  strong  inducements  for  the
three  years'        men to  re-enlist  by offering  a two weeks'        furlough
and  a  liberal   bounty.         This  secured  many re-enlistments  which
were  counted  the  same  as   new  enlistments  to  the  credit  of  the
place from which they came.        On the other hand,  many,    especially
the family men,    were war weary and longed for home.          Could they
be blamed if   the inducements  offered  had for  them little  attrac-
tion?     In the spring  of  1864 the  President  issued  a call  for  more
men,       and Weymouth had to get busy and secure recruits  for  what
was fondly hoped would be the last  campaign of the war.
General  Grant had been placed at the head of  the  armies  and
made  his   headquarters  with  the  army  in  Virginia.          At a  town
meeting  held  May 20  it  was  voted  "that  the  Treasurer  be  au-
thorized  to  borrow  $10,000  to  aid  in  recruiting  volunteer  soldiers
to  fill  the quota of this  town under the last call of the President! "
On June  8  it  was  voted  " that  the  town  appropriate  $125  to
each volunteer who shall  be recruited  in anticipation of any future
call of the President of the United States during the present year,
and  that  the  Treasurer  be  authorized  to  borrow  $10,000  or  so
much as may be necessary for  the purpose of paying the same. "
It was voted " that the Chairman of the Selectmen be authorized
to  recruit  in  anticipation  of  any future call  for  volunteers  by the
President of the United States. "
A committee   was   appointed,      consisting   of  Elias   S.   Beals ,
Nathaniel  Blanchard  and  the  selectmen,   to  prepare  resolutions  to
 - 361 - 
THE  CIVIL  WAR,       1861-65                                   353
be presented to  the same meeting,   and this  committee reported  the
following:
Resolved,       That this  town  believes  and  is  fully  satisfied  that  the  enrollment
for  this  town is  very nearly or  quite  twenty per  cent  larger  than  is  the enroll-
ment of the average towns in the district,     and that a large  number of  persons
have been  enrolled  in this  town  who ought  not  to  be  enrolled,    and  who  are
utterly  incompetent  to  perform  military  services,       and  the  town  respectfully
requests  the  proper  authorities  to  revise  the  enrollment of this  town and have
the enrollment made up in  a manner that  shall  be as  equitable as  possible.
Resolved,       That this  town  believes  that   their   boards  of  Selectmen  and As-
sessors  for  the past and present  years  will  not  compare  unfavorably in  respect
to ability and integrity with those  of  our  neighboring  towns,    and that  we feel
aggrieved  that  they have been entirely  ignored in the  whole  matter  of  making
up the enrollment of this  town,    while in  such  neighboring  towns  assessors  and
other town officers  have been appointed to that duty.
If   I   interpret  aright  the  foregoing  resolutions   the  enrollment
list  was  made up by a board  or  committee  appointed  either  by
state  or  national  authorities,   and  that  while  in  other  towns  the
town  officers  had been  placed  upon  these  boards,     in  Weymouth
the town officers had been ignored.
The inference is  that had this work been performed by the local
authorities  the 20 per cent  of  incompetents  spoken  of  would  not
have been included  in the  enrollment  list,  and the  quota  of  the
town would have been reduced  to  that extent.
Incidentally,       fewer  incompetents  would  have  gotten  into  the
service.
The  occasion  which  called  for  the  above  resolutions  was  the
resignations  of  Zachariah  L.  Bicknell  and James Humphrey from
the board  of  selectmen.         Apparently they considered  the  manner
of making up the enrollment board a reflection  upon the honor or
integrity of the town officers .
Both of them being men of broad minds they felt  that in those
trying  times  the  town had  a right  to  have at  the  helm  men in
whom implicit  confidence  could  be placed.       They were  asked  to
withdraw their resignations,   which they did.
The board of selectmen at that time consisted  of three members.
Mr.  Humphrey and  Mr.  Bicknell  served  the whole period  of  the
war.          Mr.  Allen  Vining  served  during  the years  1861  and  1862,
when he was succeeded by Mr. Noah Vining,    who remained  upon
the board many years.
At the same meeting above mentioned,   it  was  voted  " that  the
Selectmen be authorized  to  receive  in  Boston Company H of  the
Twelfth  Regiment  Mass.       Volunteers   on  their   return  from  the
war,    and that  they procure a band of  music and escort  them  free
of  expense  to  Weymouth  Landing  or  such  other  place  as  they
may agree upon.  "    This regiment was now on the front  of Peters-
burg,    and its  term of enlistment was about to  expire.
The  fourth  and  last  company  sent  out  from  Weymouth  was
Company H,      of  the  Fourth  Regiment  of  Heavy Artillery,      which
was enlisted in August of  1864 for a term of one year.
 - 362 - 
354                    MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
The officers  of  this  company were,     captain,     Andrew J.   Garey;
first   lieutenant,       Charles  A.   Morrill;      second  lieutenant,        John W.
Bates.                   This   regiment  did   useful   service   in  the  forts   around
Washington until its  discharge on June 17,     1865.
The fond  hope which  had been  cherished  that  the autumn  of
1864  was  to  see  the  end  of  the  terrible  conflict  was  doomed  to
disappointment.          Both  armies  held well  intrenched positions,     and
it  became  to  a large  extent  a question  of which must first  fail  for
want of  men and  means.            The North was confident  that the war
would close  by the defeat  of  the  Confederate  Army.           The South
must  have  seen  that this  end was inevitable,   but still  maintained
the  conflict  with  dogged  determination.          The  principal  military
event  of  the  fall  of  1864  was  Sherman's  march from Atlanta  to
the  sea,      which commenced on November 16,     and which has been
celebrated  in  song  and story.           This  army of sixty  thousand men,
marching  in  four  columns  and  living  upon  the  country  through
which  it   passed,    desolated  a fertile   region  sixty  miles  in  width
and three hundred miles long.
This event  had a most depressing effect  upon the people  of the
South  and the  Confederate  government.          It  had a corresponding
effect  to  elate  and  encourage  the  people  of  the  North  and  the
government at Washington.
The early  spring  of  1865 found the armies of General Grant well
recruited  and supplied,   and ready to deliver what proved to be the
fatal  blow  to  Lee's Army around  Richmond and Petersburg.
The  first   move was  made by Lee  in  an effort  to  open  a way
through  the  Union  lines  for  the  escape  of  his  beleaguered  army
to the south,    there to join General Johnston,   in the vain hope that
their  united  armies  might  be  able  to  prolong  the struggle.           This
effort  of General Lee failed.
On the  morning  of April  1  a  concerted  movement was  made
along  the  whole  Union front  in  an  overwhelming  assault.              The
Confederate  lines  were carried,     and that  night  Lee escaped  with
the  remnant of  his  army along  the  north  side of the Appomattox
River.               He eluded his pursuers  until April 9,   when he surrendered
to  General  Grant  at  Appomattox,      and  the  war  was  practically
at  an end.            Joy reigned supreme throughout the North.          The glad
tidings  spread  like  wildfire  from  city  to  city  and from  village  to
village.          Bells  rang,    cannons  roared,     and people  went wild  with
the lifting  of the terrible incubus which had laid its  deadly weight
upon the land for four long terrible years .
Did I   say " joy reigned  supreme? "    Well,   let it  pass.       It might
have been supreme,    but it was not unalloyed.    In many thousands
of homes there was a vacant chair.       He who left  it in the strength
of his  young manhood,    with a cheerful good-bye though his  heart
was heavy,     would return no more.        There was many a heart wound
which time did not heal.
I would not close  the  subject  of  the  Civil War leaving  the  im-
pression  that  it  was  only  by  the  men that  a self-sacrificing   and
 - 363 - 
THE  CIVIL  WAR,        1861-65                                   355
heroic part was played.         Hundreds  of  devoted  women gave  them-
selves  up to  nursing the sick and wounded who filled  the hospitals ,
bringing  cheer and comfort and hope to their  lives,     writing  letters
for  them to  the folks  at  home,   and in  general  acting  the  part  of
ministering  angels,                 at  least,       many a boy thought so.          Nor were
the  women  at  home  idle.          There  was  lint   to   be  scraped  and
bandages  to  be rolled,    which might alleviate  the  pain,      or possibly
save  the  life   or  limb  of  somebody's  boy,      and  these  occupations
were  carried  on in thousands  of  households  throughout  the  land.
Yes,      the  women did  much more than  to  say  " God speed "  with
brave words when their hearts  were breaking.
It was no light task to run the household with a family of small
children in those trying days.          Specie was at a premium and finally
went  out  of  circulation  entirely,      the  fractional   currency  being
replaced  by paper money,   familiarly  known as  shin-plasters.               At
the  time  of  greatest  disparity  between  the  gold  dollar  and  the
paper one  it  took $2.90  of  the latter  to  equal  $1  of  the  former.
As paper was all  the  money in circulation  prices  were regulated by
paper values  and ranged much as we have seen them the last  three
years,          although  some  things   were  much  higher;        for   instance,
calico   cloth   reached  60  cents  a  yard,     kerosene  oil,       50  cents  a
gallon  and various other things  in  proportion.
Many a man sent home $12 a month out of his scanty $14,     and
be  it  remembered  that  the  government  rations  were  not  upon
the  generous  scale  of  these  later  years.          The family  which  had
an adequate supply of bed linen was indeed fortunate.       The State
of  Massachusetts  was  liberal  with  the  soldiers'     families,       allowing
from $8  to $ 12  a month.         At least,    it  was thought liberal  for  those
times.              Many a family  had  no meat  upon the  table  during  the
summer months and but a scant supply at other times.            We may
well  wonder  how  the  house  mother  managed  to  keep  her  flock
from  suffering  for  want  of  food  and clothing.      Perhaps  she  was
not always able  to do so.
I  might state  here that during the war the use of bosom shirts
and  linen  collars  by men went entirely  out  of  practice.           French
flannel   for  shirts   and  paper   for   collars   were  the   order  of  the
day.
During  the  war the  town  paid  $80,320  for  the  encouragement
of enlistments.
The  State  of  Massachusetts  has  always  maintained  a  liberal
policy  toward  the  soldiers  and  sailors  who  were  engaged  in  the
Civil War.
The payments  of  state  aid  are  administered  through  the  local
authorities.          In Weymouth it  has been the custom of the selectmen
to  place as  liberal interpretation  upon the law as  is  allowable.
During the years  1861  to  1866,    inclusive,    there  was paid in  this
town the sum of $117,977 .
In the years which have elapsed since  1866,    including  1919,     aid
to  the  soldiers  and  sailors  and their families  has  been  distributed
 - 364 - 
356                    MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
to  the  amount of  $318,289 ;       in  addition  to  the  above,    the  town
has paid in  soldiers'      relief  $99,547,     making a total  of $417,836.
Massachusetts  furnished  159,165  men,     including  re-enlistments,
to  the  army,      and 26,168  to the navy from  1861 to  1865,      a total  of
185,333 .                    Of this  number,    13,942 died in the war.
Weymouth sent out 936 men,   including about  100 re- enlistments,
of whom about 120 never returned.
Benjamin  F.  Foss was the  first  man from Weymouth who was
lost.            He belonged  to  Company  F,       Eleventh   Massachusetts  In-
fantry,      and  was  killed  in  the  first  battle  of  Bull  Run,     July  21,
1861.
The last  man from Weymouth known to  have  been killed  was
Josiah   Q.   Pratt,        Company  B,        Fourth   Massachusetts   Cavalry,
who was killed at Manning,    S.  C.,    Feb.  19,     1865.
The  following   list   of  men  who  enlisted   in  the   army  from
Weymouth during  the  Civil  War is  gathered  from  the  Adjutant
General's   Report.            It   undoubtedly  contains   some   inaccuracies
and omissions,    but is  the nearest  to  a complete record of anything
we have.           There is   no even approximately complete record of  the
naval  enlistments.            The  names  below  given  are  taken  from  the
town  records.           They are,      however,     but  a fraction  of  the  number
of  those who enlisted  in the navy from Weymouth during  the war.
I regret  that  no complete record of  the naval  enlistments  from this
town is  in  existence.
The various  organizations  in  which  Weymouth men  served  are
here  given  in  the  order  in  which  they  appear  in  the  report  of
the  Adjutant  General,    commencing  with  the  three-year  infantry
regiments.                The rank given is  that held at date of  discharge;       the
age,      that given at  time of  enlistment.

We find from the foregoing list  that Weymouth was represented
in  the  Civil   War in  forty-seven  different  military  organizations.
Not all  of the names given were residents of the town at the time.
It  is   practically  impossible  to  determine accurately the number of
non- residents  included.              On the  other  hand,     quite  a good many
Weymouth  men  enlisted   to  the  credit  of  other   towns.                I find
there were  about thirty  of  those who enlisted  to  the credit  of  this
town  who  are   classed   as   deserters.          I   have  not  recorded   their
names.
To the  credit  of the town  I  would say that the greater  part  of
those  so  classed  were  men enlisted  from  out  of  town,    who,    in the
vernacular  of  the  time,     were  known  as  bounty  jumpers.              When
large  bounties  were  being  paid  for  recruits  there  were  many of
these  unprincipled  men who did  a thriving  business  by securing
bounties  from  a  number  of  towns  or  cities.      Having  enlisted  in
one  place  and  received  the bounty,    they were  on the  lookout  for
the  first  opportunity  to  desert  safely  which  presented itself.            This
was  generally  effected  before  they  left   the  state.            By assuming
another  name  and  going  to  a town where  they  were not  known
they would repeat  the operation.
When all  the towns  and cities  were exerting  themselves in filling
a quota,       the  history  of  the  man presenting  himself  was  not,       I
 - 381 - 
THE  CIVIL  WAR,       1861-65                                  373
imagine,       gone  into  very  thoroughly.          If   secured,       and  accepted
by the government,    he counted one on the  quota.
It was not an  uncommon thing  for  a man to  be  reported  as  a
deserter  through  no  fault  of  his  own.             With  the  hospitals  filled
with sick and wounded,     there  was always  a great  number of  men
separated  from  their  commands,     and when for  any  cause  one  of
these  was lost from the record  he was classed  as  a  deserter.
In  preparing this history  I have  been greatly assisted,     up to  the
time of the close  of the  Civil  War,      by having in my hands  papers
written by the late John W. Bates,    who took great interest  in  the
military  history  of  the  town  and  gathered  much  valuable  data,
no doubt with the idea that it  would be useful for  the  purpose  to
which it  is  now applied.         I  cheerfully  acknowledge  any indebted-
ness  to  Mr. Bates for  the valuable  aid  his  papers have contributed
to this work.
All  of  the  men  whose  names  are  above  recorded  received   an
honorable discharge from the service.
In  the  report  of  the  Adjutant  General  no  distinction  is   made
between  those  who  were  discharged  from  the  result   of  wounds
and  those  who  were  otherwise  physically  disabled   to   such  an
extent  as  to  necessitate  their  discharge  before  the  end  of  their
term  of  enlistment.
No effort  has  been  made in  the  foregoing  pages  to  portray  in-
dividual deeds  of  valor  or  merit,     where  all   are  presumed  to  have
done their duty in the positions assigned  them.
There  was,         however,      one  act  which  it   seems  well  to  record.
There  has  been  considerable  controversy  as  to  what organization
is  entitled  to the honor of  having raised  the first  Union colors  in
the city of Richmond after  its  evacuation by General  Lee.
I   have  made  careful  investigation  of  what  should  be  reliable
sources   of   information,      and  have  interviewed  members  of   the
regiment  a part of which was the  first  Union force to  enter  Rich-
mond,       and am satisfied  that the following is  a correct  statement  of
the facts.
Adetachment of the Fourth  Massachusetts Cavalry were the first
Union troops to enter the city,   under command of Maj.    Atherton H.
Stevens,          provost   marshal.                This   detachment   had  with  it   the
guidons   of   Company  E  and   Company  H,      but  no  stars   and
stripes.
By command of  Major Stevens  these  guidons  were  raised  over
the  State  House,     that  of   Company H being  hoisted  by Jeremiah
Quinn of Weymouth,    and were the  first  Union colors  to  be  raised
over  the   Confederate  Capitol,      where  they  flew   for  some  hours
before being replaced by the national  colors.
I  have therefore  no doubt that  a Weymouth man had an active
part  in  raising  the  first  Union colors  flown  in  Richmond after  its
evacuation.

374                   MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
THE FIRST UNION SOLDIER IN  RICHMOND
Many times  has the story been told  of the evacuation  of Rich-
mond,           Sunday,    April  2,    1865.    A southern  writer,     to  whom I  am
indebted for  the initial facts  of the following story,    said :
None who lived through that Sabbath could forget it.         Our government gone,
our  soldiers hurrying off,    women saying good-bye to husband,    lover,    brother or
friend and urging haste;       everybody who could go,   going,   and"a kingdom for  a
horse"  could not buy one (horses brought $1,000 apiece that day in gold) ;    homes
deserted,   houses aflame,    excitement everywhere,  the bustle and hurry of departure
over all, -these are a part of American history,    making thereon a page blistered
with tears for some,    and for  others illumined with symbols of triumph and glory.
Monday,      April 3,     1865,    was an eventful day for  the army of the
Union.                    During  the  night  detonations   of   exploding   gunboats
could  be heard  for  miles,      the  noise  and  shock  and  lurid  lights
adding to the wretchedness of those within the city and the anxie-
ties  of  those who beheld  its  burnings  from afar,   among these  the
advancing  army which  was  not  without uneasy  speculations  lest
Richmond  be  found   as   Napoleon  found   Moscow, -in   ashes.
General  Shepley  of  the  United  States  Army describes  the  scene
witnessed from his position near Petersburg as a most beautiful and
awful  display of  fireworks,   the  heavens  being  filled  with  bursting
shells,        red  lights,    Roman candles  and falling  stars.          The morning
light found the Fourth Massachusetts Cavalry,  under Major Stevens,
at the gates of the city,    and in  Company H of that regiment were
many Weymouth boys,    and as soon as  it  was daylight three scouts
were sent  into  the city,     one of whom was Jerry  Quinn of  Lovell's
Corner.             Two of  the  scouts  were  captured  by the  rebel  soldiers,
but Quinn entered the city  and went as  far as the  Franklin  Hotel,
but feared  to go farther.           He returned and reported the way clear
as far as the hotel,    and two companies,    Company E and Company
H,     rode  into  the fallen  city.            As they reached  the capitol building
the  rebel  flag  was flying  above it,    and Captain  Ray of  Company
H,      together  with  Tommy  Myers,       the  color  sergeant,      and  Jerry
Quinn,      started  to  pull  it  down.            Myers took with  him  the  regi-
mental  guidons,    and just  outside  the  capitol  he  slipped  and fell
on  the  slimy  pavements.          Instantly  Quinn  seized  the  flag,      and,
rushing  to  the  top of the building,    pulled down the  rebel flag  and
raised  the  United  States  flag  over the confederate  capitol.          Thus
the honor of being  the  first  Union soldier  in Richmond,     as  well  as
the credit of pulling down the rebel flag  and raising the Union flag,
belongs to  a Weymouth soldier.

SPANISH  WAR
From the close of the Civil War our country was at peace within
its  own borders  and  with  all  the  world  until  the outbreak  of  the
Spanish  War in  the spring  of 1898.    This  war was fought  princi-
pally by our navy and the regular army.

THE  WORLD  WAR
After  the  close  of  the  Spanish  War the  United  States  settled
down to  the development  of its  industries  and  arts,    feeling  secure
against  being drawn in  as  a  party  to  any European controversies .
Even after  the outbreak of war in the summer of  1914 the great
majority of  our people deluded themselves  with the belief  that we
could and must play the part  of neutrals.        So firmly was this belief
planted  in  the  hearts  of  the  people  that  it  is  probable  that  no
other  one factor  had so  much influence  in the  re- election  of  Presi-
dent  Wilson in  1916  as  the  slogan " He kept us  out of  war. "     In
view of the now known facts we can see that it was inevitable from
the  first,      if  the  war was  long  continued,    that we  should  become
involved in it.           I  think  I  can do no better  than to  here  quote  at
some length from the message of  President Wilson to  the  Congress
of the United States  on April 2,    1917 :
GENTLEMEN OF  THE  CONGRESS :    - I   have called  the  Congress  into  extraor-
dinary  session  because  there  are  serious,      very  serious,      choices  of  policy  to  be
made,      and  made  immediately,     which  it  was neither  right  nor  constitutionally
permissible  that  I  should  assume the  responsibility  of  making.          On the  third
of  February  last,       I  officially  laid  before  you  the  extraordinary  announcement
of the Imperial German Government that on and after the first  day of February
it was its purpose to put aside  all  restraint  of  law  or  of  humanity and use  its
submarines  to  sink  every  vessel  that  sought  to  approach  either  the  ports  of
Great  Britain  and Ireland or  the  western  coasts  of Europe  or  any of the  ports
controlled by the enemies of Germany within the  Mediterranean.
Vessels  of every kind,    whatever  their  flag,     their  character,     their  cargo,       their
destination,     their errand,    have been ruthlessly sent to the bottom without warn-
ing  and without  thought  of  help  or  mercy  to  those  on  board,    the  vessels  of
friendly neutrals along with those of belligerents .
Even  hospital  ships  and  ships  carrying  relief  to  the  sorely  bereaved  and
stricken  people  of Belgium,    though the latter  were  provided with  safe  conduct
through  the proscribed  areas  by the  German Government itself  and were dis-
tinguished by unmistakable  marks  of  identity,    have  been  sunk with  the  same
reckless  lack  of compassion or of principle.
The present German submarine warfare against commerce is  a warfare against
mankind.            Each nation must decide for itself how it will meet it.
The choice we make for ourselves must be made with a moderation of counsel
and a temperateness  of judgment befitting  our  character  and  our  motives  as  a
nation.
There is  one choice we cannot make,    we are incapable of making:    we will  not
choose  the  path  of  submission  and suffer  the  most  sacred  rights  of our  nation
and our  people to be ignored  or  violated.          The wrongs  against  which we now
array  ourselves  are  no common wrongs;       they  cut  to  the  very  roots  of  human
life..
I
With a profound sense of the solemn and even tragical character  of the step
am taking and of the grave  responsibilities  which it  involves,    but in unhesi-
tating obedience to what I  deem my constitutional  duty,       I  advise  that the  Con-
gress  declare  the  recent  course  of  the  Imperial  German Government to  be  in
fact nothing less  than war against  the  Government  and People  of  the  United
States;     that  it  formally  accept  the  status  of  belligerent  which  has  thus  been
thrust upon it;      and that it  take immediate steps not only to put the country in
a more thorough  state  of  defence but also  to  exert  all  its  power and employ all
its  resources to  bring  the Government of the German Empire to  terms  and end
thewar.
 - 386 - 
378                     MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
It  is  a distressing  and oppressive  duty,   Gentlemen of the  Congress,    which I
have performed  in  thus  addressing  you.           There are,   it  may be,     many months
of  fiery  trial  and sacrifice  ahead of us.           It is  a fearful thing to lead this  great
peaceful  people  into  war,       into  the  most  terrible  and  disastrous  of  all  wars,
civilization  itself  seeming to be in the balance!     God helping her,   she can do no
other.
It  is  needless  to  relate  that  the  Congress  promptly adopted the
recommendation of  the  President  and declared  that a state  of war
existed   between  the   United   States   and  the  Imperial  German
Government,     and enacted legislation for  the raising  and equipping
of  a  huge  military   and  naval  force   to   send  across   the  water.
William  J.    Bryan  once  stated,     in  an  address  aimed  against  the
enlarging  of  our  standing  army,     that  if   the  need  ever  arose,     we
could raise  a million men overnight.           We did indeed raise a million
men,                         not  overnight,    but  in  an almost  incredibly brief time,  -
and not only one,     but another and another million.
It  was  soon  apparent,    however,    that  the raising  and organizing
of a huge army and navy,   and the equipping and training of them
for   foreign   service  under  present  conditions   of  warfare,       was  a
herculean task calling  for  all  the resources of  the government.           All
the orderly  processes  of civil life and private business were at  once
revolutionized,      and  the  whole  energy   of  the  government  was
devoted  to  obtaining  great  results  in  the  briefest  possible  time,
with utter disregard to the cost.
The allied  armies  of  Europe,   with which we were to  co- operate,
were sore  pressed,    and to  all  human appearances the result  of the
war hinged upon our being able quickly to land a million or more
organized  and  trained  men in  France  and to  render  instant  and
efficient  aid  to  England with  our navy in combating the  German
submarine  menace.
Many of  the  young  men of  our  country,     including  a number
from  Weymouth,     impatient  at  the  delay  of  our  government in
entering  the  war,     had  gone  across   the  border  and  enlisted  in
Canadian organizations,    and many had enlisted in our navy,    feeling
sure  that  we should become involved in the war.
Those  thus  enlisting  from  Weymouth and  those  taken  by the
selective  draft  numbered about seven hundred and fifty.
There is  as  yet  no tabulation in the office  of the State Adjutant
General of the men who served in the World War,    showing to what
towns they are credited.

information will admit:

WELCOME  HOME  DAY
A committee  was  appointed  by the  board  of  selectmen  under
date of Feb.  17,    1919,   for the purpose of welcoming home returning
soldiers  and sailors  from their service in the army and navy of the
United States.
This committee organized by a choice of Maj.     William  L.  Swan,
chairman,      and  William J.   Holbrook,    secretary,     and as  finally  con-
stituted  comprised  the following  members :
Maj .     Wm.     L.  Swan,    Chairman.
William J. Holbrook,    Secretary.
John F.  Dwyer,    Treasurer.
Albert P.  Worthen.
Joseph A.  Fern.
Robert S.  Hoffman.
John Condon.
NathanG. Cushing.
Benjamin V. Heffernan.
Mrs. Elbridge Nash.
Mrs. George W. Perry.
Miss Lillian  Curtiss.
On Saturday,     Aug. 9,    1919,    the committee carried out the follow-
ing program for the reception of the service men:
At 1 P.M.  the service men residing in North Weymouth and Wey-
mouth Heights assembled in  uniform at  Beal's  Park,        North Wey-
mouth,    where a short band concert was rendered by the Weymouth
Band.
At 1.15  P.M.  the  service  men left  Beal's  Park in  autos  donated
and driven by the citizens of the town,   proceeding via Sea,     North,
Church and Commercial Streets to Washington Square,     Weymouth
Landing,      where  they  were joined  by  the  service  men from  that
community in uniform.
At  1.15  P.M.   there  was  a  short  band  concert  at  Washington
Square.
At 1.45 P.M.  the men were transported from Washington Square
via   Washington,        Main  and   Columbian   Streets   to   Columbian
Square,     South  Weymouth,     where  they  were  joined  by the  South
Weymouth men in  uniform.             A short  band  concert  was  given  at
Columbian Square.
At 2.15  P.M.  the  service  men were transported  from  Columbian
Square via Pleasant,    Water,    Myrtle and School Streets to Commer-
cial  Square,      East Weymouth,     where they  were joined  by the  East
Weymouth and Lovell's  Corner service men in uniform.
At 2.30 р.м.  a parade of the service men was formed in Commer-
cial   Square,        and,      led  by  a  platoon  of  Weymouth  police,      under
command of  Chief of Police Arthur  H.  Pratt,     accompanied by the
Weymouth Band,    marched via Broad Street to the Clapp Memorial
Grounds  at  Weymouth  Centre  and  passed  in  review  before  their
respective mothers,    who had been assembled on the balcony of the
Clapp  Memorial  Building,     and before  a gathering  of  about  5,000
people.
After  the  review,     a  panorama  photograph  of  the  service  men
and  of  the  army nurses  and  Yeoman  (F)    from  Weymouth  was
taken,       following  which there  was a ball  game on the grounds  be
 - 406 - 
398                     MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
tween  the  Norfolk  Club  of  South Weymouth and  Commonwealth
Shoe  Club  of  Whitman.         A second  ball  game was  held  between
two  teams  chosen from among the service men.
At the  conclusion of the second game which was called  at 6 P.M. ,
a banquet  was  served  under  a canopy  on the  grounds,       at which
about  350  of  the  service  men were served.          During  the  banquet
there was a band concert  by the Weymouth band,    and at the con-
clusion  of  the  banquet  the  following  address  by  Mr.   Bradford
Hawes,        chairman  of  the  board  of  selectmen  and  veteran  of  the
Civil  War,       was given :
It  is  my pleasant  duty - and  I  may well  say  privilege -to  welcome  home
in behalf  of the  town of  Weymouth you who have borne  an honorable part  in
the  Great  War which  has revolutionized the governmental,    social  and industrial
conditions  of the world.          When,     five  years  ago,     like  a bolt  from a clear  sky,      the
nations  of  Europe  were  drawn into  the  maelstrom  of war,    the  great  majority
of the people  of our land consoled themselves  with the  opinion  that  it  was no
affair  of  ours;     that  as  in the  past,   so  now,   the  nations  of Europe must  settle
their own controversies .
A few  there  were  with  a  prophetic  vision  which  showed them that  whether
we would or not,     it  was inevitable  that  we should be drawn into the conflict  if
we were to maintain our high standard of national honor,   to say nothing of the
duty we owed to the civilized world.
In the  spring  of  1917  it   became  evident  that the  time had come when  the
arrogant  and barbarous  acts  of  the  German government,    by which many of our
fellow citizens  lost  property and lives,    could no longer be borne by a self- respect-
ing people.           It  became further  apparent that we had to choose between  acting
with the Allied  powers  of  Europe against  Germany,    or  at  no late  time  to  meet
that  power  by  ourselves  upon  our  own soil.           A state  of  war  was  declared by
our  President  to  exist  between  the  government  of Germany and this  country,
and  measures  were  at  once  adopted  to  place  a great  army in the  field  and to
employ all the powers of  our navy in conjunction with the armies and navies of
England,       France  and Italy  in  bringing  the war to  an early  and successful  ter-
mination.
To you who are  a part  of  that  army and navy I need not take the time for
a long  recital  of the  events  which followed.        Suffice  it  to say that  by the  en-
trance of the  United  States  into  the  conflict,     the  war  was  brought  to  a  more
speedy close  than the most sanguine then thought possible.
Most of those  who went out from us  are  now returned,    and it  is  our  happy
privilege  on this  pleasant and peaceful summer day to welcome you back to our
midst.
Some of those who two years ago left  us in the full strength and hope of their
young manhood,     we shall  see  here  no  more.             They paid  the  last  full  measure
of devotion  to  the  cause  of human welfare,      which they  well  knew when they
entered  the  service  might be required  of them.         Let  us cherish  their  memories
and resolve  that  their  deaths  shall  not have been in vain,    but that the cause of
human liberty  for  which  their  lives  were  laid  down may become the  priceless
heritage of millions  yet  unborn.
When the  Grand Army of  the  Republic  which we have known for  the  last
half  century was inaugurated,   it  was one of its  cardinal  principles  " that every
man who did  his  duty in the  position  assigned him deserves  well  of his coun-
try.  "     If this  was true of those who served in the  Civil War it  is  equally true  of
those who served in this  world war,     and I  believe that as the years  roll  by you
will find that a grateful country will not forget  the sacrifices  made by those who
offered their all  on the altar of service  to humanity.
I  know that  there  are  some  2,000,000  men whose lot  it  was never  to  cross
the sea,     but I  also know that most of these regarded that fact  a hardship  rather
than otherwise.
 - 407 - 
THE  WORLD  WAR                        399
We must not  forget  that  it  was not alone  the  great  things  accomplished  by
our men on the  bloody  fields  of  France  which  hastened  the  close  of  the  war,
but the  fact  that America had the  men and means  at  hand  to  replace  those
already in the field  as fast  as might become necessary.
Whether,     therefore,    it  was your  lot  to  cross  the  sea  and have an  actual  part
in the great conflict,     or  whether you were upon this  side  awaiting  your turn,       a
grateful town to-day gives  thanks  for  the  service  rendered and rejoices  in  your
safe  return  to home and friends .
I wish to you  each  and  all  a long  and  prosperous life  in the land  which your
valor has helped to place in the leading rank among the nations of the earth.
In the evening there was a band concert,   dancing on the grounds,
singing and fireworks .
It  was a  gala day for  the town.         Buildings  and residences  in  the
town were  decorated  with  flags  and bunting,    and everywhere  the
soldiers   were  greeted  with  enthusiasm  and  joy.               The  beautiful
Clapp Memorial building and grounds,    which had been so graciously
donated by the  Davis  Bates  Clapp  Memorial Association  for  that
day,      made an ideal  place  to hold  the exercises  of  the  day,     and as
the men marched on and across the field  in company formation and
in  line,     with the  band playing  and colors  flying,    they  presented  a
sight never to be forgotten by those who witnessed it.
On Sunday,     Sept.  28,    1919,    at the Clapp Memorial Grounds,      the
committee  held  an  open- air  Memorial Service for  the  soldiers  and
sailors  from  Weymouth who gave their lives  in the World War,      the
program  for  which was as  follows :

WEYMOUTH  CAVALRY  COMPANY,      1798-18111
By  C.   C.  TOWER,      M.D.
Nearly fourscore and two years have elapsed since the formation
of  what  was  familiarly  styled,    in  this  locality,     the  Light  Horse
Troop.                   Probably no one is  now living  who has distinct  personal
recollections  of this event or of the circumstances of its  occurrence.
2
In  the  preparation  of  this  communication  the  writer  has  in-
vestigated  pretty  thoroughly  all  available  sources  of  information
which  promised  to  throw any light  on the subject.        He has con-
versed,        in  reference  to  it,     with  many aged  persons,     residents   of
Weymouth and vicinity,   and some,   natives of the town,    who have
removed  to  a distance.          It  has  also  been his  privilege  to  receive
the  testimony of  a few individuals  advanced in life  who are  now
deceased,       memoranda of  whose  statements  were  fortunately  pre-
served.              Of  the  whole  number,      living  and dead,    who were  thus
interrogated,        about  forty  had  attained  an  age  exceeding  eighty
years,             including  six  who  had  passed  their   ninetieth   birthday.
A few of  these  persons had no  recollection  whatever of  the Horse
company,    but  most of them remembered it  more or less distinctly,
while  some  contributed  interesting  items  of  information  relating
to  it,     but  none  of  them  were  able  to  tell  just  how  or  when  it
originated.
The character  of  this  organization  and the  purposes  for  which
it  was formed  have  not  always  been  clearly  understood,       even  by
our  older  citizens.        An impression  seems  to  have  prevailed  to  a
considerable  extent  that  this  was  an  independent  company,      not
1Read at meeting of Weymouth Historical Society,   May 5,   1880.
Mr.  Thomas Derby is  authority for  the  statement (confirmed  by Mr. Allen Vining)   that a
Troop of Horse existed  in Weymouth at an earlier  date.          Capt.    Thomas Pratt,   who lived  from
1705 to  1765,       commanded this  company.       Ebenezer Vinson and  David Vining  also  belonged  to
this ancient troop.

The writer  is indebted for information on the subject of this  sketch to a considerable  number of
native residents who are between seventy and eighty years of age,   and were consequently living be-
fore the troop disbanded.       Other octogenarians than those whose names are here given are resident
in the town who have no knowledge of  the  Horse  company,    having removed here subsequently
to the period of its existence.

belonging to  the military establishment of the State,    and therefore
not  conformable  to  military  discipline  and  regulations.               It   was
supposed  to  be an association of young men whose sole  object  was
equestrian   exercise   and  manly  sport.              Sufficient   evidence   has
been  obtained,      however,      to  show  that  the  cavalry  company  of
Weymouth was a  part of  the regular militia force of the  Common-
wealth.
In  the  absence  of  oral  testimony  concerning  the  origin  of  this
company the following  extracts,    copied  from official  records  pre-
served  in  the  archives  of  the State,   are  of  value  as  showing  that
the  first  steps  taken in this  direction  were  the.  presentation  of  a
formal petition to the General Court;    which petition was granted,
and  orders   from  military   headquarters   issued   for   raising   the
company.
COMMONWEALTH  OF  MASSACHUSETTS :
IN  THE HOUSE OF  REPRESENTATIVES,
JUNE 29th,  1798.
On the petition  of Samuel Bayley and others  Praying  for  Liberty  to  raise  a
Troop of  Cavalry  in  the first  Brigade and first  Division  of the Militia  of this
Commonwealth:
Resolved,    that the  said  Bayley and others  be authorized  to  raise  a Troop  of
Cavalry  in  the  first   Brigade  of  said  first   Division;       and  his  Excellency  the
Governor is  requested  to Commission such persons,    as  may be elected  according
to   Law,        Officers   of  the  same     Provided  no  one  of  the  Standing  Companies
shall be reduced to a less  number than the  Law requires.
And it   is  further  Resolved,       That the  said Troop,  when organized,   shall be
wh

It is  interesting to notice,   in connection with the resolves,    which
we have quoted and which were passed  by the  Legislature  on  the
very last  day of its  session,   that the regiment to which the  newly
organized  troop was  to  be  attached was that commanded by Col.
Joshua  Bates,        a  Weymouth  man,    and  one  doubtless  interested

in the  success of this military project of his  townsmen.               The lead-
ing petitioner,    Samuel  Bayley,  held two commissions in the com-
pany during  its  existence,    but his  name does  not  appear  in  the

Search  at  the  State  House has been  further  rewarded  by the
discovery of a " Roster of the Commissioned Officers of the Militia "
of the State,    dating back to the latter part of the last century,   and
including  the  names  of the commissioned  officers  of  the  cavalry
company of Weymouth,    their rank,   date of commission,   residence,
and in some instances the date of promotion or discharge.
From  these  official  data it  can be positively  affirmed  that  this
company of Horse was in  existence during the period from 1798 to
1811.

Lieut.        Samuel  Bayley  (1799) .              When  Captain  White  was  pro-
moted  to   major  of  battalion   or  squadron   ( for   both  terms  are
used synonymously)   Lieutenant  Bayley was commissioned captain,
and  James  Jones  took  the  vacant  office  of  lieutenant.               Captain
Bayley,  having in turn been elevated to the majorship,   the captain's
place was occupied by James Jones,    promoted,    and the position  of
lieutenant  was filled  by Elisha  Wales.         Ebenezer Hunt,     Jr. ,     is  said
by his  son,      Maj.       Elias  Hunt,     to  have resigned  his  commission of
lieutenant  about  1808  or  1809.     Daniel  Loud  was  probably  his
successor.             It  is  not known that  Ezra  Reed  served  in  any other
capacity  than  cornet.         Asa Penniman,    who succeeded  him in  this
office,      gave  place  to   Isaac  Damons  in   February,      1809,       and  in
October of the same year was commissioned lieutenant
There is  some doubt whether Lieutenant Penniman was attached
to the Weymouth company,   as he is  said to have left it  toward the
close  of  its  existence  and joined  the  Braintree  cavalry  company.
This  supposition  is   strengthened  by  the  circumstance  that  the
date  of  his  commission  as  lieutenant  corresponds  with  that  of
William  Reed,    Jr.'s  commission  as  captain,    and the  latter  officer
belonged  to  the  troop  in  Braintree,    where both  parties   resided.
It  is   probable  that  Captain  Reed  selected  his  companion,      Asa
Penniman,       as  his  lieutenant.            There  is  no doubt,      however,     that
Penniman  was  cornet  of  the  Weymouth  company.          Lieutenant
Daniel  Loud is  said  to have been chosen captain by the  company
which  disbanded  before  he received  his  commission.          He appears
to be the last  one the date of whose discharge is  officially  recorded.
Cornet  Damons,    who took  his  commission  at  the  same  date  as
Lieutenant  Loud,     probably served  as long as  the organization  was
kept  up.          The  name  of  Samuel  Arnold,       Jr. ,        of   Weymouth,        a
member  of  the  troop,    is   recorded  as   quartermaster  of  cavalry,
under date  of April  18,    1803;      discharged April  2,    1811.    Robert
Cushing of Weymouth was commissioned quartermaster of cavalry
April 1,   1815.    He would have been too young to belong to this com-
pany,    which went out of existence more than three years before.
The martial  spirit  of  the  age  when the  Horse Troop  flourished
was  far  more active  than  that  of  the  present  day.         Every  male
inhabitant  between  the  ages   of   eighteen   and  forty- five,        unless
exempted on account of disability,    was  required  by law to  be  en-
rolled  in  the  ranks  of the  militia,     and,     if   necessary,       to  perform
military  duty  in  actual  service.        During  the  early  part  of  this
century  there  existed  in  Weymouth,     in  addition  to  the  cavalry
company,   a company of artillery, ¹  which survived its  sister  organi-
zation  many years,     and  two  companies  of  ununiformed  militia.
At a later  period (about  1812)  a third militia company was estab-
lished  in  the  center  of  the  town,     and  still   later   (1820-23)    two
independent companies of infantry  were formed,   one at the Land-
ing,        the  Weymouth  Light  Infantry,    and  one  at  the  South,       the
1Thewriter has collected considerable material relating to the Artillery Company of Weymouth,
which he proposes to make use of at some future time.

Franklin  Guards,      both  of  which  the  middle-aged  citizen  of  this
day distinctly  remembers.
At the  time  the  Light  Horse  Troop  was  raised  military  en-
thusiasm  ran  unusually  high.         Old  soldiers  were  still   living  who
had seen  service  at  Louisburg  and  Quebec,    and not a few  heroes
of  the  Revolutionary  War were  in  the  prime  of  life.            Fifteen
years  of  peace and prosperity had produced the effect of reviving
rather   than  suppressing   military   ardor,      especially   among  the
young men.            Our nation was by no means on a stable footing.        A
permanent  national  army was being  established,    and  enlistments
were then going  on all  over  the country.       Applications  for  com-
missions,       as  we read  in  the public prints  of the day,    were far  in
excess  of  the  positions  to be filled.      In the  State a reorganization
of  the  militia   was  in  progress,     and  the  so-called   " Legionary
Brigade "   of  Boston  and  Chelsea was being  raised,    by which  the
force  of the first  Division was considerably augmented.
The  recent   trip   of  the   President 1   -John  Adams     to  his
native  State  had called  forth  great  martial  demonstration,    for  we
are  informed  that  " at  Marlboro  he  was  met  by  an  escort   of
Middlesex  Cavalry, "   and  " The  Boston  Cavalry  commanded  by
Rufus  G.  Amory,     Esq. ,     met the object of their respect  at  Water-
town,        where  a  Battalion  of  Horse  commanded  by  Maj.         Brown
took  up  the  escort.  "      This  grand  cavalcade  conducted  the
chief magistrate of the nation to his country seat at Quincy.         These
stirring  events,    transpiring  shortly  before  and at  the very  month
when the  first  commissions  were assigned  to  officers  of this  com-
pany,      may be  reasonably  expected  to  have had  a favorable  in-
fluence  on its  formation.
The  Horse  Troop  is   said  to  have been  composed  of  fifty- two
members,          including   four   commissioned  officers,   -captain,       two
lieutenants  and cornet.          It  is known to have had two  trumpeters
and  probably  had  the  usual  complement  of  other  non-commis-
sioned   officers.           Its   membership  was  not   exclusively   confined
within the limits of this town.        Several are believed to have resided
in  Braintree.           Asa  Penniman,     an officer  of  the  troop,       as  already
stated,      lived  there.      As other cavalry companies were in existence
in  neighboring  towns  at  the  same period,   it  is  at this  late  day
almost   impossible  to  tell   for  certainty  to  which  company  any
known  cavalryman  was  attached.            But  evidence  is   conclusive
that  most of  the  Weymouth men were members of the Weymouth
company,    except such as were officers  of a battalion.
The  troop  paraded  regularly  twice  a year,  and in its  early  ex-
istence  met  together  often,    for  drill  and equestrian  exercise.2    A
professional  instructor  is  said,      on  good  authority,     to  have been
employed at  an early period  of  its  existence  to drill  the  members
in the manoeuvers and  evolutions of military  horsemanship.            The
1 See article entitled " The President's Tour," in Columbian Centinel, Aug. 11,  1798.
2 Sometimes the Weymouth and Braintree companies indulged in a sham fight with each other
at these meetings.
 - 413 - 
WEYMOUTH  CAVALRY  COMPANY,     1798-1811                405
parades  took  place  in  various  parts  of  the  town,   and at  Brigade
and  Division  musters  out  of town.          It  has  been  reported  to  the
writer  that  a  training  of  this  company sometimes  took  place  in
Captain Jones'     pasture,     near  East Street,   in the north  part  of the
town.             This  was  probably when Captain Jones was in  command.
Mr. Josiah  Humphrey's plain near Middle Street  (land now owned
by Mr. Thomas Humphrey on Essex Street)  was one of the parade
grounds  of  the  troop,     as  was  also  Mr.  Jacob  Richards'      plain  on
Front  Street.           But  the  most  frequent  places  of  resort  for   this
purpose  were  probably  the  vicinity  of  the  Old  North  and  the
South   meeting-houses.             Sometimes   the   cavalry,        artillery    and
militia  (ununiformed infantry)  companies trained together.             These
grand  training  occasions  were  probably  enlivened  by a band  of
music.             On May 4,    1802,    such a meeting of these companies  took
place  in  front  of  the  meeting-house  in  South  Weymouth.            The
artillery  company,    commanded by Capt.     Nathaniel  Shaw,     took  a
position in the center of the line,    the militia company,   commanded
by Capt.     Asa White,    on the left,   and the cavalry company,    under
Capt.       Samuel Bayley on the right.         They " fired  by platoons  from
the right  to the left. "     On the seventh day of June following,     the
three  companies  again  met  together,     this  time  on  " the  ground
back  of  the  meeting-house  on  Jeremiah  Shaw's  land."    "At  5
o'clock,  "   according  to  the  record,    they  " formed  the  line.          Capt.
Bayley took  command of  the whole.       1st,    fired  from the right  to
the left;   2nd,   fired  right and left;    3rd,   the whole fired;   4th,    Capt.
Bayley  marched  round  the  square;     5th,     formed  the  line;       6th,
Capt.     Shaw  took  command of his  company and marched  to  the
gun-house."
Mrs.  Caleb  Joy is  authority for  the statement  that when James
Jones was chosen captain,    her father,   Noah Tirrell,    having declined
that  office,       invited  the troop  to  his  house,    in front of which they
paraded  dressed  in  gay  uniform,       and  went  through  the  sword
exercise.             According  to   her  testimony  they  were   " a  splendid
looking company."   She remembers distinctly  the orders  that were
given  to  " Draw swords !     Poise  swords! "     At the latter  command
every  sword  was pointed  forwards  over  the  horse's  head  in  true
military style.           On this  occasion  her father  stood  treat,    the toddy
being  made in  her  mother's  washtub.            One  of  the  equestrians,
David  Rice,       probably  somewhat  exhilarated  by the  good  cheer,
rode  into  the  kitchen  of  the  house,   wheeled  around  and  made a
rapid  exit,     not  however,    without breaking the floor,    the  remains of
which accident are said to be visible to this day.           Maj.      Elias  Hunt
also  testifies  that when his  father,    Ebenezer  Hunt,   Jr.,    resigned  his
position of  lieutenant,     he invited  the whole company to  his  house
and gave them a dinner.           They remained during the afternoon and
evening  and manoeuvred  in  the  bright  moonlight  in  front  of  his
residence.             His father stood at the door and gave the orders.             Fifty-
two horses were put up on this  occasion.
According  to  all  accounts  the  members  of  this   troop  were  a
 - 414 - 
406                   MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
spirited  set  of  fellows,    fond  of a good time,    high  bucks -   as has
been expressively  said       and fearless  riders.         Numerous anecdotes
concerning  them  have  been  told  the  writer:      how,     for  instance,
after   a  day's  training  they  were  accustomed  to   dash  pell-mell
through  the  streets  on  races,     in  squads,    for  their  several  rendez-
vous,                the High Enders  for  Captain Shaw's tavern,   the last  one
in  to pay for  the drinks;     how,    on a certain occasion,     one of their
number,        James  Tirrell,      collided  with  a cow,     throwing  rider  and
horse to the ground ;      how,   on another occasion Lieut.    Daniel Loud,
finding a horse cart in his way,   leaped his  charger entirely through
it   from  end  to  end  and  escaped  unhurt;       how,     again,     the  same
personage,      not  having  so  fleet  a steed  as  his  companion,     and  in
his  haste to reach the tavern,    turned too short a corner on entering
the yard and threw his horse on his  knees,  but springing from the
saddle  while  the  others  were  hitching  their  nags  he  first   reached
the bar.          It is also related that when the company was once drawn
up in front of the residence  of  Cornet  Reed,    one of their  number,
David  Loud,       filled  his  pistols  to  the  muzzle with  powder,      and,
riding  up to  the  step-stone,    discharged  both  barrels  at  the  front
door.
Mr.  Nathan Bates  relates  the following incident of his  boyhood
recollection,     which occurred in 1804,   when the troop was on parade
at Humphrey's plain.        His father,    who did not belong to the com-
pany,   sold  refreshments in a side tent,    and Sergeant Webb,     having
bought of  him two  buckets  of punch,     rode  off  astride his   horse,
with one bucket in each  hand,   to treat  his companions.           No acci-
dent happened till  he attempted to alight,   when,   on account of the
extra  weights,    the  performance  resulted  in  a fall  to  the  ground,
the  punch  being  spilled  and  himself  drenched  to  the  skin.          He
good-humoredly bore the discomfiture,    and repeated the operation,
which the second time was successfully carried out.
While these incidents go to show that the troopers were a rollick-
ing,     jovial set of men,   we are not at liberty to infer that they were
a vulgar  crowd  or  wanting  in  true  military  spirit.          On the  con-
trary,        they  included  men  of  respectability  and  influence  in  the
community,     and  were proud  of  their  organization.           The customs
of those days were different from ours.             It was then respectable  to
take  a social  glass.            The  temperance  reform  had  not  yet  made
indulgence in  alchoholic beverages disreputable.       All  partook,     and
the  quality  of the liquor drank is  said  not to have produced such
direful   effects   as   are   frequently  witnessed  at  the  present  day.
However this  may be,    it  is  hoped that this  recital  will not excite
a desire  in  any one  to  return  to  the  social  customs  of  those by-
gone days.
The equipment  of  this  troop,   according to regulations,  consisted
of  " a serviceable horse of at least fourteen hands and an-half high,
a good  saddle,    bridle,    male-pillion  and  valise;     holsters,     a breast-
plate  and  crupper,     a pair  of  boots  and spurs,    a pair of pistols,      a
 - 415 - 
WEYMOUTH  CAVALRY  COMPANY,      1798-1811                407
sabre and cartridge- box,    to  contain  twelve cartridges  for his  (each
horseman's)   pistols. "
The uniform  which is  said  to  have been  very neat  and  tasty  is
thus described :
The cap was of hard  polished  leather,      round at the  top,    having
a stiff   straight  visor  in  front  and  a  strip  of  metal  covered  with
bear skin extending over the crown from front  to  back like  a crest
or  helmet.             It  was  further  ornamented  with  a  broad,     blue  silk
band,     trimmed  with  tinsel  cord,      and  gathered  into  a  large  bow
behind,     the ends being  looped up and from which were  suspended
two  small  tassels .         Thus decorated  the  whole  head  covering  was
surmounted with  a white feather tipped with  red.
The coat  was  short  and  close  fitting,    with  a broad,      red  facing
in front and red  trimming  about  the  pockets  and borders  behind.
It had metallic bell-shaped buttons,    and a profusion of gilt  lace.
The pants which at  first  were white were afterwards changed for
blue and trimmed with red cord up the outer seams.
The sword was suspended from the shoulders  by cross-belts .              An
eyewitness  testifies   that  to  her youthful  eyes  the  soldiers  of  this
troop,      mounted on their prancing steeds and decked in their  bright
uniforms,      presented  a very imposing appearance.
Interesting  reminiscences  relating  to  the  Horse  company were
given  the  writer  some  three  years  ago  by  Mrs.  Susanna  Tirrell,
relict of the late Stephen Tirrell,   who died in 1878,    having attained
the advanced age of ninety-four years.          She stated that in  the year
1800,       in  the  month of June,   on  artillery  election  day,     she,     being
then in her sixteenth  year,    presented  to  the  company a flag,     the
gift  of her  father,      Capt.       Eliphalet  Loud.         To the last  day of  her
long  life  she preserved  to a remarkable degree her mental faculties,
and was fond  of reciting  to her friends  the language employed by
her on the occasion  referred  to.             The words  were noted down and
preserved,      and  would  be here  introduced  but  for  another circum-
stance  to which  allusion  will  now be made.            For  many years  she
had choicely  kept a scrap of old  newspaper which,   in its  integrity,
would have contained  a complete  account  of  the  presentation  of
the flag,     but,     in its  mutilated  condition,    a considerable  portion of
the article was wanting.       This piece of paper was supposed to have
been torn from a copy of the " Columbian Centinel, "  of which her
father  is  believed  to  have been  a  subscriber.           A few weeks  since
search  was  made in  the  library  of  the  Massachusetts  Historical
Society  for  a copy of  the  newspaper containing  this  article,     which
search  was  finally  rewarded  with  success.             As  will  appear,      Mrs.
Tirrell  and  the members of Capt.     Eliphalet  Loud's family made a
mistake of one year in the date of the presentation,   as it  took place
in  1799  instead  of  1800.    In the files  of  the " Centinel"  for  1799,
under date  of June  19,     was found  the  following  reference  to  the
event under the head of
 - 416 - 
408                   MILITARY  HISTORY  OF  WEYMOUTH
MILITARY.
On Monday,     3d inst . ,   the  Troop of Horse in  Weymouth,   lately formed,      made
its   public  appearance  in  complete  uniform,    commanded by Capt.    John White.
CAPT.          ELIPHALET  LOUD  having imparted to the officer  his design of pre-
senting  the  Troop with  a Standard,    at 5 o'clock  they  paraded in front  of his
house,   when the  Standard was presented to the  Cornet by his young daughter,
who with a grace and  firmness  above her years  addressed him to the following
effect:
" Respected  Citizen:  -From the  hands  of  my Parent  I  have received  this
Standard,     and,    in compliance with his wishes,   I  now present it  to you -flatter-
ing myself with the idea  that  you will  sacrifice  everything  dear to you,   even
your life  rather than desert  it;     and relying on your patriotism and firmness  in
our Country's defence,   in the hour of danger."
The Cornet  politely replied:   " I am happy in embracing the present occasion
of acknowledging the honor done me;    and return in behalf of the Troop  their
grateful  thanks.          Rest assured  I  will  sacrifice everything,   rather than  disgrace-
fullyddesert this Standard,    when unfurled in our Country's defence."
The Troop then fired  three rounds,  and at half past 6 proceeded to Lieut. 1
SAM'L  BAYLEY'S,     where  refreshment was liberally provided  for  them.             The
occasion was honored with the presence of a number of distinguished characters,
and  respectable  officers,    who acknowledged themselves highly pleased with the
display  of  military  knowledge,    which was truly surprising  from such an infant
establishment.       The conduct and exertions  of the Officers  reflected on them the
highest honor.
Taken,     as  this  extract was,   from a public print of the time when
this  notable  event  in the history of the troop took place,     it  is  of
interest   as  showing  the  estimation  in  which  the  command  was
held  by  competent  judges  of  its   appearance  on  public  parade.
The presentation  address as given differs  in only a few words from
the  language as recited to the writer by Mrs. Tirrell.2
The identical  old  flag  received  by Cornet  Reed from the hands
of  the young  maiden,    who  was  tastily  attired  in  white  on  this
memorable  occasion,     is  still  in existence.      Although it  was  never
carried in battle,   nor pierced with bullets,    the remorseless  teeth  of
time  have  left   their  imprints  upon  it.           These  have  been  in  a
measure effaced  by the skill  of needlecraft,    so that it still  appears
to  be  in  a fair  state  of preservation.          In size  it  measures  about
twenty-six  inches   square.         The  material  of  which  it  is  made  is
heavy  silk,      which  originally  might  have  been  of  a  light  buff  or
cream color,     but is  now of a faded yellow.       It is  trimmed on three
of  its  edges  with a deep fringe  of a golden color,   the untrimmed
edge being attached  to the staff.          On its face is  a representation of
the national bird,   holding in its beak the motto " E pluribus  unum. "
Underneath is  the inscription -" Cavalry,    1st Brigade,   1st Div'n. "

Of the causes which led  to  the disbanding of the Horse company
it  is  impossible definitely  to  write.         Whether they were of a politi-
cal  character,    as  has  been  suggested,    or  whether  they  were  in
accordance  with  orders  promulgated  from  a military  source,       or
attributable  to  an  increasing  lack  of  interest  in  the  organization
cannot  now be  positively  ascertained.            The records  fail  to  show
that  any  orders  were  issued  from  headquarters  to  disband  the
company.             Information obtained from the roster  and other official
documents tallies  completely with declaration  made by the  oldest
survivors  of  the  period  that  the troop disbanded before  the  War
of 1812.    These bold cavaliers  therefore  never had the opportunity

1814 during their  active operations  in the defence of our seaboard.

In conclusion the writer  regrets  his  inability  to  have presented
more  facts  in  relation  to  the  subject  upon which  he has  written,
but will  feel  amply paid for his efforts  if he has succeeded  in  con-
tributing  anything  of  interest   pertaining  to  the  history  of  the
noble  old  town of  which  he is  only  an adopted  citizen.              He ex-
presses  the  hope that  if  his  communication be  published  it  may
recall   to  some  reader  reminiscences  of  this  military  organization
which may be worthy of record.         It is very probable that by making
public  the  names of  the  members  already  obtained,     more  names
may be secured.         Other relics  may be stored away in  chest,     closet
or  attic,       forgotten  or  unprized.       It  would  be  very  desirable  to
obtain  a pair  of pistols,     a sabre,     or  some  article  of  uniform.            It
has been ascertained  that one of the old cavalry caps was in exist-
ence till  a recent date.        Should  any person,    whether a member of
the  Historical   Society  or  not,       become  cognizant  of  any  facts ,
reminiscences  or relics,     he is  earnestly  invited  to  contribute  them
to the society for preservation.

EARLY  LIBRARIES  IN  SOUTH  WEYMOUTH
From an Address by Rev. W. H.  BOLSTER at the Dedication of the Fogg Library,
Sept.  14,    1898
At a meeting of a number of the inhabitants of ye South Parish in Weymouth,
at ye house of Lieut  Nath'l  Shaw,    innholder,    on ye 17th  of July,      1800,                   The
expediency of establishing  a Library in this  end of ye Town,   was taken into con-
sideration;      whereupon L't.     Sam'l  Bayley was chosen  Moderator,    & Mr.  David
Joy Jun'r,      Clerk of ye Meeting.
The meeting was then adjourned to ye Meeting House,    to  be on ye 7th  of
August,   1800.    At ye above mentioned adjournment,    a standing committee was
chosen to form regulations for ye said proposed Library,   consisting of ye following
Gents,      Doc't  James Torrey,    Rev'd Simeon  Williams,     Eliphalet  Loud Esq,     Mr.
Ezra Pratt & Mr. Sam'l Torrey.        Also Doc't James Torrey was chosen Librarian.
The above committee met on ye 14th of August 1800,    and chose  Simeon Wil-
liams Clerk to ye committee;    also agreed to lay ye following regulations before ye
Proprietors for their acceptance.
Then follows  the  rules  and regulations  for the practical working
of the library under thirteen articles,   with the record of their adop-
tion in the following words :
The above regulations being laid before  ye  Proprietors  on ye 25th  of August
1800,     by ye committee,   at ye schoolhouse near Mr. Joseph Vinings,   were accepted
by a unanimous vote.        The  Proprietors  then  separated,   leaving  their  standing
committee  already  named  & their  Librarian  to  execute  their  respective  trust
devolved upon them in these regulations.         Entered in this book from the original
papers,   by
SIMEON  WILLIAMS,
Scribe to ye Committee.

This  completes  the list  of  the original  proprietors  of the Social
Library.                The shares  were  50 cents  each,    and seventy- one  shares
were  subscribed   by  sixty-four   individuals,       making  $35.50   the
original  fund  with  which  the library  began.         But here  follows  in
the  record  contained  in  this  ancient  book an entry  which  was a
surprise  to  your  historian  for  the  intimation  of  the  one-time  ex-
istence  of  a library  in  the  South  Parish,     of  which  he  had  never
heard  until  he  unexpectedly  stumbled  upon the  evidence  of  its
existence  in this old record-book.
The entry is  as follows :
Catalogue of Books from Pondplain Library,    Received into the Social Library,
South End of Weymouth,    as agreed on by the  Committee of the two Libraries,
on the last of August,    1808,   entered Nov. 4th.
Then follows  a  list  of  about  twelve  volumes,     mostly  sermons,
all  valued  at  $13.50,     which  is  equal  to  nine  shares  of  the  Social
Library.
The following persons are the proprietors of the above shares & have a right to
the privileges  of the Library by complying with the rules and regulations of said
Library,               Dea.      Sam'l  Blanchard,     Benj'n Agar,    Tho's  Blanchard,   Capt.    Deme-
trius  Thayer,        David  Shaw,    Benj'n Joy,    Eliphalet Loud Esq.,  Johnathan Agar,
Warren Shaw.
The first  catalogue of  books in the library,    written evidently by
the hand of  Rev. Mr. Williams,   contains a list  of one hundred and
sixty- two  volumes,    without  any  attempt  at  classification.             The
first  printed  catalogue      at what date it  is  impossible to  ascertain
contains  a list  of two hundred and forty- two volumes,     arranged
under  the  heads  of  Theological,    Biographical,     Historical,     Poetical
and Miscellaneous.
This  library  was kept in  Derby Hall,    which was  located on the
spot where the  Opera House now stands .
No doubt  this  Social  Library  had a history  of much interest  in
this  community.           The records  through  the  thirty- five  years  of its
existence  as  a public library  are  broken  and fragmentary,    but the
natural  question,      what  finally  became  of  it,    fortunately  we can
answer.               The last  record contained  in the book is the following :

Monday the  13th day of July,   1835,   the committee appointed to make sale  of

The next  movement,     so  far  as  can be ascertained,    towards  the
formation  of  a public library in  this  part of  the town,    occurred  in
1863,       and resulted  in  the formation of  the  Mutual Library  Asso-
ciation  of  South  Weymouth.       All  written  records  of this  library
seem to  have perished in  the  fire  through which it  passed when it
was finding  a temporary  home in  the  Rogers  Building,     so  called,
in 1886.
The following  letter  from  the  Rev.  S.   H.  Hayes  relates  to  the
Library:
...
14 HAWTHORN ST. ,
CAMBRIDGE,    Sept.  12,   1898.
You allude to the old " Mutual Library Association. "    It  stirs  precious
memories.
Forty years  ago I  became a resident  of South Weymouth.          In the autumn of
that year a society for Mutual Improvement was formed.           Its laws like the British
Constitution  were  unwritten  but  never  forgotten.         The society  was known as
"The Mutual."
It had a President,     Secretary and  Committees.      Any young person of either
sex who would bring a written question suitable  for conversation and lay  it  on
the Table,   should be a member.        It met every Friday night.         The President took
up a question and asked some one to answer it  and then another,   till  it  became a
matter  of  quiet,    social conversation.        The President  was careful  to put in now
and then a question he was anxious the young people should consider.
quiet,
Books now became necessary.          The place was searched for books and then the
idea of a library was forced upon us and the library was started,    first  by a ques-
tion laid on the table,  then referred,   as many questions were,   to some one to answer
at the next  meeting,   and it  was often done in a written essay;      and here possibly
was the root of the splendid outgrowth you are to rejoice over on Wednesday.
Rev.  S.   H.  HAYES.
The library  acquired  some twelve or fourteen hundred volumes.
It  over-lived the inauguration of the Tufts'       Library at Weymouth
Landing,      but  when arrangements  were  perfected  for  distributing
the books of the Tufts'     Library in this  part of the town,    the use-
fulness  of  the  Mutual  Library  was,     of  course,    superseded  by  the
new and larger library.

416                                THE  FOGG  LIBRARY
JOHN  S.   FOGG
THE  FOGG  LIBRARY
It  has  been  made possible  by the  generous  bequest  of  the  late
John S.  Fogg,     who set  apart in his  will  $50,000 to found and per-
petuate " in  that  part of  Weymouth known as South Weymouth,  "
a free  public  library.
If   there  was  in  all   this  a  desire  on  the  part  of  the  donor  to
perpetuate  his  own name and  memory  among his  old  neighbors
and  friends,       as  there  probably  was,      he has  gratified  his  desire  in
the  noblest  way by his  bequest  for  this  library.           It  was  a praise-
worthy desire  accomplished  in a most meritorious  way.
 - 425 - 
THE  TUFTS  LIBRARY                           417
THE TUFTS  LIBRARY
The Tufts  Library  of  Weymouth was founded in  1879  through
the generosity  of  Quincy Tufts  and his  sister,      Miss  Susan  Tufts,
who gave to  the town,    by will,   a fund for  the  establishment  of  a
library  for  the  benefit  of  the  citizens   of  Weymouth.              This  was
supplemented  by an appropriation  of  $ 1,000  from  the  town and
$2,000  raised  by private  subscription.         A part  of  the  fund  con-
sisted  of  two buildings,   the  lower  story  of one of which was fitted
up for the library.
The first  meeting of the trustees was held on March 12,     1879,    at
which time the board  organized  by electing  Zecheriah  L.  Bicknell
as president,    and John J.  Loud as clerk and treasurer.       A librarian
was engaged,    books  were purchased  and prepared  for  circulation,
and on the  first  of January  of  the  year  1880  the  library,      with  a
collection  of about 2,300 volumes,    was opened to the public.
Especial credit should be given to Frank W. Lewis,     a member of
the  first   board  of  trustees,      who  by  his   tireless   and  invaluable
service,      was  instrumental  in placing  the  library  on  a strong  and
enduring foundation.
Under  the  efficient  administration  of  the  first  librarian,        Miss
Caroline A.  Blanchard,    to whose faithful  and disinterested  service
is  due in large  measure the success  of the library,    it  soon became
not only an educational  power  and a source  of  enjoyment  to  the
citizens  of the town,    but  also  attained  an honorable place  among
the  libraries  of  the  State.         Considering  its   size  and  the  money
expended,     it  ranked second to none in the  Commonwealth.
Early  in  the  history  of  the  library,    delivery  stations  were  es-
tablished   in   all   wards  outside   that   in  which  the  library   was
located,     affording,    as  far  as  possible,    equal  privileges  to  residents
in  all  parts  of the  town.           These stations  are still  maintained with
the  exception of  that in  Ward 1,     which was discontinued  in  June
of last  year  (1922) ,   when the North Weymouth branch was opened.
The library occupied  the building in which it  had its  first  home
until  it  outgrew the accommodations  provided.         At a special  town
meeting  held  March 21,     1891,     it  was voted to raise  $22,000 for  the
purpose of erecting  a public library  building  on the  land  in  Ward
3 donated by the Tufts family.
In  preparation for  the  erection  of a  new building,   the old  one in
which  the  library  was  then  housed  was  moved  to   Commercial
Street  where  the  Gem Theatre  now  stands.          The new building,
the  present  home of  the  library,     begun  in  1891,     was  finished  in
July of  1892,     and formally opened on October 6 of that year.
The  first   board  of  trustees  included  Noah  Vining,       Everett  C.
Bumpus,         Frank  W.  Lewis,      James  Humphrey,     Alanson  A.   Hol-
brook,         John  J.   Loud,      E.  Atherton  Hunt,     Zecheriah  L.   Bicknell,
Amos   S.     White,          and   the   selectmen   ex   officio:         Thomas   H.
Humphrey,     John W. Bartlett,    William Nash,   Augustus J.  Richards
and Jacob Baker.
